In GPU-resident online matching after shared feature extraction, candidate-limited matching was 16.3 times faster and used 93.6 times fewer estimated operations than full-archive one-layer cross-attention. These results establish coarse-to-fine retrieval as an effective strategy for exact study-level image-report linkage in large radiology archives.

papers.title: 2D anomaly detection of fatal cerebral hemorrhage on postmortem CT
papers.text: 2D anomaly detection of fatal cerebral hemorrhage on postmortem CT. Postmortem computed tomography (PMCT) is increasingly used in forensic medicine, yet image interpretation remains largely manual and time-consuming, and supervised deep learning is constrained by the scarcity of annotated forensic datasets. This study investigated whether diffusion-based generative models can detect fatal cerebral haemorrhage on PMCT through reconstruction-based anomaly detection, using solely image-level labels derived from the documented cause of death. Postmortem brain CT examinations acquired at a single forensic institute between 2011 and 2025 were retrospectively analyzed, comprising 265 healthy subjects and 33 cases of fatal intracranial haemorrhage. After automated brain extraction, slice selection and intensity normalization, two diffusion frameworks were trained: an unsupervised denoising diffusion probabilistic model (AnoDDPM) trained on healthy anatomy alone, and a weakly supervised classifier-guided diffusion model exploiting image-level labels. Anomaly scores were derived from the reconstruction error between each slice and its pseudo-healthy reconstruction, and detection was assessed at the image level using 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. AnoDDPM achieved an AUROC of 0.928 (95% CI 0.812-0.989) and an AUPRC of 0.794 (95% CI 0.429-0.946), whereas the classifier-guided model reached an AUROC of 0.991 (95% CI 0.984-0.997) with an AUPRC of 0.960 (95% CI 0.855-0.994). These results demonstrate excellent feasibility of diffusion-based anomaly detection for forensic PMCT and indicate that weak, image-level supervision substantially improves detection, thereby supporting the future development of automated triage tools for postmortem brain imaging.

papers.title: A semi-supervised diffusion model for automated segmentation of vascular plaques.
papers.text:
A semi-supervised diffusion model for automated segmentation of vascular plaques..

Purpose

Segmenting vascular plaques in the carotid arteries, aorta, and iliac arteries on CT is important because plaque burden relates to cardiovascular and stroke risk and can guide treatment. However, manual labeling is often infeasible and time-consuming across large vascular regions. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) can leverage unlabeled CT data to enable accurate plaque segmentation with only limited labels.

Methods

We applied a diffusion-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) method for vascular plaque segmentation in non-contrast CT by formulating the task as multi-class segmentation of plaques and 26 adjacent anatomical structures. The method employs a teacher-student architecture with a shared diffusion encoder to learn domain-invariant feature representations and separate teacher and student decoders to decouple labeled and unlabeled data, reducing overfitting and improving robustness. To address the severe class imbalance caused by the small size of plaques, we developed a plaque-aware oversampling strategy and a labeled-data-guided training for the shared encoder and student decoder. We used 142 NIH non-contrast CT scans, divided into 119 training scans and 23 validation scans. We externally evaluated the method on 95 scans from the University of Wisconsin and 50 scans from Medipol University Mega Hospital and compared its performance with supervised nnU-Net and a strong SSL baseline.

Results

The improved SSL method significantly outperformed the original SSL method and supervised training with the same architecture when using 14 labeled training scans ( p<0.0001 ). With these 14 labeled training scans, it achieved DSC values of 58.8% and 82.3% on CTRATE and Renal Donor, respectively, within 2.7--2.8 percentage points of the same architecture trained with all 119 training scans labeled.

Conclusion

The SSL method segments plaques in the carotid, aortic, and iliac arteries with performance approaching that of fully supervised training while using only 14 labeled training scans, supporting scalable plaque burden assessment.

papers.title: Benchmarking Classification Tasks of Chest X-ray AI Across Multinational Public and Private Datasets: a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study
papers.text: Benchmarking Classification Tasks of Chest X-ray AI Across Multinational Public and Private Datasets: a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study. Chest X-ray (CXR) AI models are increasingly proposed for triage, screening, and rule-out, where the operating point is fixed to miss few abnormalities. Most evaluations instead report threshold-free discrimination on a few public benchmarks, leaving clinically usable performance and generalisability to unseen institutional cohorts poorly characterised. We retrospectively evaluated 10 published CXR classification models on 12 datasets from six countries: seven public benchmarks and five institutional cohorts from China, Japan, and Germany. Models spanned convolutional networks, vision-language models, a question-answering foundation model, and a repurposed encoder. Only image-level classification was assessed; segmentation, detection, and report generation were out of scope. Source labels were harmonised to a common vocabulary. The primary outcome was specificity at 95% sensitivity; PPV at 95% sensitivity and AUROC were secondary outcomes. Estimates weighted each diagnostic task equally, with 95% CIs. MAVL and MedKLIP had the highest overall specificity at 95% sensitivity (0.37 [95% CI 0.31-0.44] and 0.37 [0.30-0.44]) and kept that ranking on tasks evaluable for every model. Their PPV was 0.18 (0.13-0.24) and 0.19 (0.13-0.25): most flagged examinations would be false positives. Specificity was lower on institutional cohorts than on public benchmarks for most models, by 0.13 for MAVL, 0.15 for DenseNet, and 0.09 for MedKLIP. No model was best for every finding, country, lesion extent, or prevalence stratum; specificity fell from 0.34 for diffuse to 0.15 for focal findings. At 95% sensitivity, the best current models clear only about a third of truly negative examinations, and public-benchmark performance overstates what they achieve on unseen institutional data. Operating-point-aware evaluation and external validation on institutional cohorts should precede deployment.

papers.title: AnyCXR: Human Anatomy Segmentation of Chest X-ray at Any Acquisition Position using Multi-stage Domain Randomized Synthetic Data with Imperfect Annotations and Conditional Joint Annotation Regularization Learning
papers.text: AnyCXR: Human Anatomy Segmentation of Chest X-ray at Any Acquisition Position using Multi-stage Domain Randomized Synthetic Data with Imperfect Annotations and Conditional Joint Annotation Regularization Learning. Robust anatomical segmentation of chest X-rays (CXRs) remains challenging due to the scarcity of comprehensive annotations and the substantial variability of real-world acquisition conditions. We propose AnyCXR, a unified framework that enables generalizable multi-organ segmentation across arbitrary CXR projection angles using only synthetic supervision. The method combines a Multi-stage Domain Randomization (MSDR) engine, which generates over 100,000 anatomically faithful and highly diverse synthetic radiographs from 3D CT volumes, with a Conditional Joint Annotation Regularization (CAR) learning strategy that leverages partial and imperfect labels by enforcing anatomical consistency in a latent space. Trained entirely on synthetic data, AnyCXR achieves strong zero-shot generalization on multiple real-world datasets, providing accurate delineation of 54 anatomical structures in PA, lateral, and oblique views. The resulting segmentation maps support downstream clinical tasks, including automated cardiothoracic ratio estimation, spine curvature assessment, and disease classification, where the incorporation of anatomical priors improves diagnostic performance. These results demonstrate that AnyCXR establishes a scalable and reliable foundation for anatomy-aware CXR analysis and offers a practical pathway toward reducing annotation burdens while improving robustness across diverse imaging conditions.

papers.title: MedVersa: A Generalist Foundation Model for Diverse Medical Imaging Tasks.
papers.text:
MedVersa: A Generalist Foundation Model for Diverse Medical Imaging Tasks..

Background

Current medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems are often limited to narrow, task-specific applications, which constrains their impact on routine clinical care. Generalist models that can learn from multimodal inputs and produce flexible outputs across imaging workflows may better support scalable, real-world deployment.

Methods

We developed MedVersa, a generalist foundation model trained on tens of millions of compiled medical instances from diverse imaging scenarios. MedVersa is designed to accept heterogeneous inputs, including images and clinical text, and generate outputs such as classifications, segmentations, and narrative reports. We evaluated MedVersa on nine medical imaging tasks against leading task-specialized systems, and we conducted blinded radiologist assessments of AI-generated and human-written reports, as well as prospective user studies measuring report-writing time and discrepancy rates.

Results

Across tasks, MedVersa achieved performance that was competitive with or exceeded that of specialist systems. In blinded evaluations of chest radiograph reports, radiologists judged AI-generated and human-written reports to be clinically equivalent in 64% of all cases, with equivalence rising to 91% for normal studies. In user studies, the use of MedVersa was associated with notable reductions in report writing time and clinically relevant discrepancies compared with standard reporting workflows.

Conclusions

MedVersa demonstrates that a single, flexible, multimodal foundation model can match or surpass task-specialized medical imaging systems while supporting radiologist efficiency and consistency. These findings highlight the potential of generalist multimodal AI systems to advance AI-enabled medical imaging workflows and augment clinical expertise.

papers.title: Role of Three-Dimensional Convolution Neural Networks (3D-CNN) in Image Processing and Recognition in Oncology: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.text: Role of Three-Dimensional Convolution Neural Networks (3D-CNN) in Image Processing and Recognition in Oncology: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.. Three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs) have transformed oncology imaging, excelling in tumor detection, classification, segmentation, and prognosis prediction. Unlike traditional two-dimensional CNNs, 3D CNNs effectively analyze volumetric medical imaging data, enhancing spatial feature extraction and diagnostic accuracy across modalities, including CT, MRI, PET, and ultrasound. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of 3D CNNs across 22 studies, of which 11 were eligible for quantitative synthesis. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC were 0.72, 0.73, and 0.77, respectively, with a diagnostic odds ratio of 10.38, indicating favorable discriminative ability. Subgroup analyses demonstrated superior accuracy in lung cancer and CT-based models, with DenseNet and ResNet architectures outperforming traditional CNNs. Technical innovations-including multi-modal fusion, spatial context integration, and explainable AI techniques-enhance model robustness and clinician trust. However, substantial heterogeneity (I² > 95%) across studies, attributable to differences in imaging protocols, dataset quality, and model design, underscores the need for standardized methodologies. Persistent challenges include computational demands, annotation variability, and generalization limitations. Future directions should prioritize the integration of explainable AI, PACS-compatible user interfaces, and federated learning frameworks to bridge institutional gaps. This review highlights the considerable promise of 3D CNNs in advancing precision oncology, while also identifying the infrastructural and methodological refinements necessary for widespread clinical adoption.

papers.title: Multi-Backbone U-Net segmentation and interpretable hybrid deep learning classification for lung cancer detection in chest CT images.
papers.text:
Multi-Backbone U-Net segmentation and interpretable hybrid deep learning classification for lung cancer detection in chest CT images..

Background

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and its early and accurate diagnosis from chest CT imaging is complicated by overlapping radiological features between benign and malignant lesions, as well as by the limited cross-institution validation and interpretability reported in much of the existing computer-aided diagnosis literature. This study evaluates the effectiveness of U-Net architectures integrated with different pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) backbones for automated lung segmentation and lung cancer classification in chest CT images, with an emphasis on rigorous, leakage-free validation and cross-institution generalizability relevant to clinical practice.

Methods

A balanced internal dataset of 832 chest CT images (416 cancerous and 416 non-cancerous cases, NIDCH, Bangladesh) was preprocessed using Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) and resized to 224 × 224 pixels. U-Net models with three CNN backbones (VGG16, ResNet50, and Xception) were implemented for lung segmentation, with pseudo-labels verified against expert-annotated masks. A standalone CNN and three hybrid classifiers combining CNN feature extraction with machine learning algorithms (Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting) were then evaluated, alongside a Vision Transformer baseline. All models were assessed using subject-level fivefold cross-validation, followed by fully independent external testing on a second, structurally distinct dataset (IQ-OTH/NCCD; 110 subjects) without retraining. Performance was measured using Dice coefficient, IoU, accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC, with 95% confidence intervals and statistical significance testing.

Results

For segmentation, U-Net with the Xception backbone achieved the best overall performance (Dice: 0.9581 ± 0.0104; IoU: 0.9163 ± 0.0167). For classification, the CNN + SVM hybrid model achieved the highest internal cross-validation accuracy (98.21% ± 0.68%) and AUC (0.9881 ± 0.0041), significantly outperforming the standalone CNN (p = 0.041), and retained the strongest performance under external validation (92.73% accuracy), with the smallest accuracy drop among all evaluated models. Ablation analyses confirmed substantial contributions from CLAHE preprocessing and U-Net segmentation, and Grad-CAM analysis showed that segmentation constrains classifier attention to anatomically plausible lung regions.

Conclusion

Integrating U-Net segmentation with hybrid CNN-based classification provides an accurate and reasonably generalizable framework for lung cancer detection, offering a methodological foundation for future clinically oriented computer-aided diagnosis research, pending prospective, multi-institution validation.

papers.title: Benchmarking Deep Learning for NSCLC PET/CT Segmentation on a Histologically Confirmed Vietnamese Dataset: Validation and Generalization.
papers.text: Benchmarking Deep Learning for NSCLC PET/CT Segmentation on a Histologically Confirmed Vietnamese Dataset: Validation and Generalization.. Accurate segmentation of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) on positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) is an essential prerequisite for automated metabolic tumor volume (MTV) quantification and staging. Although deep learning models achieve high performance on large-scale datasets, their generalization across different clinical domains is limited by variations in imaging protocols and patient demographics. This study aims to evaluate several deep learning architectures and investigate a transfer learning strategy to mitigate domain shift. Three architectures, including ResNet-backbone 3D U-Net, nnU-Net v2, and Swin UNETR, were benchmarked from scratch and compared with a fine-tuned nnU-Net initialized with AutoPET II weights. Results on the internal dataset showed that the fine-tuned nnU-Net achieved a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 83.4 ± 6.5%, a 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 5.1 ± 3.6 mm, and a precision of 89.6 ± 8.2%. Compared to the nnU-Net v2, the fine-tuned nnU-Net improved the absolute DSC by 6.8% while reducing local training time by 37.5% by bypassing the initial feature-learning phase. The fine-tuned nnU-Net model also demonstrated a high correlation between the MTV and the ground truth (Pearson r = 0.96, p < 0.001), indicating its potential as a reliable automated approach for quantitative MTV extraction and NSCLC prognostic-related analysis.

papers.title: High-Frequency Enhancement and Dual-Model Ensemble for Language-Guided COVID-19 Pneumonia Lesion Segmentation.
papers.text: High-Frequency Enhancement and Dual-Model Ensemble for Language-Guided COVID-19 Pneumonia Lesion Segmentation.. Accurate segmentation of COVID-19 pneumonia lesions in chest X-ray (CXR) images is critical for disease quantification and clinical decision-making. However, existing methods suffer from blurred lesion boundaries, missed detection of tiny lesions, and limited generalization performance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a language-guided multimodal medical image segmentation method integrating high-frequency enhancement and a dual-model ensemble. The method is developed along three dimensions: frequency-domain detail enhancement, spatial alignment optimization, and dual-model ensemble. First, a frequency-domain decomposition-based high-frequency enhancement module is designed to mitigate detail attenuation caused by encoder downsampling. Second, a two-dimensional (2D) spatial position encoding module is introduced to improve the spatial alignment between text descriptions and visual regions. Third, a dual-model ensemble architecture with differentiated frequency-domain masks is constructed to address the performance ceiling of individual models. Finally, experiments on two public datasets with different imaging modalities and data characteristics demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing single-modal and multimodal baseline methods and achieves competitive performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, verifying the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework. On the QaTa-COV19 dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 91.85% and the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) reaches 84.98%. On the multi-institutional MosMedData+ dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 78.48% and the mIoU reaches 64.66%. The proposed method provides effective technical support for clinical diagnosis and follow-up assessment of pneumonia.

papers.title: PET/CT radiomics for noninvasive histologic risk stratification in resected lung adenocarcinoma: a single-system development and internal validation study.
papers.text: PET/CT radiomics for noninvasive histologic risk stratification in resected lung adenocarcinoma: a single-system development and internal validation study.. Preoperative histologic characterisation of lung adenocarcinoma is typically available only after resection. We evaluated whether fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) radiomics could predict histologic patterns and pathologic risk features using a hierarchical modelling strategy. This retrospective cohort study included patients from three imaging facilities within a single academic health system. Radiomic features were extracted from preoperative PET/CT and CT segmentations; preprocessing included feature filtering, standardisation, redundancy reduction, and ComBat harmonisation. Penalised generalised linear model (GLMNET), random forest, and XGBoost models were trained with stratified cross-validation and evaluated in independent test sets. Outcomes included mucinous phenotype, non-mucinous histologic subtype, histologic grade, spread through air spaces (STAS), vascular invasion, and visceral pleural invasion (VPI). Eligible patients had primary lung adenocarcinoma treated by curative-intent resection, with preoperative PET/CT or thin-section CT and histopathologic review available; patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy, non-adenocarcinoma histology, or rare adenocarcinoma variants were excluded. The histologic reference standard was central review by a single thoracic pathologist per the 2021 WHO/IASLC (World Health Organization/International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer) classification, blinded to imaging and radiomic results. From 300 candidate radiomic variables (147 PET-derived, 153 CT-derived), models were developed using a 75%/25% stratified train-test split within the same single-institution cohort; the test set therefore represents internal, not external, validation. Among 254 patients, 255 tumours were analysed. Binary identification of poorly differentiated tumours (grade 3 vs. grade 1-2) achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) 0.767 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.624-0.897], area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC) 0.854 (95% CI: 0.723-0.952), and satisfactory calibration [Brier Score 0.170; Brier Skill Score (BSS) 0.23]. VPI yielded a moderate global signal (ROC-AUC 0.691, 95% CI: 0.518-0.841). Non-mucinous subtype classification showed preserved probabilistic ranking despite limited categorical accuracy (balanced accuracy 0.614). Models for mucinous phenotype, STAS, and vascular invasion showed limited discrimination; VPI in the small-tumour subgroup was constrained by insufficient positive events. PET/CT radiomics supported probabilistic preoperative risk stratification of lung adenocarcinoma, particularly for identifying poorly differentiated tumours. These results support radiomics as a complementary preoperative tool pending external validation.

papers.title: A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP-HMM challenge.
papers.text:
A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP-HMM challenge..

Background

Manual radiotherapy treatment planning is labor-intensive, subjective, and highly variable across planners and institutions. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for estimating achievable three-dimensional (3D) dose distributions for a given plan (hereafter: dose prediction) by directly mapping patient anatomy and beam geometry to voxel-wise dose. However, achieving robust generalization across diverse anatomical sites, prescriptions, and institutions remains a major challenge, particularly under computational constraints required for clinical deployment.

Purpose

We sought to develop and evaluate a generalizable, computationally efficient 3D dose prediction framework capable of spanning heterogeneous multi-site and multi-cohort datasets, as defined in the 2025 AAPM Generalizable Dose Prediction for Heterogeneous Multi-Cohort and Multi-Site (GDP-HMM) Grand Challenge. Our goal was to design a model that not only achieved state-of-the-art voxel-wise accuracy but also maintained clinically meaningful dose-volume and geometric characteristics across diverse cases.

Methods

We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose-prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture, which was originally introduced as a high-capacity convolutional backbone for medical image segmentation and is well suited to volumetric dense prediction tasks. The network accepted multimodal inputs comprising CT, PTV/OAR masks, beam and angle plates, and scalar plan metadata. A composite loss function combined voxel-wise L1, body-masked weighted L1, structure-wise moment-matching, and gradient-based penalties to jointly preserve spatial fidelity and dosimetric accuracy. The model was trained on the fixed GDP-HMM dataset consisting of 2876 training plans, 356 validation plans, and a held-out test set of 498 plans using random 3D patches and evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE), homogeneity index (HI), and conformity indices (CI100%, CI50%). Ablation studies quantified the contribution of each loss component to overall performance. Statistical comparisons used paired Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction.

Results

The proposed model achieved a mean voxel-wise MAE of 2.04 Gy on the validation set, outperforming the challenge baseline (2.54 Gy). An ensemble with the baseline further improved MAE to 1.94 Gy on the validation set and 2.071 Gy on the held-out test set, corresponding to the lowest test-set MAE and first-place overall ranking in the GDP-HMM Challenge. Predicted dose distributions preserved key plan characteristics, with ΔHI, ΔCI100%, and ΔCI50% narrowly centered around zero, indicating consistent target coverage and dose conformity. Protocol-specific evaluations for head-and-neck and lung cohorts demonstrated close alignment with reference plans, with no systematic degradation in OAR endpoints. Ablation experiments showed that removing gradient-based terms increased MAE by 0.50 Gy, while excluding the moment-matching term increased MAE by 0.06 Gy confirming that both gradient- and moment-based constraints enhanced spatial and dosimetric fidelity.

Conclusion

We present a generalizable 3D dose prediction framework that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while satisfying stringent runtime requirements (< 3s per case on < 24 GB GPU memory). By integrating gradient-aware and moment-based constraints within a MedNeXt backbone, the model preserved clinical DVH endpoints and geometric plan features. These findings demonstrate that carefully engineered loss formulations are pivotal for cross-institutional generalization. The framework offers a foundation for rapid dose prediction that could accelerate treatment planning, reduce inter-planner variability, and enable intelligent automation in radiotherapy workflows.

papers.title: DINOv3-SAM: Fusing Semantic and Anatomical Foundation Models for Robust Medical Image Classification.
papers.text: DINOv3-SAM: Fusing Semantic and Anatomical Foundation Models for Robust Medical Image Classification.. Robust medical image classification remains a persistent challenge due to heterogeneous acquisition protocols, label noise, and subtle inter-class variability. In chest radiography, these difficulties are compounded by shortcut learning from non-anatomical artifacts and projection variability, which severely undermine generalization. To address these limitations, we propose DINOv3-SAM, a dual-encoder framework that synergistically integrates complementary visual representations. The architecture combines a self-supervised DINOv3 vision transformer, which captures global semantic context, with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder, which provides anatomy-aware spatial features. The two feature streams are spatially aligned and adaptively refined through a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which emphasizes informative channels and diagnostically relevant regions prior to classification. Notably, only the final DINOv3 layers are fine-tuned while SAM remains frozen, yielding a computationally efficient framework with only 5.3 million trainable parameters. We evaluate DINOv3-SAM across five public datasets spanning diverse modalities and diagnostic tasks: pediatric pneumonia classification, cardiomegaly detection, large-scale RSNA pneumonia detection, COVID-19 radiography, and dermatological lesion classification. A unified stratified train/validation/test protocol ensures consistent and fair evaluation across both binary and multi-class settings. Each configuration was trained three times with different random seeds, and comprehensive comparisons against reproduced CNN baselines and published state-of-the-art methods, supported by statistical significance testing, demonstrate improvements across most datasets and metrics. The proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% (±3.06) on pediatric pneumonia, 97.24% (±0.77) accuracy (AUC 0.998 ±0.001) on COVID-19 radiography, and a mean AUC of 0.8705 (±0.0445) on the challenging RSNA benchmark. These results underscore the efficacy of fusing self-supervised semantic representations with segmentation-informed anatomical cues to enhance robustness against dataset bias, acquisition variability, and cross-domain shifts. The proposed approach offers a reliable foundation for multi-dataset and multi-modality medical image classification in research-oriented decision-support systems.

papers.title: A review of medical image segmentation research based on bibliometrics.
papers.text: A review of medical image segmentation research based on bibliometrics.. BackgroundMedical image segmentation is a fundamental step in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning, and its research landscape has expanded rapidly with the advancement of artificial intelligence. A systematic bibliometric overview of this field is therefore needed to clarify its intellectual structure and emerging trends.ObjectiveTo provide a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the global research landscape, developmental trends, collaboration networks, and emerging hotspots in the field of medical image segmentation over the past decade.MethodsA bibliometric analysis was performed on 21,437 publications related to medical image segmentation, indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2016 to 2025. The analysis systematically examined publication outputs, country-level contributions, author collaboration networks, journal distributions, and keyword co-occurrence patterns.ResultsThe annual publication count increased remarkably from 25 in 2016 to 5,207 in 2025. China contributed the largest share with 11,556 publications, followed by the United States (3,272) and India (1,924). Core researchers formed stable intra-team collaborations, though inter-team cooperation remained limited. Keyword and citation analyses identified deep learning, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Transformers, U-Net, and their variants as dominant methodological themes. Case studies on skin and lung segmentation revealed differential research attention and international collaboration patterns across anatomical targets. A historical trajectory analysis showed methodological evolution from traditional image processing to fully convolutional networks and U-Net, and subsequently to hybrid architectures integrating attention mechanisms and Transformers.ConclusionMedical image segmentation has experienced substantial growth, driven by deep learning innovations. Future research may increasingly focus on multimodal foundation models capable of generalizable segmentation across diverse clinical scenarios. This bibliometric review offers researchers a valuable reference for understanding the intellectual structure and frontiers of the field.

papers.title: CT radiomics combined with 3D deep learning interpretable model to predict the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor plus platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC: a three-center retrospective cohort study
papers.text:
CT radiomics combined with 3D deep learning interpretable model to predict the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor plus platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC: a three-center retrospective cohort study. Abstract

Background Platinum‑based chemotherapy combined with PD‑1 inhibitors serves as standard systemic treatment for unresectable stage IIIB–IV non‑small‑cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in both first‑line and later‑line settings; however, primary resistance causes substantial treatment‑response heterogeneity. Tissue‑based biomarkers including PD‑L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are limited by invasive biopsy requirements and high costs, whereas routine thin‑slice chest CT non‑invasively captures intratumoral spatial heterogeneity. We constructed a multimodal interpretable AI model integrating clinical variables, three‑dimensional (3D) radiomics and pre‑trained 3D‑DenseNet latent features to predict immunochemotherapy response and evaluate its cross‑center generalizability. Methods We retrospectively enrolled 378 advanced NSCLC patients receiving PD‑1 inhibitor plus platinum‑based chemotherapy from three tertiary hospitals. Three‑dimensional regions of interest (ROIs) of primary tumors were manually double‑blinded segmented. Following three‑step feature filtering, four models were built: clinical‑only, radiomics‑only, standalone 3D deep learning (DL), and multimodal fusion. Center 1 data were split into training (n = 66) and internal validation (n = 35) sets; Centers 2 and 3 formed two fully independent external test sets (n = 81 and n = 196). Model performance was evaluated via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and decision curve analysis (DCA). Ablation, multi‑classifier and subgroup analyses assessed robustness. SHAP and 3D Grad‑CAM enabled model interpretation; TCGA‑TCIA datasets supported immunological mechanism exploration, and an interactive prediction platform was developed. Results Only pathological subtype and treatment line exerted clinical predictive effects. The fusion model achieved competitive AUCs: training 0.909, internal validation 0.946, external‑test‑1 0.848, external‑test‑2 0.893. Although standalone 3D DL attained marginally higher AUC in training cohort, fusion outperformed clinical‑only and radiomics‑only models across all cohorts (all P < 0.05). 3D DL features represented the major predictive contributor. The model maintained AUC > 0.87 across most subgroups; calibration and DCA verified favorable consistency and clinical net benefit. SHAP‑Grad‑CAM visualized decision logic, and transcriptomic data associated CT‑defined high‑risk phenotypes with immunosuppressive microenvironments and reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration. Conclusions This low‑cost interpretable multimodal AI based on routine chest‑CT non‑invasively predicts immunochemotherapy resistance for advanced NSCLC across treatment lines. Validated by two external cohorts, it demonstrates complementary predictive value of radiomic and DL signatures and offers a standardized imaging tool for personalized immunotherapy stratification.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Ultrasound Imaging: Opportunities for Improving Diagnostic Accuracy in Gulf Health Care.
papers.text: Artificial Intelligence in Ultrasound Imaging: Opportunities for Improving Diagnostic Accuracy in Gulf Health Care.. Ultrasound imaging is widely used across cardiology, hepatology, obstetrics, breast and thyroid imaging, and emergency care because it is real-time, noninvasive, and relatively accessible. However, its diagnostic performance remains influenced by operator experience, image quality, scanner settings, and interpretation variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising support tool for ultrasound, assisting with image acquisition, quality assessment, view classification, segmentation, measurement, lesion characterization, and structured reporting. This narrative review summarizes recent developments in AI-assisted ultrasound imaging, emphasizing its technical foundations, clinical applications, validation challenges, and relevance to Gulf health care systems. Current evidence suggests that AI may improve workflow efficiency, reduce interobserver variability, and support diagnostic decision-making in selected ultrasound tasks, particularly when models are trained and tested on large, diverse data sets. Nevertheless, the clinical readiness of many AI tools remains constrained by retrospective study designs, single-center data sets, limited external validation, vendor-dependent image variability, and insufficient prospective evaluation. These limitations are particularly salient in Gulf health care, where ultrasound services are delivered across heterogeneous public, private, military, and academic institutions that use different equipment, workflows, and operator training backgrounds. Gulf countries are well-positioned to adopt AI-enabled ultrasound because of the ongoing digital health transformation and emerging regulatory frameworks, including the Saudi SFDA guidance and the UAE AI governance initiatives. However, responsible implementation will require region-specific, multicenter, multivendor validation, transparent reporting of model performance and failure cases, clinician training, and privacy-preserving data governance. AI should therefore be viewed not as a replacement for ultrasound professionals but as a decision-support technology that may improve consistency, efficiency, and diagnostic confidence when carefully validated in real-world clinical settings.

papers.title: Integrating Heterogeneous Real-World Cancer Data for Semantic Interoperability in Oncology and Medical Imaging: Development and Validation of the Cancer Image Europe Hyperontology.
papers.text:
Integrating Heterogeneous Real-World Cancer Data for Semantic Interoperability in Oncology and Medical Imaging: Development and Validation of the Cancer Image Europe Hyperontology..

Background

Semantic interoperability in health care, essential for seamless integration of information systems, is partially achieved through the use of terminologies and common data standards that define the semantic structure of data. Various complexities arise when using real-world health care data, including different interpretations of terms and concepts and gaps in domain coverage in standard terminologies. However, ensuring compatibility becomes increasingly challenging when big data are distributed across diverse repositories that use heterogeneous health care standards and overlapping terminologies. Ontologies are key solutions to bridge these gaps, enabling consistent semantic interoperability and data harmonization.

Objective

We aim to develop and validate a hyperontology within the EUCAIM (Cancer Image Europe) project to semantically integrate and harmonize clinical, biological, and imaging metadata, along with associated data from heterogeneous, disparate cancer image data models, to achieve semantic interoperability in oncology and medical imaging. The hyperontology will be used to support several EUCAIM components, including the extract, transform, and load process; federated query; image annotation and segmentation; and ultimately, AI-federated processing.

Methods

The ontology development process combines real-world data from a network of European projects on cancer imaging (AI for Health Imaging) with their semantic mappings, as well as conceptual unpacking and modeling of the Minimal Common Oncology Data Elements (mCODE) specifications. The mCODE is a core set of structured data elements for oncology electronic health records. The building process is supported by ontology grounding, layering, and modularization. We adopted this hybrid approach to simplify ontology design, semantically reflect oncology's essential entities and their interactions, and enhance the extensibility and reusability of the hyperontology. We initiated ontology development with a set of competency questions derived from the provided knowledge, which helped clarify the ontology's scope and requirements and identify inconsistencies or incomplete information. We also assessed whether the requirements were fulfilled by formalizing the competency questions using SPARQL.

Results

We developed a FAIR hyperontology that semantically integrates and harmonizes clinical, biological, and imaging metadata and data spread across disparate sources. The ontology also captures and accurately represents oncology and medical imaging. The hyperontology, which covers various cancer types, is rich in axiomatizations and patterns, supporting the semantic understanding and harmonization of heterogeneous data. Additionally, semantic mappings are established across data models and standards, ensuring the efficient and meaningful sharing and integration of health care data. Finally, we evaluated the ontology model and demonstrated its applicability using real-world prostate and breast cancer use cases.

Conclusions

EUCAIM's hyperontology is a valuable effort that provides a unifying framework for the essentials of oncology and medical imaging, facilitating communication among disparate and heterogeneous cancer image data models. The ontology model is evaluated and validated using multiple methods, demonstrating compliance with the specified ontological requirements. Challenges include ensuring that the ontology is scalable, extensible, and applicable, given the complexity and dynamic nature of the application domain.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Review of Radiodiagnosis in Indian Perspectives.
papers.text: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Review of Radiodiagnosis in Indian Perspectives.. Artificial intelligence (AI) has become the most transformative development in radiology since digital imaging, with deep learning algorithms demonstrating validated-and in controlled settings superior-performance across pulmonary nodule detection, breast cancer screening, tuberculosis (TB) triage, acute stroke identification, and glioma segmentation. Over 950 AI/machine learning-enabled medical devices have received clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as of 2024, ∼75% within radiology, yet a consequential knowledge gap persists: fewer than 30% of practising radiologists can critically evaluate an AI study and fewer than 20% have received formal AI training. This review addresses that gap by providing a clinically accessible account of core AI concepts, major neural network architectures-including convolutional neural networks, U-Net, generative adversarial networks, vision transformers, and foundation models-the complete model development and validation workflow, and validated clinical applications across all major imaging modalities. We give dedicated attention to the Indian context, where an acute radiologist deficit of 1:50,000 against the World Health Organization-recommended ratio of 1:10,000, a 26% share of the global TB burden, and heterogeneous imaging infrastructure make AI both urgently necessary and uniquely demanding of local validation; we discuss the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, federated learning, and the domestic ecosystem of Qure.ai, Niramai, and Sigtuple as structural enablers, as well as algorithmic bias, explainability, and regulatory frameworks. We conclude that AI literacy is no longer optional: the radiologist's role is not threatened by AI but transformed by it-from film reader to AI-augmented clinical imaging physician capable of extending world-class diagnostic care to underserved populations across India and globally.

papers.title: A personalized breast prosthesis volume customization method based on preoperative MRI imaging for post-mastectomy breast cancer patients.
papers.text: A personalized breast prosthesis volume customization method based on preoperative MRI imaging for post-mastectomy breast cancer patients.. Conventional breast prosthesis selection for mastectomy patients faces poor fitting accuracy, privacy exposure and complicated operation. In this preliminary feasibility study, we proposed and feasibility-verified a personalized volume customization method based on preoperative MRI and publicly available open-source tooling. A representative cohort of three breast MRI cases with distinct breast volumes and bilateral symmetry characteristics were analyzed with fully open-source 3D Slicer for segmentation, 3D reconstruction and voxel-based volumetric measurement, using the public Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI dataset. Intra-method agreement between the voxel-based label mapping method and the closed surface fitting method was less than 0.5% across all cases, and the resulting per-breast mean volumes were 1228.15, 507.49, and 635.08 mL (bilateral totals 2456.30, 1014.97, and 1270.16 mL), spanning a wide spectrum from large to small breast sizes and thereby providing a diversified basis for validating the robustness of the proposed method across different anatomical types. Breast volume is known to vary widely across individuals and populations, so the three case volumes are reported here as descriptive findings rather than as validation against any external reference. Target volumes were determined according to unilateral and bilateral mastectomy scenarios. High-quality 3D models and accurate volume quantification were obtained successfully, and a mapping model linking individual volumetric parameters to commercial prosthesis sizes was constructed as a step toward clinical translation. This non-invasive method is privacy-friendly, posture-independent in terms of volume, and avoids postoperative physical exposure, thereby relieving psychological distress. The guiding "volume conservation with morphological assessment" principle adopted in this study informs personalized external breast prosthesis selection; its longer-term morphological-remodeling dimension (patient-specific prosthesis design) lies beyond this feasibility study and is reserved for future work, offering a reproducible, privacy-friendly methodological framework for prospective validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Integrating AI for Human-Centric Breast Cancer Diagnostics: A Multi-Scale and Multi-View Swin Transformer Framework
papers.text: Integrating AI for Human-Centric Breast Cancer Diagnostics: A Multi-Scale and Multi-View Swin Transformer Framework. Despite advancements in Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems, breast cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths among women worldwide. Recent breakthroughs in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown significant promise in development of advanced Deep Learning (DL) architectures for breast cancer diagnosis through mammography. In this context, the paper focuses on the integration of AI within a Human-Centric workflow to enhance breast cancer diagnostics. Key challenges are, however, largely overlooked such as reliance on detailed tumor annotations and susceptibility to missing views, particularly during test time. To address these issues, we propose a hybrid, multi-scale and multi-view Swin Transformer-based framework (MSMV-Swin) that enhances diagnostic robustness and accuracy. The proposed MSMV-Swin framework is designed to work as a decision-support tool, helping radiologists analyze multi-view mammograms more effectively. More specifically, the MSMV-Swin framework leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to isolate the breast lobe, reducing background noise and enabling comprehensive feature extraction. The multi-scale nature of the proposed MSMV-Swin framework accounts for tumor-specific regions as well as the spatial characteristics of tissues surrounding the tumor, capturing both localized and contextual information. The integration of contextual and localized data ensures that MSMV-Swin's outputs align with the way radiologists interpret mammograms, fostering better human-AI interaction and trust. A hybrid fusion structure is then designed to ensure robustness against missing views, a common occurrence in clinical practice when only a single mammogram view is available.

papers.title: Optimizing Breast Cancer Detection in Mammograms: A Comprehensive Study of Transfer Learning, Resolution Reduction, and Multi-View Classification
papers.text: Optimizing Breast Cancer Detection in Mammograms: A Comprehensive Study of Transfer Learning, Resolution Reduction, and Multi-View Classification. Mammography, an X-ray-based imaging technique, remains central to the early detection of breast cancer. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have enabled increasingly sophisticated computer-aided diagnostic methods, evolving from patch-based classifiers to whole-image approaches and then to multi-view architectures that jointly analyze complementary projections. Despite this progress, several critical questions remain unanswered. In this study, we systematically investigate these issues by addressing five key research questions: (1) the role of patch classifiers in performance, (2) the transferability of natural-image-trained backbones, (3) the advantages of learn-to-resize over conventional downscaling, (4) the contribution of multi-view integration, and (5) the robustness of findings across varying image quality. Beyond benchmarking, our experiments demonstrate clear performance gains over prior work. For the CBIS-DDSM dataset, we improved single-view AUC from 0.8153 to 0.8343, and multiple-view AUC from 0.8483 to 0.8658. Using a new comparative method, we also observed a 0.0217 AUC increase when extending from single to multiple-view analysis. On the complete VinDr-Mammo dataset, the multiple-view approach further improved results, achieving a 0.0492 AUC increase over single view and reaching 0.8511 AUC overall. These results establish new state-of-the-art benchmarks, providing clear evidence of the advantages of multi-view architectures for mammogram interpretation. Beyond performance, our analysis offers principled insights into model design and transfer learning strategies, contributing to the development of more accurate and reliable breast cancer screening tools. The inference code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/dpetrini/multiple-view.

papers.title: A Versatile Foundation Model for AI-enabled Mammogram Interpretation
papers.text: A Versatile Foundation Model for AI-enabled Mammogram Interpretation. Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women globally. Mammography is essential for the early detection and diagnosis of breast lesions. Despite recent progress in foundation models (FMs) for mammogram analysis, their clinical translation remains constrained by several fundamental limitations, including insufficient diversity in training data, limited model generalizability, and a lack of comprehensive evaluation across clinically relevant tasks. Here, we introduce VersaMammo, a versatile foundation model for mammograms, designed to overcome these limitations. We curated the largest multi-institutional mammogram dataset to date, comprising 706,239 images from 21 sources. To improve generalization, we propose a two-stage pre-training strategy to develop VersaMammo, a mammogram foundation model. First, a teacher model is trained via self-supervised learning to extract transferable features from unlabeled mammograms. Then, supervised learning combined with knowledge distillation transfers both features and clinical knowledge into VersaMammo. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we established a benchmark comprising 92 specific tasks, including 68 internal tasks and 24 external validation tasks, spanning 5 major clinical task categories: lesion detection, segmentation, classification, image retrieval, and visual question answering. VersaMammo achieves state-of-the-art performance, ranking first in 50 out of 68 specific internal tasks and 20 out of 24 external validation tasks, with average ranks of 1.5 and 1.2, respectively. These results demonstrate its superior generalization and clinical utility, offering a substantial advancement toward reliable and scalable breast cancer screening and diagnosis.

papers.title: Long-Term Volumetric Increase of a Free Omental Flap in Breast Reconstruction: A Case Report with a Focus on Body Weight Correlation.
papers.text: Long-Term Volumetric Increase of a Free Omental Flap in Breast Reconstruction: A Case Report with a Focus on Body Weight Correlation.. A 53-year-old woman underwent breast reconstruction using a free omental flap following the resection of a phyllodes tumor in the right breast. Postoperative volumetric analysis was retrospectively conducted over 5 years using computed tomography and three-dimensional imaging software. The omental flap demonstrated a 157% increase in volume compared with the immediate postoperative size. A positive correlation (r = 0.93) was observed between body weight and flap volume. Our report is just a single case; therefore, further studies are required to elucidate our hypothesis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report to describe this association in an omental flap used for breast reconstruction. These findings may support appropriate surgical planning and postoperative follow-up in reconstructive breast surgery.

papers.title: Dosimetric Comparison of Five Radiotherapy Techniques in Left-Sided Breast Cancer Patients Following Breast-Conserving Surgery.
papers.text:
Dosimetric Comparison of Five Radiotherapy Techniques in Left-Sided Breast Cancer Patients Following Breast-Conserving Surgery..

Objective

This study aims to compare and evaluate the dosimetric characteristics of five radiotherapy techniques in left-sided breast cancer patients following breast-conserving surgery. The five radiotherapy techniques include three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3D-CRT), fixed-field intensity-modulated radiation therapy (ff-IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), hybrid 3D-CRT with IMRT (CRT + IMRT), and hybrid 3D-CRT with VMAT (CRT + VMAT).

Patients and methods

Ten patients with left-sided breast cancer who received postlumpectomy radiotherapy at the Department of Radiation Oncology, First Hospital of Qinhuangdao, between June 1, 2020, and June 1, 2021, were randomly enrolled in this study. For each patient, five distinct treatment plans were designed using the five aforementioned techniques (3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, CRT + IMRT, and CRT + VMAT) based on identical computed tomography (CT) imaging datasets. Dosimetric parameters for the tumor target volume, organs at risk (OARs), and normal tissues (defined as body minus planning target volume [PTV], termed B-P) were analyzed and compared using dose-volume histograms (DVHs) and isodose distributions.

Results

The CRT + VMAT technique demonstrated superior PTV dose coverage, conformity, and homogeneity compared to 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, and CRT + IMRT (p < 0.05). In contrast, the VMAT technique achieved significantly lower V30 (%) values for bilateral lungs and ipsilateral lung than 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, CRT + IMRT, and CRT + VMAT (p < 0.05). The CRT + IMRT technique reduced V5 (%) values for bilateral lungs, ipsilateral lung, and heart compared to 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, and CRT + VMAT (p < 0.05). Finally, 3D-CRT required the fewest monitor units (MUs) and shortest treatment time among all techniques (p < 0.05).

Conclusion

Clinicians may tailor radiotherapy plans to individual patients based on the distinct dosimetric profiles of each technique. For patients requiring optimal PTV dose distribution, the CRT + VMAT technique is suggest. For enhanced cardiopulmonary protection (e.g., reduced lung/heart doses), ff-IMRT or CRT + IMRT may be prioritized. Additionally, 3D-CRT should be the first choice for patients needing rapid fractionated treatment due to its efficiency in minimizing MUs and treatment time.

papers.title: Breast Cancer Screening in Rural West Texas: Access Barriers, Follow-Up Fragmentation, and AI-Enabled Oncology Care Delivery.
papers.text: Breast Cancer Screening in Rural West Texas: Access Barriers, Follow-Up Fragmentation, and AI-Enabled Oncology Care Delivery.. Breast cancer screening can reduce mortality, but its benefit depends on timely diagnostic resolution and access to treatment. This narrative review examines screening in rural West Texas as an oncology care-delivery continuum, integrating evidence on geographic and financial barriers, abnormal-result follow-up, navigation, regional screening programs, and artificial intelligence (AI). Mobile mammography and community outreach can improve initial access; their effectiveness depends on diagnostic capacity, clear referral responsibilities, accessible communication, and tracking through resolution. Regional evidence supports attention to structural barriers and workforce distribution, although breast-specific capacity data remain limited. A proposed regional framework links outreach and mammography with navigation, diagnostic imaging, biopsy, multidisciplinary referral, and treatment initiation. AI-assisted image interpretation, risk prediction, and follow-up coordination are distinct applications with different evidence and workload implications. Evidence from organized screening programs supports selected imaging applications, but does not establish a reduction in total clinical workload or improved diagnostic completion in rural West Texas. AI should therefore be considered an optional, locally evaluated adjunct after the pathway needed to act on its outputs is established. Program assessment should extend beyond mammography volume to diagnostic completion, time to treatment, workload, and equity.

papers.title: Cost-Effectiveness, Budget Impact and Value of Information of Artificial-Intelligence-Supported Detection of Breast, Lung, Colorectal and Cervical Cancer in the Philippines: A Decision-Analytic Modelling Study
papers.text: Cost-Effectiveness, Budget Impact and Value of Information of Artificial-Intelligence-Supported Detection of Breast, Lung, Colorectal and Cervical Cancer in the Philippines: A Decision-Analytic Modelling Study. The economic value of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported cancer detection in the Philippines remains uncertain. This study evaluated opportunistic AI reading and AI-supported screening programmes for breast, lung, colorectal and cervical cancer from the public-payer perspective. A decision-analytic model integrated stage shift, precursor-lesion prevention, budget impact and value-of-information analyses using published inputs, 7% discounting and 10,000 probabilistic draws. At PHP 250 per read, opportunistic AI reading would avert approximately 270 deaths per annual cohort at a net cost of PHP 0.93 billion and PHP 628,000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY). Only computer-aided colonoscopy approached the benchmark of one gross domestic product per capita (PHP 220,000 per QALY). Combined opportunistic reading met this benchmark at AI prices of PHP 50 or less. Increasing screening uptake from 1% to 20% would avert approximately 4750 deaths per annual cohort at PHP 14.0 billion annually, with a five-year budget impact of PHP 56 billion. Further research had greatest value for lung and breast screening programmes and opportunistic colonoscopy. Auto-contouring could expand annual radiotherapy capacity to 19,100–23,900 courses. Cost-effectiveness depends on software pricing, prevention benefits and affordable acquisition; conditional reimbursement should prioritise Philippine evidence on incremental detection and prevalence. AI-supported cancer detection offers substantial health gains but requires affordable implementation to achieve cost-effectiveness. This study identifies actionable pricing thresholds and research priorities to guide evidence-based reimbursement and equitable cancer screening in the Philippines.

papers.title: Mammography datasets and artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection: challenges, bias, and future directions
papers.text: Mammography datasets and artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection: challenges, bias, and future directions.

papers.title: Nonlinear association between age and volumetric breast density in Japanese women.
papers.text:
Nonlinear association between age and volumetric breast density in Japanese women..

Background

Volumetric breast density (VBD) is influenced by age, body mass index (BMI), and reproductive factors, yet the shape of the age-VBD association and age-specific VBD distributions in Japanese women remain incompletely characterized. We examined the associations of age, BMI, menopausal status, and parity with software-derived VBD and characterized age-specific VBD distributions, including the proportion of women with VBD ≥ 7.5%.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 719 asymptomatic Japanese women undergoing screening mammography (mean age, 58.7 ± 12.6 years; range, 20-87 years) in whom no breast lesion was identified. VBD was quantified using Volpara Density. Age was modeled using restricted cubic splines, adjusted for BMI, menopausal status, and parity. Regression analyses used 672 complete cases. Mean VBD ≥ 7.5% defined volumetrically dense breasts.

Results

Overall, 72.7% (523/719) had VBD ≥ 7.5%. Mean VBD was 17.34%, 13.41%, 11.01%, and 11.72% at ages 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79 years, respectively, and 16.81% versus 11.85% in pre- versus postmenopausal women. Age was associated with VBD (P < 0.001), with significant nonlinearity (P = 0.027); adjusted VBD was lower with increasing age until the mid-60s and then largely plateaued. Higher BMI (β = -1.08; 95% CI, - 1.20 to - 0.97; P < 0.001) and parity (β = -2.21; 95% CI, - 3.43 to - 0.98; P < 0.001) were independently associated with lower VBD, whereas menopausal status was not (β = -1.07; 95% CI, - 2.85 to 0.71; P = 0.239).

Conclusions

Age was nonlinearly associated with VBD in Japanese women, plateauing after the mid-60s. VBD ≥ 7.5% was common, while BMI and parity remained independently associated with lower VBD.

papers.title: Clinical Implications of Background Parenchymal Enhancement on Breast MRI.
papers.text: Clinical Implications of Background Parenchymal Enhancement on Breast MRI.. Breast MRI is an essential tool for breast cancer detection, evaluation, and characterization, offering greater sensitivity than mammography and ultrasound. Normal breast tissue demonstrates variable enhancement on MRI, known as background parenchymal enhancement (BPE), which reflects the physiologic enhancement of fibroglandular tissue after gadolinium administration. Initially considered an incidental finding, BPE is now recognized as a dynamic imaging feature influenced by several factors, including age, menopausal status, exogenous hormone use, and prior breast cancer treatments. Increasing evidence supports its clinical relevance since variations in BPE have been associated with differences in breast cancer risk, lesion detection, and imaging interpretation. Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is emerging as an important imaging biomarker with potential applications in risk stratification, evaluation of disease extent, and monitoring response to neoadjuvant therapy. Differences in BPE patterns may also correlate with tumor biology and molecular subtypes, further supporting its role in personalized breast imaging assessment. This article provides a comprehensive review of BPE, highlighting its biologic basis, imaging characteristics, and clinical implications in breast cancer care. It also examines the evolving role of artificial intelligence tools in the assessment and quantification of BPE, which may improve standardization and integration into clinical decision-making and research.

papers.title: Comparison of Two Deep Learning Models and Their Combination for 1-year Lung Cancer Detection in Two Screening Cohorts.
papers.text: Comparison of Two Deep Learning Models and Their Combination for 1-year Lung Cancer Detection in Two Screening Cohorts.. Purpose To evaluate the performance of Sybil, a Medical Open Network for Artificial Intelligence (MONAI)-based nodule model, and their combination for 1-year lung cancer detection in two screening cohorts: the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the Pamplona International Early Lung Cancer Action Program (P-IELCAP). Materials and Methods Baseline low-dose CT (LDCT) examinations from the NLST and the P-IELCAP were analyzed. A prespecified OR-stacked composite model combining Sybil, a MONAI-based nodule model, and a safety-net rule (MONAI-detected nodule > 6 mm with detection confidence > 0.95) was developed and evaluated for 1-year lung cancer detection. Model discrimination was assessed by using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and operating-point performance metrics were calculated. Results A total of 5110 baseline LDCT examinations were analyzed, including 2343 from NLST and 2767 from P-IELCAP, with 65 lung cancers diagnosed within 1 year. Mean age, mean pack-years, and percentage of female participants were 61.6 years ± 5.1 (SD), 57.3 pack-years ± 24.8, and 39.4% (923 of 2343), respectively, in NLST and 56.0 years ± 9.5, 34.4 pack-years ± 21.5, and 28.6% (791 of 2767), respectively, in P-IELCAP. Lung cancer incidence (per 1000 person-years) was higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (17.7 vs 8.7; P = .006). Mean Sybil 1-year lung cancer probabilities (scaled by 1000 for presentation) were also higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (16.4 vs 9.9; P < .01). Sybil achieved an AUC of 0.93 in both cohorts, whereas the MONAI-based model achieved AUCs of 0.90 in NLST and 0.79 in P-IELCAP. The composite model missed two of 65 1-year lung cancers while correctly classifying 2731 of 4965 (55.0%) noncancer examinations as negative, yielding a sensitivity of 63 of 65 (96.9%) and a positive predictive value of 63 of 2297 (2.7%). Conclusion For 1-year lung cancer detection with LDCT, the composite AI model achieved high sensitivity while maintaining acceptable specificity. Keywords: Applications-CT, Thorax, Pulmonary, Sybil, MONAI, NLST, P-IELCAP, Lung Cancer, Low Dose Computed Tomography Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

papers.title: Evaluation of artificial intelligence algorithms from Lunit for detection of breast cancer with mammogram in a South-East Asian population.
papers.text: Evaluation of artificial intelligence algorithms from Lunit for detection of breast cancer with mammogram in a South-East Asian population.. PurposeTo conduct a pre-clinical evaluation of a commercially available artificial intelligence system, Lunit AI, as an independent mammography reader and compare its performance with human readers.Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study analyzed a double-reader population-based mammographic screening cohort of women at an academic women's hospital in Singapore from 2010 to 2017. Lunit AI performance was compared with single-reader (SRR) and double-reader radiologist (DRR) assessment using AUC-ROC, specificity, sensitivity and accuracy.Results1,982 women 35-87 years without breast implants or prior breast cancer were included. The cohort comprised 193 histopathologically confirmed breast cancers, 1,299 healthy controls and 490 histopathologically proven benign recalls. Mean age was 55.7 ± 9.7 years for with cancer and 52.9 ± 8.5 years without cancer.Lunit AI achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.874 (95% CI: 0.843-0.905) compared with 0.811 (95% CI: 0.783-0.840) for SRR assessment and 0.863 (95% CI: 0.846-0.880) for DRR assessment. Compared with SRR, Lunit AI demonstrated higher specificity (81.0% vs 72.6%, p < 0.001), lower sensitivity (80.3% vs 89.6%, p = 0.013) and higher accuracy (80.9% vs 74.3%, p < 0.001). Compared with DRR, Lunit AI demonstrated higher specificity (81.0% vs 72.6%, p < 0.001), lower sensitivity (80.3% vs 100%, p < 0.001) and higher accuracy (80.9% vs 75.3%, p < 0.001). The apparent 100% sensitivity of DRR reflects the retrospective study design and should not be interpreted as true screening sensitivity. Lunit AI detected 156 of 193 cancers and missed 34 cancers of which the majority of the missed cases were 22 cases (64.7%) of microcalcifications.ConclusionLunit AI model shows promising performance in a Southeast Asian population with high AUC-ROC, specificity and accuracy. However it shows lower sensitivity for subtle microcalcifications. These results suggest that Lunit AI may not be suitable as a fully independent reader but as an adjunct to enhance existing clinical workflows in mammographic screening.

papers.title: Interpretable Retinal Disease Prediction Using Biology-Informed Heterogeneous Graph Representations
papers.text: Interpretable Retinal Disease Prediction Using Biology-Informed Heterogeneous Graph Representations. Interpretability is crucial for utilizing machine learning models as clinical decision support tools for medical diagnostics. However, most state-of-the-art image classifiers based on neural networks are not interpretable. As a result, clinicians often resort to known biomarkers to guide diagnosis, although biomarker-based classification often suffers from drastic information loss compared to raw medical images. This work proposes a method that preserves the rich imaging information while simultaneously enhancing the interpretability of predictions for diabetic retinopathy staging from optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) images. The core contribution of our method is a novel biology-informed heterogeneous graph representation that models retinal vessel segments, intercapillary areas, and the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) in a human-interpretable way. This graph representation allows us to frame diabetic retinopathy staging as a graph-level classification task, which we solve using an established, efficient graph neural network architecture. We compare our method against established methods, including classical biomarker-based classifiers, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and vision transformers in predicting the clinically assigned DR stage based on color fundus photography images. We find stage agreement rates of our method and alternative vision model based classifiers saturating at AUC-ROC values of 84%. Crucially, we use our biology-informed graph to provide explanations of great detail. Our approach surpasses existing methods in precisely localizing and identifying abnormal vessels and non-perfusion areas. Our approach sets the stage for the interpretable identification of patients who require special attention due to their traceable microvascular changes, only observable using the details of OCTA images.

papers.title: Evaluating Fundus-Specific Foundation Models for Diabetic Macular Edema Detection
papers.text: Evaluating Fundus-Specific Foundation Models for Diabetic Macular Edema Detection. Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is a leading cause of vision loss among patients with Diabetic Retinopathy (DR). While deep learning has shown promising results for automatically detecting this condition from fundus images, its application remains challenging due the limited availability of annotated data. Foundation Models (FM) have emerged as an alternative solution. However, it is unclear if they can cope with DME detection in particular. In this paper, we systematically compare different FM and standard transfer learning approaches for this task. Specifically, we compare the two most popular FM for retinal images-RETFound and FLAIR-and an EfficientNetB0 backbone, across different training regimes and evaluation settings in IDRiD, MESSIDOR-2 and OCT-and-Eye-FundusImages (OEFI). Results show that despite their scale, FM do not consistently outperform fine-tuned CNNs in this task. In particular, EfficientNet-B0 consistently achieves competitive or superior performance across evaluation settings, with FLAIR being the most competitive foundation model, consistently outperforming RETFound. These findings suggest that FMs do not necessarily provide an advantage for fine-grained ophthalmic tasks such as DME detection, even after fine-tuning, highlighting lightweight CNNs as strong baselines in data-scarce environments.

papers.title: DR-LiteNet: A Lightweight Explainable Hybrid CNN Framework for Imbalanced Diabetic Retinopathy Grading via Adaptive SMOTE Fusion
papers.text: DR-LiteNet: A Lightweight Explainable Hybrid CNN Framework for Imbalanced Diabetic Retinopathy Grading via Adaptive SMOTE Fusion. Automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading from colour fundus photographs is held back by two compounding challenges: severe class imbalance across five severity grades and the heavy computational cost of large scale architectures in resource constrained clinical settings. We introduce DR-LiteNet, a dual branch hybrid convolutional neural network that tackles both problems at once. The CNN branch extracts 1,280 dimensional deep features through EfficientNetB0, while the handcrafted (HC) branch produces a compact 51 dimensional lesion descriptor capturing vessel density, exudate intensity, texture entropy, and HSV colour histograms. Concatenating both branches yields a 1,331-d hybrid embedding, on which Adaptive SMOTE (ADASYN) is applied during training to synthesise minority class feature vectors, correcting distributional skew without touching the image space. A two phase training protocol first warms up the classification head on balanced features, then fine tunes the full network end to end. Grad CAM saliency maps deliver post-hoc clinical explainability. Tested on APTOS 2019 under five fold stratified cross validation, DR-LiteNet reaches 88.77% +/- 0.61 accuracy, a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.884 +/- 0.010, and a macro F1 of 0.792 +/- 0.008 with only 4.69 M parameters beating ResNet50 (23.5 M) by DeltaQWK = 0.022 while staying practical on a single Google Colab T4 GPU. The source code of this project is available at: https://github.com/Nishi-Kanta-Paul/DR-LiteNet.

papers.title: Polyp Matching Using Deep Learning
papers.text: Polyp Matching Using Deep Learning. A key challenge in colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) analysis is accurately identifying whether multiple images depict the same polyp, which is critical to avoid over-counting and unnecessary clinical interventions. Additionally, this prevents prolonged follow-up colonoscopies where endoscopists search for duplicate polyps without precise localization. This study presents a novel contrastive learning-based approach to polyp matching using a Siamese neural network architecture. The model was trained on a dataset from the Danish CareForColon2015 trial. The dataset comprises 5,103 image pairs of confirmed same polyp and 5,103 pairs of different polyps, annotated by experienced clinicians. The proposed model employs ResNet variants (ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50), DenseNet121 and EfficientNet B0/B3 as backbones and utilizes contrastive learning with cosine vector distance metric for classification. Experimental results demonstrate high classification accuracies of up to 92% and AUC values close to 0.98. These results suggest that automated polyp matching has the potential to reduce polyp over-counting, improve patient risk stratification, and reduce unnecessary follow-up colonoscopies.

papers.title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
papers.text: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification. Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.

papers.title: Segment What It Can Draw: Querying a Text-to-Image Generator with Its Own Images for Skin Lesion Segmentation
papers.text: Segment What It Can Draw: Querying a Text-to-Image Generator with Its Own Images for Skin Lesion Segmentation. Skin lesion segmentation without annotated masks requires the target to be specified through other cues. Existing approaches rely on dermoscopy-specific rules, annotation-derived model priors, or user-selected regions. A general text-to-image diffusion transformer offers a text interface to the target, but its concept-word attention is unreliable on dermoscopy images: in the model's attention-output space, the word-derived skin-to-lesion direction is poorly aligned with the direction separating real skin from real lesions. We show that the direction derived from generated healthy-skin and lesion images is substantially better aligned. Based on this finding, we propose GENIQ, a training-free method that constructs initial skin and lesion prototypes from generated images and refines them using the most skin-like and lesion-like patches from unlabelled dermoscopy images. It scores test patches along the refined direction and applies a gated threshold to suppress contextual spill-over around small lesions. Without inference-time annotations or additional models, GENIQ achieves Dice scores of 0.85-0.88 on three dermoscopy test sets. It outperforms zero-shot and word-based attention methods on all three sets, and a hand-designed dermoscopy pipeline in Dice and IoU on two.

papers.title: Reliable Retinal Screening with Foundation Models under Distribution Shift
papers.text:
Reliable Retinal Screening with Foundation Models under Distribution Shift. Abstract

Reliable deployment of deep learning classifiers for retinal disease screening requires accurate in-distribution classification, effective out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and well-calibrated predictions under distribution shift. This study investigates the open-world reliability of the EyeCLIP foundation model and evaluates whether calibration-oriented fine-tuning improves performance under external-domain shift. A three-class fundus classification task comprising diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and normal images was constructed using APTOS2019, G1020, and ORIGA, with ORIGA held out entirely for external evaluation.
