Standard balanced fine-tuning was compared with calibration-oriented fine-tuning and a frozen-feature linear probe. Five OOD scoring methods were evaluated alongside post-hoc temperature scaling and accept–reject analysis. Performance was assessed using classification, OOD detection, and calibration metrics. Standard balanced fine-tuning out-performed calibration-oriented fine-tuning in in-distribution accuracy (0.928 vs. 0.781), k-nearest-neighbor OOD detection (AUROC 0.938 vs. 0.878), and post-hoc OOD calibration (ECE 0.081 vs. 0.450). The calibration-oriented model misclassified 69% of normal ORIGA images as glaucoma. At 25% overall rejection, standard balanced fine-tuning rejected 50.9% of OOD samples while falsely rejecting 1.6% of in-distribution samples. Standard balanced fine-tuning combined with post-hoc calibration and feature-space k-nearest-neighbor abstention provides a simple and effective strategy for improving the reliability of open-world retinal screening.

papers.title: Lung Cancer Classification from CT Images: A Comparative Study of SVM, Modified CNN, and EfficientNet–SVM Hybrid Models
papers.text:
Lung Cancer Classification from CT Images: A Comparative Study of SVM, Modified CNN, and EfficientNet–SVM Hybrid Models. Abstract

This paper proposes a computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) framework that combines four complementary classification paradigms on the publicly available IQ-OTH/NCCD CT dataset with 1,097 slices across benign, malignant, and normal classes from 110 patients. The framework comprises: (i) an image-processing pipeline employing Gaussian smoothing, histogram equalization, Canny edge detection, and morphological closing, (ii) Otsu-based lung segmentation followed by handcrafted feature extraction combining statistical Local Binary Pattern (LBP), gradient, and shape descriptors, (iii) a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier benchmarked under a systematic ablation of three kernels and six class-balancing strategies (SMOTE, ADASYN, Borderline-SMOTE, Random Over-Sampling, SMOTE–Tomek, and cost-sensitive class weighting), (iv) a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and a modified CNN architecture enriched with batch normalization, and (v) a hybrid EfficientNet–SVM model that separates deep representation learning from maximum-margin decision-boundary fitting. The modified CNN achieves the highest overall test accuracy of 99.41% with a macro F1-score of 0.99, while the SVM with the RBF kernel under Random Over-Sampling reaches 98.81% balanced accuracy and the hybrid CNN–SVM attains 98.00% test accuracy. The result demonstrates both robust-ness across classes and competitiveness against recent state-of-the-art models on the same dataset.

papers.title: Adaptive Squeeze-and-Shrink Image Denoising for Improving Deep Detection of Cerebral Microbleeds.
papers.text: Adaptive Squeeze-and-Shrink Image Denoising for Improving Deep Detection of Cerebral Microbleeds.. Deep learning for medical image analysis requires large quantities of high-quality imaging data for training purposes, which could be often less available due to existence of heavy noise in particular imaging modalities. This issue is especially obvious in cerebral microbleed (CMB) detection, since CMBs are more discernable on long echo time (TE) susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) data, which are unfortunately much noisier than those with shorter TE. In this paper we present an effective unsupervised image denoising scheme with application to boosting the performance of deep learning based CMB detection. The proposed content-adaptive denoising technique uses the log-determinant of covariance matrices formed by highly correlated image contents retrieved from the input itself to implicitly and efficiently exploit sparsity in PCA domain. The numerical solution to the corresponding optimization problem comes down to an adaptive squeeze-and-shrink (ASAS) operation on the underlying PCA coefficients. Obviously, the ASAS denoising does not rely on any external dataset and could be better fit the input image data. Experiments on medical image datasets with synthetic Gaussian white noise demonstrate that the proposed ASAS scheme is highly competitive among state-of-the-art sparsity based approaches as well as deep learning based method. When applied to the deep learning based CMB detection on the real-world TE3 SWI dataset, the proposed ASAS denoising could improve the precision by 18.03%, sensitivity by 7.64%, and increase the correlation between counts of ground truth and automated detection by 19.87%.

papers.title: 3D-StyleGAN: A Style-Based Generative Adversarial Network for Generative Modeling of Three-Dimensional Medical Images.
papers.text: 3D-StyleGAN: A Style-Based Generative Adversarial Network for Generative Modeling of Three-Dimensional Medical Images.. Image synthesis via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) of three-dimensional (3D) medical images has great potential that can be extended to many medical applications, such as, image enhancement and disease progression modeling. Current GAN technologies for 3D medical image synthesis must be significantly improved to be suitable for real-world medical problems. In this paper, we extend the state-of-the-art StyleGAN2 model, which natively works with two-dimensional images, to enable 3D image synthesis. In addition to the image synthesis, we investigate the behavior and interpretability of the 3D-StyleGAN via style vectors inherited form the original StyleGAN2 that are highly suitable for medical applications: (i) the latent space projection and reconstruction of unseen real images, and (ii) style mixing. The model can be applied to any 3D volumetric images. We demonstrate the 3D-StyleGAN's performance and feasibility with ~12,000 three-dimensional full brain MR T1 images. Furthermore, we explore different configurations of hyperparameters to investigate potential improvement of the image synthesis with larger networks. The codes and pre-trained networks are available online: https://github.com/sh4174/3DStyleGAN.

papers.title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cardiac Segmentation: Towards Structure Mutual Information Maximization
papers.text: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cardiac Segmentation: Towards Structure Mutual Information Maximization. Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches have recently succeeded in various medical image segmentation tasks. The reported works often tackle the domain shift problem by aligning the domain-invariant features and minimizing the domain-specific discrepancies. That strategy works well when the difference between a specific domain and between different domains is slight. However, the generalization ability of these models on diverse imaging modalities remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces UDA-VAE++, an unsupervised domain adaptation framework for cardiac segmentation. We show that the evidence lower bound of VAE-based domain adaptation penalizes the mutual information between the image and the latent space, including the structure information that segmentation relies on. Maximizing the structure mutual information removes this penalty on the structure information, while the remaining information is still compressed. To estimate this term, we develop a novel Structure Mutual Information Estimation (SMIE) block with a global estimator, a local estimator, and a prior information matching estimator to maximize the mutual information between the reconstruction and segmentation tasks. Specifically, we design a novel sequential reparameterization scheme that enables information flow and variance correction from the low-resolution latent space to the high-resolution latent space. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark cardiac segmentation datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art qualitatively and quantitatively. The code is available at https://github.com/LOUEY233/Toward-Mutual-Information

papers.title: 3D UX-Net: A Large Kernel Volumetric ConvNet Modernizing Hierarchical Transformer for Medical Image Segmentation.
papers.text: 3D UX-Net: A Large Kernel Volumetric ConvNet Modernizing Hierarchical Transformer for Medical Image Segmentation.. The recent 3D medical ViTs (e.g., SwinUNETR) achieve the state-of-the-art performances on several 3D volumetric data benchmarks, including 3D medical image segmentation. Hierarchical transformers (e.g., Swin Transformers) reintroduced several ConvNet priors and further enhanced the practical viability of adapting volumetric segmentation in 3D medical datasets. The effectiveness of hybrid approaches is largely credited to the large receptive field for non-local self-attention and the large number of model parameters. We hypothesize that volumetric ConvNets can simulate the large receptive field behavior of these learning approaches with fewer model parameters using depth-wise convolution. In this work, we propose a lightweight volumetric ConvNet, termed 3D UX-Net, which adapts the hierarchical transformer using ConvNet modules for robust volumetric segmentation. Specifically, we revisit volumetric depth-wise convolutions with large kernel (LK) size (e.g. starting from 7 × 7 × 7) to enable the larger global receptive fields, inspired by Swin Transformer. We further substitute the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) in Swin Transformer blocks with pointwise depth convolutions and enhance model performances with fewer normalization and activation layers, thus reducing the number of model parameters. 3D UX-Net competes favorably with current SOTA transformers (e.g. SwinUNETR) using three challenging public datasets on volumetric brain and abdominal imaging: 1) MICCAI Challenge 2021 FLARE, 2) MICCAI Challenge 2021 FeTA, and 3) MICCAI Challenge 2022 AMOS. 3D UX-Net consistently outperforms SwinUNETR with improvement from 0.929 to 0.938 Dice (FLARE2021) and 0.867 to 0.874 Dice (Feta2021). We further evaluate the transfer learning capability of 3D UX-Net with AMOS2022 and demonstrates another improvement of 2.27% Dice (from 0.880 to 0.900). The source code with our proposed model are available at https://github.com/MASILab/3DUX-Net.

papers.title: Investigating and Improving Latent Density Segmentation Models for Aleatoric Uncertainty Quantification in Medical Imaging
papers.text: Investigating and Improving Latent Density Segmentation Models for Aleatoric Uncertainty Quantification in Medical Imaging. Data uncertainties, such as sensor noise, occlusions or limitations in the acquisition method can introduce irreducible ambiguities in images, which result in varying, yet plausible, semantic hypotheses. In Machine Learning, this ambiguity is commonly referred to as aleatoric uncertainty. In image segmentation, latent density models can be utilized to address this problem. The most popular approach is the Probabilistic U-Net (PU-Net), which uses latent Normal densities to optimize the conditional data log-likelihood Evidence Lower Bound. In this work, we demonstrate that the PU-Net latent space is severely sparse and heavily under-utilized. To address this, we modify the training objective to introduce the entropy-regularized Sinkhorn Divergence in the latent space, which promotes homogeneity across all latent dimensions, effectively improving gradient-descent updates and latent space informativeness. Applied to public datasets of various clinical segmentation problems, our proposed methodology achieves the best Empirical Wasserstein Distance on every dataset compared against preceding latent variable models for probabilistic segmentation. The results indicate that encouraging a homogeneous latent space significantly improves latent density modeling for medical image segmentation.

papers.title: Full-resolution MLPs Empower Medical Dense Prediction
papers.text: Full-resolution MLPs Empower Medical Dense Prediction. Dense prediction is a fundamental requirement for many medical vision tasks such as medical image restoration, registration, and segmentation. The most popular vision model, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), has reached bottlenecks due to the intrinsic locality of convolution operations. Recently, transformers have been widely adopted for dense prediction for their capability to capture long-range visual dependence. However, due to the high computational complexity and large memory consumption of self-attention operations, transformers are usually used at downsampled feature resolutions. Such usage cannot effectively leverage the tissue-level textural information available only at the full image resolution. This textural information is crucial for medical dense prediction as it can differentiate the subtle human anatomy in medical images. In this study, we hypothesize that Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are superior alternatives to transformers in medical dense prediction where tissue-level details dominate the performance, as MLPs enable long-range dependence at the full image resolution. To validate our hypothesis, we develop a full-resolution hierarchical MLP framework that uses MLPs beginning from the full image resolution. We evaluate this framework with various MLP blocks on a wide range of medical dense prediction tasks including restoration, registration, and segmentation. Extensive experiments on six public well-benchmarked datasets show that, by simply using MLPs at full resolution, our framework outperforms its CNN and transformer counterparts and achieves state-of-the-art performance on various medical dense prediction tasks.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Guided Dynamic Pseudo-Label Enhancement for Semi-Supervised Left Atrial Segmentation
papers.text: Uncertainty-Guided Dynamic Pseudo-Label Enhancement for Semi-Supervised Left Atrial Segmentation. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common atrial-origin arrhythmia. Left atrial image segmentation is critical for timely diagnosis and intervention. The traditional manual annotation is inefficient and inconsistent. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has thus become a practical way to alleviate the annotation bottleneck in medical imaging. Existing SSL segmentation methods still suffer from fixed confidence thresholds, accumulated pseudo-label noise, and insufficient local perturbations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a semi-supervised medical image segmentation method based on uncertainty-guided dynamic pseudo-label enhancement. This method dynamically adjusts the confidence threshold to better adapt to the dynamic characteristics of data distribution and feature changes. And it introduces an uncertainty-guided region mixing (UMIX) module, which uses prediction entropy to identify high uncertainty regions and achieves data enhancement through cross-sample feature replacement. UniMatch serves as the backbone, with strong and weak perturbations applied at both image and feature levels to enable more effective supervised learning and improve segmentation. The proposed method was compared against competing methods on two public datasets. Through comparative experiments with other methods on two public datasets, together with ablation studies, we validated the superior performance of the proposed method in image segmentation tasks and the effectiveness of its individual components.

papers.title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images
papers.text: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images. We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.

papers.title: A review of medical image segmentation research based on bibliometrics.
papers.text: A review of medical image segmentation research based on bibliometrics.. BackgroundMedical image segmentation is a fundamental step in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning, and its research landscape has expanded rapidly with the advancement of artificial intelligence. A systematic bibliometric overview of this field is therefore needed to clarify its intellectual structure and emerging trends.ObjectiveTo provide a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the global research landscape, developmental trends, collaboration networks, and emerging hotspots in the field of medical image segmentation over the past decade.MethodsA bibliometric analysis was performed on 21,437 publications related to medical image segmentation, indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2016 to 2025. The analysis systematically examined publication outputs, country-level contributions, author collaboration networks, journal distributions, and keyword co-occurrence patterns.ResultsThe annual publication count increased remarkably from 25 in 2016 to 5,207 in 2025. China contributed the largest share with 11,556 publications, followed by the United States (3,272) and India (1,924). Core researchers formed stable intra-team collaborations, though inter-team cooperation remained limited. Keyword and citation analyses identified deep learning, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Transformers, U-Net, and their variants as dominant methodological themes. Case studies on skin and lung segmentation revealed differential research attention and international collaboration patterns across anatomical targets. A historical trajectory analysis showed methodological evolution from traditional image processing to fully convolutional networks and U-Net, and subsequently to hybrid architectures integrating attention mechanisms and Transformers.ConclusionMedical image segmentation has experienced substantial growth, driven by deep learning innovations. Future research may increasingly focus on multimodal foundation models capable of generalizable segmentation across diverse clinical scenarios. This bibliometric review offers researchers a valuable reference for understanding the intellectual structure and frontiers of the field.

papers.title: PG-HSAM: Prototype-Guided Hierarchical Segment Anything Model for Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Annotations
papers.text:
PG-HSAM: Prototype-Guided Hierarchical Segment Anything Model for Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Annotations. Abstract

Adapting segmentation foundation models to medical images with limited annotations requires effective use of semantic information without substantially increasing model complexity. We propose PG-HSAM, an extension of H-SAM that introduces prototype prior fusion (PPF) and balanced pixel-to-prototype contrastive regularization (BPC). PPF maintains exponential-moving-average class prototypes, converts pixel-to-prototype similarities into a semantic probability prior, and fuses this prior with the first-stage prediction before hierarchical refinement. BPC regularizes the same feature space with class-balanced pixel sampling. For binary segmentation, foreground and background prototypes are jointly normalized to construct the semantic prior. The prototype memory is non-trainable, and BPC is used only during training. Under the limited-label protocols of H-SAM, PG-HSAM achieves mean Dice scores of 80.49%, 85.20%, and 83.51% on Synapse, LA, and PROMISE12, respectively. Compared with H-SAM, the gains are 0.81, 1.26, and 6.56 percentage points, while Synapse HD95 decreases from 18.35 to 13.70. Ablation and hyperparameter studies further verify the contributions of PPF and BPC and show that the improvement is obtained without increasing the model parameter count.

papers.title: TRiST: Topology-Reinforced Swin Transformer for Medical Image Analysis
papers.text: TRiST: Topology-Reinforced Swin Transformer for Medical Image Analysis. Medical images contain topological patterns, such as connected components and loops, at scales ranging from small lesions to organ boundaries. Although hierarchical Vision Transformers have advanced medical image analysis, they do not explicitly incorporate topology throughout their multiscale representations. We propose Topology-Reinforced Swin Transformer (TRiST), a framework that integrates topological information into feature construction, refinement, and attention. First, a Hierarchical Multi-Scale Topology Representation algorithm computes 2D persistent homology (H0 and H1) independently at four native Swin stages, producing descriptors aligned with each stage's token grid rather than downsampling fine-scale topology. Second, a Band-Aware H0/H1 Residual Refinement module uses gated residual networks to process short-, medium-, and long-persistence information separately. Third, a Persistence-Band Progressive Attention Bias converts stage-specific descriptors into learned key-saliency scores that directly modify shifted-window attention logits. We instantiate TRiST as Topo-SwinV2-B for classification and Topo-Swin-UNet for segmentation, preserving the underlying Swin-based backbones. Experiments on five medical image datasets show consistent improvements over Swin-based baselines and competitive performance relative to existing topology-augmented methods.

papers.title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
papers.text: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling. Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.

papers.title: Boundary-weighted logit consistency improves calibration of segmentation networks.
papers.text: Boundary-weighted logit consistency improves calibration of segmentation networks.. Neural network prediction probabilities and accuracy are often only weakly-correlated. Inherent label ambiguity in training data for image segmentation aggravates such miscalibration. We show that logit consistency across stochastic transformations acts as a spatially varying regularizer that prevents overconfident predictions at pixels with ambiguous labels. Our boundary-weighted extension of this regularizer provides state-of-the-art calibration for prostate and heart MRI segmentation.

papers.title: A Multimodal Feature Distillation with Mamba-Transformer Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Incomplete Modalities
papers.text: A Multimodal Feature Distillation with Mamba-Transformer Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Incomplete Modalities. Existing brain tumor segmentation methods usually utilize multiple Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) modalities in brain tumor images for segmentation, which can achieve better segmentation performance. However, in clinical applications, some modalities are often missing due to resource constraints, resulting in significant performance degradation for methods that rely on complete modality segmentation. In this paper, we propose a Multimodal feature distillation with Mamba-Transformer hybrid network (MMTSeg) for accurate brain tumor segmentation with missing modalities. We first employ a Multimodal Feature Distillation (MFD) module to distill feature-level multimodal knowledge into different unimodalities to extract complete modality information. We further develop an Unimodal Feature Enhancement (UFE) module to model the semantic relationship between global and local information. Finally, we built a Cross-Modal Fusion (CMF) module to explicitly align the global correlations across modalities, even when some modalities are missing. Complementary features within and across modalities are refined by the Mamba-Transformer hybrid architectures in both the UFE and CMF modules, dynamically capturing long-range dependencies and global semantic information for complex spatial contexts. A boundary-wise loss function is employed as the segmentation loss of the proposed MMTSeg to minimize boundary discrepancies for a distance-based metric. Our ablation study demonstrates the importance of the proposed feature enhancement and fusion modules in the proposed network and the Transformer with Mamba block for improving the performance of brain tumor segmentation with missing modalities. Extensive experiments on the BraTS 2018 and BraTS 2020 datasets demonstrate that the proposed MMTSeg framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods when modalities are missing.

papers.title: MATCH: Multi-faceted Adaptive Topo-Consistency for Semi-Supervised Histopathology Segmentation
papers.text: MATCH: Multi-faceted Adaptive Topo-Consistency for Semi-Supervised Histopathology Segmentation.

papers.title: Subcortical Masks Generation in CT Images via Ensemble-Based Cross-Domain Label Transfer
papers.text: Subcortical Masks Generation in CT Images via Ensemble-Based Cross-Domain Label Transfer. Subcortical segmentation in neuroimages plays an important role in understanding brain anatomy and facilitating computer-aided diagnosis of traumatic brain injuries and neurodegenerative disorders. However, training accurate automatic models requires large amounts of labelled data. Despite the availability of publicly available subcortical segmentation datasets for Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), a significant gap exists for Computed Tomography (CT). This paper proposes an automatic ensemble framework to generate high-quality subcortical segmentation labels for CT scans by leveraging existing MRI-based models. We introduce a robust ensembling pipeline to integrate them and apply it to unannotated paired MRI-CT data, resulting in a comprehensive CT subcortical segmentation dataset. Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed framework. Furthermore, using our generated CT dataset, we train segmentation models that achieve improved performance on related segmentation tasks. To facilitate future research, we make our source code, generated dataset, and trained models publicly available at https://github.com/alxw0671/CT_Subcortical_Segmentation, marking the first open-source release for CT subcortical segmentation to the best of our knowledge.

papers.title: Confidence-Calibrating Regularization for Robust Brain MRI Segmentation Under Domain Shift
papers.text: Confidence-Calibrating Regularization for Robust Brain MRI Segmentation Under Domain Shift. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibits strong zero-shot performance on natural images but suffers from domain shift and overconfidence when applied to medical volumes. We propose \textbf{CalSAM}, a lightweight adaptation framework that (i) reduces encoder sensitivity to domain shift via a \emph{Feature Fisher Information Penalty} (FIP) computed on 3D feature maps and (ii) penalizes overconfident voxel-wise errors through a \emph{Confidence Misalignment Penalty} (CMP). The combined loss, \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CalSAM}}\) fine-tunes only the mask decoder while keeping SAM's encoders frozen. On cross-center and scanner-shift evaluations, CalSAM substantially improves accuracy and calibration: e.g., on the BraTS scanner split (Siemens$\to$GE) CalSAM shows a $+7.4\%$ relative improvement in $\mathrm{DSC}$ (80.1\% vs.\ 74.6\%), a $-26.9\%$ reduction in $\mathrm{HD95}$ (4.6 mm vs.\ 6.3 mm), and a $-39.5\%$ reduction in $\mathrm{ECE}$ (5.2\% vs.\ 8.6\%). On ATLAS-C (motion corruptions), CalSAM achieves a $+5.3\%$ relative improvement in $\mathrm{DSC}$ (75.9\%) and a $-32.6\%$ reduction in $\mathrm{ECE}$ (5.8\%). Ablations show FIP and CMP contribute complementary gains ($p<0.01$), and the Fisher penalty incurs a modest $\sim$15\% training-time overhead. CalSAM therefore delivers improved domain generalization and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates for brain MRI segmentation, while retaining the computational benefits of freezing SAM's encoder.

papers.title: Latent Representation Learning from 3D Brain MRI for Latent Analysis and Prediction in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.text: Latent Representation Learning from 3D Brain MRI for Latent Analysis and Prediction in Multiple Sclerosis. Neurological diseases can cause significant cognitive impairment, yet linking brain structure to cognitive function remains challenging due to the limitations of conventional methods and the black-box nature of deep learning. We propose InfoVAE-Med3D, an adaptation of InfoVAE for three-dimensional brain MRI that learns informative latent representations by relaxing the mutual information regularization penalty between inputs and latent representations. We evaluated the method on a healthy control (HC) dataset (\(n=6{,}503\)) with age and sex information and a multiple sclerosis (MS) dataset (\(n=916\)) with age, sex, and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) scores. Two-dimensional visualizations revealed sex-related clustering and smooth transitions in grey and white matter volumes. Removing the mutual information regularization penalty generally improved MRI reconstruction and brain age and SDMT prediction using support vector regression, outperforming other variational autoencoder variants and achieving competitive performance with deep learning predictors, particularly on the MS dataset. InfoVAE-Med3D provides informative latent representations for investigating brain-related characteristics and supports latent-space analysis and imaging biomarker discovery for cognitive impairment, particularly in MS.

papers.title: Anatomically-Guided Attention for False Positive Reduction in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.text:
Anatomically-Guided Attention for False Positive Reduction in Brain Tumor Segmentation. Abstract

U-Net-based brain tumor segmentation can produce false positives in anatomically implausible locations, which inflate tumor volume estimates and reduce clinical trust. We investigate whether injecting an anatomical location prior into the network's attention can reduce these errors. We propose a prior informed attention gate that conditions U-Net features on empirical tumor-location prior maps computed from the training annotations, applied as a residual spatial gate at the bottleneck and at every decoder stage. Using the BRISC dataset of 2D contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI slices (glioma, meningioma and pituitary tumor), we compare the proposed model with a vanilla U-Net and a learned-gate ablation under identical training, using 3-fold cross-validation and a held-out test set of 860 images. We evaluate Dice, IoU, precision, recall, Hausdorff distance, HD95 and a dedicated far false-positive measure. The proposed model matched the baseline in Dice (0.709 versus 0.708) and showed a slightly lower but non-significant HD95 (36.5 versus 37.9 px, p = 0.26); it did not significantly reduce far false positives (49.7 versus 48.0 px, p = 0.82). A simple location prior injected through a spatial gate is therefore insufficient on BRISC, and stronger prior integration, longer training and additional datasets are needed to establish any benefit.

papers.title: Revisiting the MS paradox: automated 2.5D FLAIR segmentation and DTI microstructural profiling reveals dissociation between lesion burden and reference-like intralesional tract profiles
papers.text: Revisiting the MS paradox: automated 2.5D FLAIR segmentation and DTI microstructural profiling reveals dissociation between lesion burden and reference-like intralesional tract profiles.

papers.title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
papers.text: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis. Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fréchet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.

papers.title: MDF-Net: A Decoupled Multimodal Fusion Network with Contrastive Learning for Reliable Brain Tumor Segmentation on Multi-sequence MRI.
papers.text: MDF-Net: A Decoupled Multimodal Fusion Network with Contrastive Learning for Reliable Brain Tumor Segmentation on Multi-sequence MRI.. Accurate segmentation of brain tumors from multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is critical for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal disease monitoring. Multimodal MRI provides complementary information across sequences, yet this complementarity is entangled with substantial cross-modal redundancy. Prevailing coupled fusion schemes merge modalities into a single shared space, where discriminative tumor-specific cues and redundant shared content are blended indiscriminately, an effect further aggravated by cross-scale feature inconsistency and by the difficulty of delineating small enhancing lesions. To address these issues, we recast multimodal segmentation as a decoupled representation learning problem and propose a Multimodal Decoupled Fusion Network (MDF-Net) that explicitly disentangles the fused representation into complementary and non-redundant components. At its core, a Tri-Branch Decoupling (TBD) module separates the fused features into spatial, channel, and instance components, and a Feature Contrastive Learning (FCL) objective enforces their complementarity while suppressing inter-branch redundancy. To provide scale-aware and locally coherent features for decoupling, an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module and a Local Window Self-Attention (LWSA) module jointly model multi-scale context and local dependencies, while a dedicated Small Lesion Refinement (SLR) module improves the delineation of small and ambiguous enhancing tumors through multi-scale detection and boundary-aware refinement. Extensive experiments on two publicly available benchmarks, BraTS 2023 and FeTS 2022, demonstrate that MDF-Net achieves competitive and well-balanced performance relative to recent state-of-the-art methods across tumor sub-regions and multiple evaluation metrics, with particularly accurate whole-tumor boundary delineation. Ablation studies and feature-space visualizations further confirm that explicit decoupling yields a more structured embedding space and that each component makes a complementary contribution to segmentation performance.

papers.title: 2D U-Net Framework for Multiclass Automated Segmentation of Healthy Structures, Ischemic Stroke, and Glioblastoma in the Rat Brain.
papers.text: 2D U-Net Framework for Multiclass Automated Segmentation of Healthy Structures, Ischemic Stroke, and Glioblastoma in the Rat Brain.. Rodents are essential for preclinical brain disease research, including stroke, tumors, and neurodegenerative disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables longitudinal brain tissue visualization, but accurate segmentation is crucial for meaningful analysis. This study introduces a multitask 2D U-Net, a convolutional neural network designed for automated segmentation and quantification of brain regions, ischemic stroke lesions, and tumors in rats using T<sub>2</sub>-weighted imaging (T<sub>2</sub>-wi) and T<sub>2</sub>-relaxation maps. The model was evaluated on the following three MRI datasets: (i) segmentation of multiple brain regions in healthy rats, (ii) ischemic stroke lesions using T<sub>2</sub>-relaxation maps, and (iii) glioblastoma tumors using T<sub>2</sub>-wi. Performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient (DC), Hausdorff distance (HD), sensitivity (SEN), and volume ratio (VR), comparing network outputs against semiautomatic ground truths and existing models. A total of 1949 images from 111 rats were analyzed, expanded to 5847 through data augmentation. After correcting an animal-level train/test partitioning that prevented data leakage between subjects, the model achieved robust accuracy across all tasks (DC = 0.80-0.96, HD = 0.83-2.16 mm, SEN = 0.75-0.96, VR = 0.89-1.10), showing a strong correlation ( ρ=0.82-0.99 ) with manual annotations. This framework improves segmentation accuracy, robustness, and applicability across different MRI settings and conditions, addressing issues like interrater variability and time inefficiency when analyzing rodent brain MRI data. Datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NOBEL-MRI/Rat-Datasets.

papers.title: Evaluating Boundary-Aware Losses for U-KAN on BraTS 2023 Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.text:
Evaluating Boundary-Aware Losses for U-KAN on BraTS 2023 Brain Tumor Segmentation. Abstract

Background:: Boundary-aware loss functions are intended to improve segmentation by penalizing spatial errors that may be insufficiently represented by region-based objectives. Whether they provide meaningful and reproducible benefits when incorporated into U-KAN for brain tumor segmentation remains unclear.

Methods:

: We compared five loss configurations in separate 2D and 3D U-KAN pipelines using multimodal MRI from the BraTS 2023 adult glioma dataset: a region-based baseline, fixed Boundary Loss, Staged Boundary Loss, a Generalized Surface Loss composite, and standalone Boundary Difference-over-Union loss. Each configuration was trained with three seeds in each pipeline, producing 30 runs. Performance was assessed using regional and macro Dice, the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), run-level consistency, and patient-level paired comparisons against the corresponding baseline.

Results:

: In 2D, Staged Boundary Loss achieved the highest mean macro Dice (0.8139 versus 0.8001) and reduced mean HD95 (22.55 versus 34.81~mm). Patient-level comparisons favored this configuration, but its overlap improvement was concentrated in whole-tumor segmentation and it exceeded the baseline in only one of three matched seed comparisons. In 3D, Staged Boundary Loss produced only small descriptive improvements in macro Dice (0.89794 versus 0.89698) and HD95 (3.645 versus 3.736~mm), with no significant favorable patient-level difference after multiplicity correction. The other boundary-aware configurations did not consistently outperform the baselines, and standalone Boundary Difference-over-Union exhibited substantial instability in one 2D run.

Conclusions:

: Boundary-aware training did not provide a consistent advantage over region-based objectives. Staged Boundary Loss was the most promising configuration, but its benefits were pipeline-dependent and not reliably reproduced across training runs.

papers.title: Towards Generalist Biomedical AI.
papers.text:
Towards Generalist Biomedical AI..

Background

Medicine is inherently multimodal, requiring the simultaneous interpretation and integration of insights between many data modalities spanning text, imaging, genomics, and more. Generalist biomedical artificial intelligence systems that flexibly encode, integrate, and interpret these data might better enable impactful applications ranging from scientific discovery to care delivery.

Methods

To catalyze development of these models, we curated MultiMedBench, a new multimodal biomedical benchmark. MultiMedBench encompasses 14 diverse tasks, such as medical question answering, mammography and dermatology image interpretation, radiology report generation and summarization, and genomic variant calling. We then introduced Med-PaLM Multimodal (Med-PaLM M), our proof of concept for a generalist biomedical AI system that flexibly encodes and interprets biomedical data including clinical language, imaging, and genomics with the same set of model weights. To further probe the capabilities and limitations of Med-PaLM M, we conducted a radiologist evaluation of model-generated (and human) chest x-ray reports.

Results

We observed encouraging performance across model scales. Med-PaLM M reached performance competitive with or exceeding the state of the art on all MultiMedBench tasks, often surpassing specialist models by a wide margin. In a side-by-side ranking on 246 retrospective chest x-rays, clinicians expressed a pairwise preference for Med-PaLM Multimodal reports over those produced by radiologists in up to 40.50% of cases, suggesting potential clinical utility.

Conclusions

Although considerable work is needed to validate these models in real-world cases and understand if cross-modality generalization is possible, our results represent a milestone toward the development of generalist biomedical artificial intelligence systems. (Funded by Alphabet Inc. and/or a subsidiary thereof.).

papers.title: Expert-level vision-language foundation model for real-world radiology and comprehensive evaluation
papers.text: Expert-level vision-language foundation model for real-world radiology and comprehensive evaluation. Radiology is a vital and complex component of modern clinical workflow and covers many tasks. Recently, vision-language (VL) foundation models in medicine have shown potential in processing multimodal information, offering a unified solution for various radiology tasks. However, existing studies either pre-trained VL models on natural data or did not fully integrate vision-language architecture and pretraining, often neglecting the unique multimodal complexity in radiology images and their textual contexts. Additionally, their practical applicability in real-world scenarios remains underexplored. Here, we present RadFound, a large and open-source vision-language foundation model tailored for radiology, that is trained on the most extensive dataset of over 8.1 million images and 250,000 image-text pairs, covering 19 major organ systems and 10 imaging modalities. To establish expert-level multimodal perception and generation capabilities, RadFound introduces an enhanced vision encoder to capture intra-image local features and inter-image contextual information, and a unified cross-modal learning design tailored to radiology. To fully assess the models' capability, we construct a benchmark, RadVLBench, including radiology interpretation tasks like medical vision-language question-answering, as well as text generation tasks ranging from captioning to report generation. We also propose a human evaluation framework. When evaluated on the real-world benchmark involving three representative modalities, 2D images (chest X-rays), multi-view images (mammograms), and 3D images (thyroid CT scans), RadFound significantly outperforms other VL foundation models on both quantitative metrics and human evaluation. In summary, the development of RadFound represents an advancement in radiology generalists, demonstrating broad applicability potential for integration into clinical workflows.

papers.title: How Well Can Modern LLMs Act as Agent Cores in Radiology Environments?
papers.text: How Well Can Modern LLMs Act as Agent Cores in Radiology Environments?. Radiology, with its heterogeneous modalities, anatomies, and evolving protocols, is a natural yet high-stakes testbed for agentic AI. As LLMs grow more capable and tool ecosystems such as MCP and Agent Skills more complex, their capability boundaries in radiology remain unclear. We introduce RadA-BenchPlat, a two-layer benchmark spanning idealized reasoning and real-world execution: a synthetic layer with 2.2k clinician-verified records, 24.2k QA pairs, and 10 tool categories under diverse availability settings; and a real-environment layer pairing 165 2D/3D cases with executable tools for grounding, diagnosis, and report generation. We find that high completion rates under idealized settings do not carry over to real environments, where the best agents trail their upper bound by approximately 15% and drop to 0.327 on long-chain tasks. Prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, multi-agent coordination) and AutoTB (on-the-fly synthesis of missing tools) mitigate execution drift and breakdowns in difficult scenarios, lifting execution success to 94.5%, yet remain not fully reliable. Overall, our findings suggest that radiology agents are no longer limited to conceptual demonstrations, but are beginning to show potential for real-world applications. Project repository: https://github.com/MAGIC-AI4Med/RadABench

papers.title: A Multimodal Biomedical Foundation Model Trained from Fifteen Million Image-Text Pairs.
papers.text:
A Multimodal Biomedical Foundation Model Trained from Fifteen Million Image-Text Pairs..

Background

Biomedical data are inherently multimodal, comprising physical measurements and natural-language narratives. A generalist biomedical artificial intelligence (AI) model needs to simultaneously process different modalities of data, including text and images. Therefore, training an effective generalist biomedical model requires high-quality multimodal data, such as parallel image-text pairs.

Methods

Here, we present PMC-15M, a novel dataset that is two orders of magnitude larger than existing biomedical multimodal datasets, such as MIMIC-CXR, and spans a diverse range of biomedical image types. PMC-15M contains 15 million biomedical image-text pairs collected from 4.4 million scientific articles. Based on PMC-15M, we have pretrained BiomedCLIP, a multimodal foundation model, with domain-specific adaptations tailored to biomedical vision-language processing.

Results

We conducted extensive experiments and ablation studies on standard biomedical imaging tasks from retrieval to classification to visual question answering (VQA). BiomedCLIP achieved new state-of-the-art results in a wide range of standard datasets, substantially outperforming prior approaches. Intriguingly, by large-scale pretraining on diverse biomedical image types, BiomedCLIP even outperforms state-of-the-art radiology-specific models, such as BioViL, in radiology-specific tasks such as Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) pneumonia detection.

Conclusions

BiomedCLIP is a fully open-access foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on various biomedical tasks, paving the way for transformative multimodal biomedical discovery and applications. We release our models at aka.ms/biomedclip to facilitate future research in multimodal biomedical AI.

papers.title: PadChest-GR: A Bilingual Chest X-Ray Dataset for Grounded Radiology Report Generation.
papers.text:
PadChest-GR: A Bilingual Chest X-Ray Dataset for Grounded Radiology Report Generation..

Background

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered radiology report generation (RRG) aims to create free-text radiology reports from clinical imaging. Grounded radiology report generation (GRRG) augments RRG by including the localization of individual findings on the image. Currently, to our knowledge, no manually annotated chest x-ray (CXR) datasets exist on which to train GRRG models.

Methods

In this article, we present a dataset called PadChest-GR (grounded reporting), which is derived from the CXR dataset, PadChest, and aimed at training GRRG models to analyze CXR images. First, we selected a subset of studies from PadChest that contained images with frontal projection; studies that were originally labeled as suboptimal and those involving pediatric patients were excluded. Then, using Generative Pretrained Transformer 4 in Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service, we processed reports to extract sentences with single findings, translate them from Spanish into English, link them to the existing PadChest finding and location labels, and classify the finding progression. A team of 14 radiologists discarded studies with poor image quality or issues relating to the report or findings list and then manually annotated the findings using bounding boxes to surround regions of interest in each image.

Results

We curated a public bilingual dataset of 4555 CXR studies with grounded reports, of which 3099 were abnormal and 1456 were normal. Each report contains complete lists of sentences describing individual present (positive) findings and absent (negative) findings in English and Spanish. In total, PadChest-GR contains 7037 positive-finding sentences and 3422 negative-finding sentences. Every positive-finding sentence is associated with up to two independent sets of bounding boxes labeled by different readers and has categorical labels for finding type, locations, and progression.

Conclusions

PadChest-GR is a manually curated dataset designed to train GRRG models to understand and interpret radiological images and generated text. By including detailed localization and comprehensive annotations of all clinically relevant findings, PadChest-GR provides a valuable resource for developing and evaluating GRRG models from CXR images. (Funded by the Microsoft Corporation.).

papers.title: Structure is Supervision: Multiview Masked Autoencoders for Radiology
papers.text: Structure is Supervision: Multiview Masked Autoencoders for Radiology. Building robust medical machine learning systems requires pretraining strategies that exploit the intrinsic structure present in clinical data. We introduce Multiview Masked Autoencoder (MVMAE), a self-supervised framework that leverages the natural multi-view organization of radiology studies to learn view-invariant and disease-relevant representations. MVMAE combines masked image reconstruction with cross-view alignment, transforming clinical redundancy across projections into a powerful self-supervisory signal. We further extend this approach with MVMAE-V2T, which incorporates radiology reports as an auxiliary text-based learning signal to enhance semantic grounding while preserving fully vision-based inference. Evaluated on a downstream disease classification task on three large-scale public datasets, MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, and PadChest, MVMAE consistently outperforms supervised and vision-language baselines. Furthermore, MVMAE-V2T provides additional gains, particularly in low-label regimes where structured textual supervision is most beneficial. Together, these results establish the importance of structural and textual supervision as complementary paths toward scalable, clinically grounded medical foundation models.

papers.title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
papers.text: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation. Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

papers.title: Comparative reasoning in radiology artificial intelligence: longitudinal and reference-case approaches.
papers.text: Comparative reasoning in radiology artificial intelligence: longitudinal and reference-case approaches.. Artificial intelligence (AI) in radiology remains predominantly examination-centric, whereas clinical interpretation frequently depends on comparison across time or with relevant prior cases. This narrative review examines comparative reasoning in radiology AI through two related but clinically distinct forms: longitudinal reasoning, which compares examinations from the same patient over time, and reference-case reasoning, which uses clinically analogous cases from other patients to support interpretation. We propose a capability hierarchy that distinguishes simple access to comparative information from higher-level capabilities, including selection of relevant historical context, anatomical and lesion-level correspondence, characterization of interval change, temporal-state interpretation, multi-interval trajectory reasoning, and entity-specific assessment of clinical similarity. This distinction matters because providing prior examinations or retrieving visually similar cases does not itself demonstrate meaningful comparative reasoning. We review developments in prior-examination selection, registration, lesion tracking, temporal vision-language modeling, treatment-response assessment, analogous-case retrieval, and longitudinal report generation. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluation strategies that determine whether model performance depends appropriately on clinically relevant comparative information rather than on additional input volume, global image similarity, acquisition characteristics, or other shortcuts. Key challenges include incorrect prior selection, lesion mismatching, temporal inconsistency, clinically irrelevant reference-case retrieval, data leakage, misleading comparative language, and propagation of historical errors. Future progress will require models that preserve entity identity, reason coherently across multi-visit imaging histories, identify clinically informative reference cases, and demonstrate benefit under realistic clinical conditions. Comparative reasoning is therefore a necessary step in the transition from examination-level toward patient-level radiology AI.

papers.title: ESR Essentials: MRI of the scrotum-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology.
papers.text: ESR Essentials: MRI of the scrotum-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology.. While conventional ultrasonography (US) remains the first-line imaging modality for scrotal pathology, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has emerged as a valuable problem-solving tool for indeterminate US findings. Owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast, functional imaging capabilities, and operator independence, mpMRI allows for the precise localization and characterization of scrotal lesions. This paper from the European Society of Urogenital Radiology Scrotal and Penile Imaging Working Group provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of scrotal mpMRI for a general radiologist. It details optimized imaging protocols, recommending a standard sequence of T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and subtracted dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging. The article highlights key clinical indications, including the characterization of intratesticular and paratesticular masses, local staging of testicular germ cell tumors, and differentiation between germ cell and sex cord-stromal neoplasms. This paper familiarizes radiologists with normal MRI appearances and MRI findings of common scrotal diseases. Evidence-based recommendations for reporting basic MRI examinations of the scrotum are also provided. The potential of advanced techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging and proton MR spectroscopy, and the future integration of artificial intelligence and radiomics, are also discussed. We hope the implementation of these recommendations into radiological practice will enhance diagnostic confidence and promote standardized practice in scrotal MRI for radiologists. KEY POINTS: While conventional ultrasound is the first-line modality for scrotal pathology, it can yield inconclusive findings regarding complex mass characterization and local tumor staging. Multiparametric MRI combines anatomical and functional data to accurately characterize scrotal masses, localize impalpable, undescended testes, and provide precise local tumor staging. Scrotal multiparametric MRI serves as a valuable problem-solving tool that enhances diagnostic confidence in sonographically indeterminate cases, prevents unnecessary radical orchiectomies, supports testis-sparing surgery or active surveillance, and standardizes radiological reporting templates to optimize personalized patient management.

papers.title: Development of an Electronic Clinical Quality Measure for Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality in Diagnostic CT in Adults.
papers.text: Development of an Electronic Clinical Quality Measure for Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality in Diagnostic CT in Adults.. The Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality for Diagnostic CT in Adults (ExRad) measure is the first automated radiology outcome measure adopted by CMS. We describe its development, specification, calculation, and adoption. Beginning in 2018, the measure was developed under a CMS cooperative agreement following the Measures Management System Blueprint, with oversight from a multidisciplinary Technical Expert Panel. ExRad evaluates each adult diagnostic CT examination in three steps. First, the examination is assigned to 1 of 19 CT categories defined by anatomic region and clinical indication using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification and Current Procedural Terminology codes. Second, size-adjusted radiation dose and image noise are computed from the DICOM dose report and pixel data; because clinical and radiology data reside in separate systems, translation software inside the hospital firewall performs the linkage and calculations automatically. Third, dose and noise are compared with category-specific thresholds derived from a reader study in which 125 radiologists rated the image quality of 734 CT examinations. An examination is out of range if either value exceeds its threshold, and the measure score is the percentage of eligible examinations that are out of range. Testing across 32 facilities in eight health systems confirmed the availability, accuracy, validity, and reproducibility of all data elements, and the National Quality Forum endorsed the measure in 2021. CMS adopted ExRad in 2023 into hospital inpatient, hospital outpatient, and clinician quality reporting programs, with voluntary reporting beginning in 2025. It is the sole outcome measure in the Diagnostic Radiology MIPS (Merit-Based Incentive Payment System) Value Pathway.

papers.title: RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models.
papers.text:
RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models..

Purpose

Variability in chest X-ray (CXR) reporting hinders training and evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology report generation. Our previous study showed that Structured Radiology Report Generation (SRRG)-style supervision improves VLM-based CXR reporting over free-text supervision. Here, we examine this finding in a larger multi-institutional setting and address a key preprocessing challenge: reliable free-text-to-structured-report conversion using open-source small language models (SLMs).

Methods

We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-3B using free-text and SRRG-style structured supervision across 10 institutions covering 97K samples. We then propose RadStructAgent, an agentic framework that converts free-text CXR reports into structured reports using SLMs, combining LLM-based orchestration, judge feedback, and feedback-guided revision. RadStructAgent is evaluated on 1,000 free-text CXR reports using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.

Results

For the report generation task, structured supervision improves Qwen2.5-VL-3B over free-text supervision, increasing GREEN from 0.494 to 0.539, with similar gains across other clinical metrics. For the structuring task, RadStructAgent improves both clinical quality (GREEN) and anatomy-level assignment (RadFAA): for Qwen3-4B, from 0.844 to 0.867 and 0.883 to 0.891; for Qwen3-8B, from 0.863 to 0.881 and 0.889 to 0.902.

Conclusion

Structured supervision remains effective for VLM-based CXR report generation when evaluated in a larger multi-institutional setting. RadStructAgent shows that open-source SLMs can be strengthened through agentic verification and refinement, providing a resource-efficient approach for offline and privacy-preserving structured report preparation. Our code, prompt templates, and configuration files are publicly available at: https://github.com/badhon1512/RadStructAgent .

papers.title: Evaluation of knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of interventional radiology among the Jordanian population.
papers.text:
Evaluation of knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of interventional radiology among the Jordanian population..

Background

Interventional Radiology (IR) comprises multiple minimally invasive techniques that aid in the diagnosis and treatment of a plethora of conditions. However, some studies worldwide indicate low public awareness, with IR often conflated with Diagnostic Radiology (DR). No prior study has evaluated this knowledge gap in Jordan. This study aims to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of IR among the Jordanian population.

Methods

A cross-sectional, questionnaire-based survey was distributed via social media and convenience sampling. The survey, available in both English and Arabic, assessed demographics, awareness, procedural knowledge, and attitudes toward IR. A total of 429 participants were analyzed using R software. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, and multivariable logistic regression.

Results

Slightly over half (52.2%) of participants had heard of IR. Self-assessed knowledge was low (67.6% "Poor/Very poor"), and 73.9% were confused about the difference between IR and DR. While 72.0% preferred IR over surgery in a hypothetical choice, only 44.1% definitively agreed to undergo an IR procedure when advised. Awareness was significantly lower among females and those in non-medical occupations. High rates of misattribution were observed, with only 18.2% correctly identifying MRI as a DR procedure.

Conclusion

There is a significant public knowledge gap regarding IR in Jordan, creating an "awareness-preference paradox." Despite a theoretical preference for minimally invasive IR treatments, a lack of concrete knowledge hinders real-world acceptance. Targeted educational initiatives are needed to clarify the role of IR and improve the utilization of these therapeutic options.

Plain language summary

Interventional radiology uses minimally invasive procedures guided by medical imaging and can offer an alternative to some types of surgery. This study surveyed people in Jordan to understand their knowledge and views of interventional radiology and related imaging services. This study found that awareness and understanding of interventional radiology were generally low, many people confused it with diagnostic imaging, but most said they would prefer a minimally invasive treatment option. This matters because better public education could help people make informed healthcare decisions and improve access to available treatment options.

papers.title: CT-PrepAgent: Bounded Policy and Controlled Execution for Adaptive CT Data Preparation
papers.text: CT-PrepAgent: Bounded Policy and Controlled Execution for Adaptive CT Data Preparation. Heterogeneous computed tomography (CT) acquisitions and diverse downstream task requirements limit the transferability of fixed data preparation workflows across data sources and tasks. Existing approaches typically rely on manually designed or dataset-specific rules, making it difficult to accommodate changes in acquisition conditions and analytical objectives without manual intervention. Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown promise for automating medical workflows, yet their potential for adaptive CT data preparation remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose CT-PrepAgent, which enables adaptive CT data preparation through a bounded policy and controlled deterministic execution. Deterministic inspection constructs structured data--task profiles, from which a policy decides an eligible DICOM series or predefined preprocessing profile, while the controlled execution flow guards, resolves, executes, and verifies the decision with bounded recovery when enabled and safe quarantine otherwise. Across three public CT segmentation tasks, CT-PrepAgent derived data-task adaptive preprocessing decisions and achieved the highest macro-average Dice. On two private raw-DICOM cohorts, CT-PrepAgent increased verified output yield from 61.7\% to 70.0\% and yielded similar registration metrics on common verified outputs. Controlled fault and replay tests validate bounded recovery, safe quarantine, and policy-free replay under tested fault and drift settings.

papers.title: VLM-Assisted Routing and HU-Traceable DICOM Adaptation for Lumbar CT HU Measurement: A Deployment-Oriented Pilot Technical Evaluation.
papers.text: VLM-Assisted Routing and HU-Traceable DICOM Adaptation for Lumbar CT HU Measurement: A Deployment-Oriented Pilot Technical Evaluation.. Automated lumbar computed tomography (CT) Hounsfield unit (HU) measurement can support opportunistic osteoporosis screening, but heterogeneous Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) inputs often disrupt automated workflows before measurement. We evaluated a local Qwen2.5-VL-7B vision-language model (VLM)-assisted front end for suitability routing, input planning, and HU-traceable DICOM-derived field-of-view/orientation adaptation upstream of an unchanged single-slice lumbar CT HU workflow. The VLM was restricted to routing and planning. In a 20-case FUJIFILM pilot cohort, observed HU output availability was higher with the front-end-assisted route than with direct processing (12/20 versus 5/20), while paired automatic-success cases showed excellent agreement with post hoc manual ImageJ (version 1.54g) measurements (ICC(A,1) = 0.997; MAE = 4.64 HU). Public DICOM stress testing further demonstrated improved workflow robustness across heterogeneous datasets. These findings support the use of a deployment-oriented front-end strategy to improve the auditability and robustness of automated lumbar CT HU measurement while preserving an unchanged downstream measurement workflow.

papers.title: Annotating anatomy and pathology in the National Lung Screening Trial computed tomography images
papers.text: Annotating anatomy and pathology in the National Lung Screening Trial computed tomography images. Large-scale public medical imaging datasets contribute critically to translational research. When accompanied by rich clinical and multi-omics data, they can stimulate exploratory research and enable secondary analyses. Expert annotations of such imaging collections can support the development of new image analysis tools. Continuous enrichment of images with image-derived data makes them more usable for researchers without expertise in image analysis or access to large-scale computational resources. The National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) released a rich longitudinal dataset that includes Computed Tomography (CT) images for over 26,000 patients. We introduce three Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) formatted datasets, complementing NLST CT images, shared as analysis results in the National Cancer Institute Imaging Data Commons (IDC). Two of those (IDC NLSTSeg and IDC NLSTSybil) contain DICOM-harmonized annotations and extracted measurements (for 581 and 601 NLST patients, respectively) shared earlier using research formats (Sybil and NLSTseg). The third one (TotalSegmentator-CT-Segmentations) contains volumetric segmentations generated using TotalSegmentator and radiomics features for each segment for 26,194 NLST patients.

papers.title: Sharing standardized image-derived data in computational pathology using DICOM
papers.text: Sharing standardized image-derived data in computational pathology using DICOM. Development and evaluation of computational pathology methods require access to large and diverse datasets. Over the past decade, various initiatives invested significantly into collecting, centralizing, and sharing pathology imaging data. In contrast, sharing of image-derived data such as region-of-interest delineations or segmentation masks is less well developed. In this work, we describe our approach to encoding and sharing image-derived pathology data in a standardized manner within the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Imaging Data Commons (IDC), a platform that hosts and provides public access to de-identified radiology and pathology data. The IDC relies on the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) standard for data harmonization, yet the adoption of DICOM for pathology image-derived content has remained largely unexplored until now. Here, we present five representative datasets harmonized by conversion from their original representations into DICOM and shared publicly in the IDC. We demonstrate the benefits of this harmonization, describe contributions to critical open-source tooling, and discuss technical considerations relevant to broader adoption of DICOM for pathology image-derived data.

papers.title: Instant3D: A Lightweight Open-Source GUI Frontend for TotalSegmentator-Based Medical Image Segmentation and 3D Reconstruction.
papers.text: Instant3D: A Lightweight Open-Source GUI Frontend for TotalSegmentator-Based Medical Image Segmentation and 3D Reconstruction.. Automatic segmentation is increasingly used in medical imaging, but many tools require command-line operation and environment setup. TotalSegmentator provides open-source multiorgan segmentation for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, yet its routine use may be challenging for nontechnical users. Herein, we describe the design, implementation, and functionality of Instant3D, a lightweight, open-source graphical user interface (GUI) frontend for TotalSegmentator. Instant3D was developed in Python using PyQt6. It accepts DICOM folders, NIfTI files, and NRRD files as input and allows users to select regions of interest (ROIs) through a suggestion-enabled interface. The GUI executes TotalSegmentator as the backend. Default outputs include STL meshes for 3D visualization and NIfTI segmentation images, with optional SVG masks and CSV files containing volumetric measurements. SVG masks are interoperable with SegRef3D for slice-level review and refinement of automated segmentation results. Batch processing is supported. Functionality was tested using representative CT and MRI datasets. Instant3D successfully imported supported formats, executed TotalSegmentator through the GUI, and generated expected outputs, including STL, NIfTI, SVG, and CSV files. Representative datasets demonstrated successful workflow completion and compatibility with SegRef3D. Batch processing generated organized output files for multiple input datasets, confirming workflow feasibility. Instant3D simplifies TotalSegmentator execution and facilitates generation of reusable 3D reconstruction outputs. While not a replacement for comprehensive visualization platforms, it complements them by providing a streamlined workflow for ROI selection, batch processing, and multiformat export. Instant3D may serve as a practical tool for research, education, quantitative imaging, and 3D model generation.

papers.title: End-to-End PET/CT Interpretation and Quantification with an LLM-Orchestrated AI Agent: A Real-World Pilot Study.
papers.text: End-to-End PET/CT Interpretation and Quantification with an LLM-Orchestrated AI Agent: A Real-World Pilot Study.. Although deep learning models have improved individual PET analysis, image processing, and quantification tasks, end-to-end automation from raw DICOM data to quantitative clinical reporting remains limited, particularly in heterogeneous real-world settings. Methods: As a proof-of-concept, an autonomous large language model (LLM)-orchestrated multitool agent for end-to-end PET/CT interpretation was developed. A reasoning-based, text-based LLM selected appropriate series from raw DICOM, coordinated registration and SUV conversion, invoked segmentation and detection tools, generated maximum-intensity projections, called a vision-enabled LLM for interpretation, and synthesized structured draft reports. The system was retrospectively evaluated in 170 patients undergoing baseline [18F]FDG PET/CT for lung cancer staging, with clinical reports serving as the reference standard. Results: The agent successfully completed the full end-to-end workflow from raw DICOM selection to structured draft report generation without human intervention in all 170 examinations. Primary tumor detection achieved 100% sensitivity. For nodal involvement, sensitivity was 84.8% and specificity was 39.4%, whereas distant metastasis detection showed 70.2% sensitivity and 65.0% specificity. Discrepancy analysis of 58 nodal and 57 metastatic mismatch cases revealed systematic false-positive findings related to reactive or physiologic uptake and false-negative findings involving small-volume or anatomically atypical metastases. Conclusion: LLM-orchestrated PET/CT agents enabled workflow-level automation from raw DICOM to quantification and structured draft reporting under real-world conditions. Although primary tumor detection was highly reliable, nodal and metastatic assessment revealed systematic limitations, supporting a collaborative role with continued expert oversight in complex clinical scenarios.

papers.title: MCP-MedImg: Enabling Standardized PACS-AI Integration through the Model Context Protocol
papers.text:
MCP-MedImg: Enabling Standardized PACS-AI Integration through the Model Context Protocol. Abstract

Background: The proliferation of AI-assisted diagnostic models in medical imaging has created a fragmented integration landscape with PACS systems, leading to redundant development, inconsistent security compliance, and disconnected clinical workflows. Most AI diagnostic products exist as standalone Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), limiting scalability, auditability, and clinical adoption. Existing integration solutions (Direct Plugin, DICOM Router, VNA) are point-to-point adaptations without unified semantic layers. While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides tool invocation frameworks for AI agents, it lacks dedicated extensions for the medical imaging domain. Critically, global regulators (FDA, NMPA, EU) are converging on total product life cycle (TPLC) approaches demanding continuous post-market surveillance, yet no standardized protocol supports such surveillance at scale. Objective: We propose MCP-MedImg, an open reference architecture and protocol specification for interoperable integration and governance of AI services in medical imaging ecosystems, allowing AI capabilities to be discovered, invoked, monitored, and governed across heterogeneous healthcare environments without replacing existing PACS infrastructures. Methods: MCP-MedImg extends MCP with a four-layer architecture: Transport (DICOMweb-compatible, with dicom-mcp upward compatibility), Security and Compliance (PHI de-identification plus 14-column audit trail), AI Orchestration (model routing and version management), and Application Semantics (inspection-driven routing, lesion encoding, conditional human-in-the-loop verification). The specification defines six core information model entities and a tiered conformance model (five mandatory requirements, seven optional extensions). A reference implementation based on Orthanc PACS and nnU-Net validates protocol consistency, workflow, multi-model routing, DICOM SR/SEG generation, and audit trails.
