Results: The reference implementation demonstrated end-to-end interoperability, standardized service registration, structured result integration (DICOM SR/SEG), and auditable tracking of AI lifecycle events. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 D, end-to-end latency under realistic clinical conditions was: LIDC-IDRI lung nodule CT (200 volumes, mean 5.4 s, P99 22.6 s) and MSD Heart cardiac MRI (10 volumes, mean 18.2 s, P99 27.6 s, 5-fold ensemble Dice 0.9324). Validation comprised 132 passing tests across 10 verification scenarios.

Conclusions:

MCP-MedImg aims to transform AI-assisted diagnosis from standalone software into auditable, service-oriented capabilities with conditional human-in-the-loop verification—directly addressing the regulatory surveillance gap and establishing foundations for governable public infrastructure in healthcare AI. By defining a tiered conformance model, the protocol enables incremental adoption: from minimal compliance (Level 1) through full production deployment (Level 3). The service-oriented delivery model, with built-in audit trails, configurable verification, and standardized output generation, significantly enhances clinical trust, lowers deployment barriers, and accelerates the adoption of AI-assisted diagnosis in routine clinical practice.

papers.title: M4DTrack: A DICOM-Based Imaging Informatics Workflow for User-Supervised 4DCT Lung Tumor Motion Reporting.
papers.text: M4DTrack: A DICOM-Based Imaging Informatics Workflow for User-Supervised 4DCT Lung Tumor Motion Reporting.. Four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) is routinely used in radiotherapy simulation to evaluate respiration-induced tumor motion, but the motion information is often reviewed visually rather than captured as structured, phase-resolved data. We developed and evaluated M4DTrack, a DICOM-based imaging-informatics workflow for user-supervised 4DCT lung tumor motion analysis and structured, exportable three-dimensional center-of-mass (CoM) motion reporting. M4DTrack imports phase-resolved DICOM CT images, groups images by respiratory phase, displays linked axial/coronal/sagittal views, supports crosshair-based tumor localization and HU inspection, and applies seed or linked 3D-box initialization with sequential phase-to-phase HU-volume propagation. An 8-case lower-lobe lung 4DCT dataset (80 respiratory phases) was analyzed. Directional amplitudes, 3D vector amplitude, maximum phase-wise displacement, and agreement with independent ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were quantified. HU-weighted CoM amplitudes were 2.44 ± 1.44 mm, 2.64 ± 1.37 mm, and 6.04 ± 2.48 mm in X, Y, and Z patient-coordinate directions, respectively. Mean 3D vector amplitude was 7.26 ± 2.50 mm, and mean maximum phase-wise 3D displacement was 6.20 ± 2.10 mm. Biases versus ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were 0.01, - 0.84, and 0.23 mm for X, Y, and Z, respectively, with a 3D vector amplitude bias of - 0.29 mm. M4DTrack provides a user-supervised imaging-informatics bridge between qualitative 4DCT cine review and structured quantitative motion documentation. The pilot results support feasibility for generating exportable, phase-resolved tumor-motion metrics while preserving user-supervised review of 4DCT artifacts, HU-capture uncertainty, adjacent anatomy, and differences between CoM-based and extent-based measurements.

papers.title: Meta-CLIP: Metadata-Conditioned Contrastive Learning for Zero-Shot Disease Inference
papers.text: Meta-CLIP: Metadata-Conditioned Contrastive Learning for Zero-Shot Disease Inference. Medical vision--language pretraining learns transferable representations from paired images and radiology reports, yet differences in scanners and acquisition protocols can impair transfer. Existing approaches primarily enrich clinical semantics, leaving structured acquisition information in DICOM headers underused. We introduce Meta-CLIP, a metadata-conditioned contrastive framework that uses acquisition similarity to reweight cross-modal negatives during pretraining. A kernel over numerical and categorical DICOM fields defines a bounded pairwise margin. This margin increases the contribution of acquisition-similar negatives, emphasizing distinctions among studies that share imaging conditions. The kernel remains fixed during image--text optimization, and inference follows the standard dual-encoder architecture without requiring metadata. We evaluate Meta-CLIP on chest radiography and volumetric chest CT through zero-shot classification, appearance perturbations, grounding, and representation analyses. On CT-RATE, Meta-CLIP improves macro-AUROC over CT-CLIP by 1.41 points, with a 95\% paired bootstrap confidence interval of 0.96--1.85 points. It also achieves the highest macro-AUROC on four of five CXR benchmarks. An exploratory BrgSA evaluation extends the analysis to another CT backbone. These findings support acquisition metadata as a practical training-time prior for medical vision--language learning. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: Boundary-weighted logit consistency improves calibration of segmentation networks.
papers.text: Boundary-weighted logit consistency improves calibration of segmentation networks.. Neural network prediction probabilities and accuracy are often only weakly-correlated. Inherent label ambiguity in training data for image segmentation aggravates such miscalibration. We show that logit consistency across stochastic transformations acts as a spatially varying regularizer that prevents overconfident predictions at pixels with ambiguous labels. Our boundary-weighted extension of this regularizer provides state-of-the-art calibration for prostate and heart MRI segmentation.

papers.title: MATCH: Multi-faceted Adaptive Topo-Consistency for Semi-Supervised Histopathology Segmentation
papers.text: MATCH: Multi-faceted Adaptive Topo-Consistency for Semi-Supervised Histopathology Segmentation.

papers.title: Vessel Segmentation for Fundus Images Based on High-Resolution Networks with Gamma Correction and CLAHE Preprocessing.
papers.text: Vessel Segmentation for Fundus Images Based on High-Resolution Networks with Gamma Correction and CLAHE Preprocessing.. Retinal vessel segmentation plays a crucial role in the early diagnosis and treatment of ophthalmic diseases, yet manual segmentation methods are time-consuming and prone to human error. The increasing demand for automated solutions has led to the exploration of deep learning-based approaches that improve segmentation accuracy and efficiency. However, existing methods often struggle with poor image resolution, a lack of robustness across datasets, and challenges in detecting fine vessel structures, limiting their applicability in large-scale clinical settings. To address these limitations, this study proposes a deep learning-based framework using high-resolution network (HRNet) combined with an advanced preprocessing pipeline, including grayscale conversion, gamma correction, CLAHE, and normalization, to enhance image quality for segmentation. The proposed HRNet-based framework was evaluated on two publicly available datasets, DRIVE and CHASE_DB1. It achieved the highest sensitivity of 0.8193 on DRIVE and the highest specificity of 0.9807 on CHASE_DB1, demonstrating its capability to balance fine vessel detection and false positive reduction. These findings indicate that the proposed framework effectively improves the segmentation accuracy of ophthalmoscope images, enhancing its potential for clinical decision-making in ophthalmology.

papers.title: Intraparotid Facial Nerve Segmentation: A Reproducibility Study of Manual Segmentation on Neurographic Sequences.
papers.text:
Intraparotid Facial Nerve Segmentation: A Reproducibility Study of Manual Segmentation on Neurographic Sequences..

Background and purpose

Preoperative delineation of the intraparotid facial nerve using advanced MR neurography may aid surgical planning of parotid tumors, reducing complications. However, the reliability of manual segmentation for depicting the nerve pathway has not been extensively investigated. This study aimed to assess the reproducibility of manual segmentation of the intraparotid facial nerve on neurographic MRI sequences.

Materials and methods

Neurographic MR data sets from 7 patients with unilateral benign parotid tumors were analyzed using 2 imaging sequences: double-echo steady-state (DESS) and T1 variable flip angle TSE (VFA-TSE) with gadolinium. Two faculty head and neck radiologists and 2 radiology trainees independently segmented the intraparotid facial nerve in both tumorous and healthy glands using 3D Slicer. Given the absence of a measurement standard, segmentation reliability was quantified through mean pair-wise error, interobserver segmentation agreement for anatomic nerve branches, and reliability profiles along the nerve course. Comparisons by imaging sequence, gland status, and radiologist experience were performed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction.

Results

The mean pair-wise error was 1.58 [95% CI: 1.38-2.04] mm for the trunk, 3.20 [95% CI: 2.94-4.50] mm for the inferior division, and 3.58 [95% CI: 2.29-5.99] mm for the superior division. The VFA-TSE sequence showed lower pair-wise segmentation errors than the DESS sequence, particularly for the trunk (1.26 [95% CI: 0.84-2.10] mm vs 1.85 [95% CI: 1.55-2.37] mm), although no comparisons reached statistical significance after correction for multiple testing. Nerve segments near tumors exhibited increased segmentation errors and greater interobserver variability. No significant differences were observed between radiologists of differing experience. The trunk showed high interobserver agreement, whereas peripheral branches displayed lower consistency, more frequent nonsegmentation, and increased subdivision instances.

Conclusions

Manual segmentation of the intraparotid facial nerve is reproducible for the trunk but remains challenging for peripheral branches. VFA-TSE may offer an advantage over DESS for trunk delineation, whereas radiologist experience level does not appear to limit segmentation reliability. Standardized segmentation protocols can mitigate the impact of prior experience, but imaging sequence choice may influence segmentation reproducibility. Further research should refine the neurographic sequence and explore automated segmentation techniques to improve consistency in presurgical planning of parotid tumors.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Segmentation of Peritoneal Cancer Index Regions from CT Imaging
papers.text: Deep Learning-Based Segmentation of Peritoneal Cancer Index Regions from CT Imaging. Peritoneal metastases (PM) are staged using the surgically determined Peritoneal Cancer Index (sPCI), which requires invasive laparoscopic assessment. Although CT is routinely used for preoperative evaluation, imaging-based assessment of PM extent remains challenging and is often less structured than surgical PCI scoring. A recent consensus study defined radiological PCI (rPCI) regions for cross-sectional imaging. We present the first deep learning approach to automatically segment 13 rPCI regions on CT. 62 contrast-enhanced CT scans were retrospectively collected across the full PCI range. Each scan was annotated into non-overlapping rPCI regions by one researcher, reviewed by a second, with disagreements resolved by a radiologist. Using five-fold cross-validation, we compared nnU-Net and Swin UNETR with Dice, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) and Average Surface Distance (ASD). We introduce an anatomically constrained pipeline that trains on merged super-regions and splits them during post-processing using TotalSegmentator landmarks at the hips and the ligament of Treitz. On this 62-scan cohort, the baseline nnU-Net reached an overall Dice of 0.81 and outperformed Swin UNETR (0.76). The proposed pipeline improved the overall Dice to 0.84 and reduced boundary error (HD95 13.7 to 11.8 mm; ASD 4.1 to 3.4 mm), with the largest gains in the small-bowel regions, approaching the interobserver Dice of 0.87. Automated rPCI region segmentation on CT is feasible and approaches interobserver agreement. Encoding anatomical boundary constraints substantially improves segmentation quality in the most challenging regions. This provides a reproducible foundation for non-invasive, imaging-based PCI assessment. The main limitations are the single-center cohort and the small interobserver subset.

papers.title: From Convolution to Transformer: A Comparative Study of U-Net Variants for Brain Tumor and Retinal Vessel Segmentation
papers.text: From Convolution to Transformer: A Comparative Study of U-Net Variants for Brain Tumor and Retinal Vessel Segmentation. Medical image segmentation plays an important role in computer aided diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. U-Net has been widely used for biomedical image segmentation because of its encoder decoder structure and skip connections. However, conventional convolution based U-Net models may have limited ability to capture long range dependencies and global contextual information, which can affect performance in complex segmentation tasks. This paper presents a comparative study of five U-Net based architectures: U-Net 3D, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin UNETR. The models are evaluated on two benchmark datasets: BraTS 2023 for brain tumor segmentation and DRIVE for retinal vessel segmentation. Experimental results show that Swin UNETR achieves the best overall performance, with Dice scores of 0.8965 on BraTS 2023 and 0.8078 on DRIVE. The results suggest that transformer based U-Net variants are effective for segmentation tasks requiring global contextual modeling, while residual learning remains useful for fine structure segmentation. This study provides practical insights into model selection for medical image segmentation across volumetric MRI and retinal imaging tasks.

papers.title: Segmentation Confidence for Arbitrary CNNs
papers.text: Segmentation Confidence for Arbitrary CNNs. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used for medical image segmentation. However, they lack an inherent measure of confidence. Existing methods for estimating prediction uncertainty often require a custom network architecture and/or dedicated training setups and need to be trained from scratch. In addition, the deduction of a single confidence score per input from the uncertainty maps is not always straightforward. In this study, we explore voxel-based uncertainty estimation methods that can be added to existing segmentation pipelines without training from scratch. We also propose a novel method to estimate a single confidence score from the uncertainty maps. Our evaluations on different ROIs and modalities suggest that our confidence score can predict segmentation performance in unseen data.

papers.title: Development and evaluation of automated organ segmentation models for abdominal ultrasound in injured children
papers.text:
Development and evaluation of automated organ segmentation models for abdominal ultrasound in injured children. BackgroundAccurate organ segmentation in pediatric focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) is an important prerequisite for automated image analysis and image quality assessment, but manual segmentation is time-intensive, subject to inter- and intra-observer variability, and limits the scalability of deep learning dataset development. Although deep learning has shown promise for ultrasound organ segmentation, its application to pediatric FAST has not been evaluated.

ObjectiveTo describe the development and evaluation of deep learning models to automatically localize and segment six abdominal organs in pediatric FAST.

MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study using a convenience sample of archived FAST examinations from 200 injured children evaluated at a Level I pediatric trauma center. Emergency ultrasound fellowship-trained physicians manually segmented six key abdominal organs. Annotated image-mask pairs were split into training and test sets in an 80:20 ratio. We developed or fine-tuned U-Net, EVIT U-Net, UltraSAM, and nnU-Net models to automatically segment the bladder, kidney, liver, spleen, spine, and diaphragm. Segmentation accuracy was assessed using the Dice-Sorensen Coefficient (DSC) compared with manual annotations. Pediatric emergency ultrasound experts reviewed previously unlabeled FAST clips and rated the acceptability of model-generated organ masks.

ResultsThe dataset included 1,807 manually annotated image-mask pairs from 200 pediatric FAST clips. Using an 80:20 split with no overlap between video clips, 1,446 image-mask pairs were used for training and 361 for testing. Across all models and organs, mean DSC was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75-0.84). Mean DSC was highest for the kidney and bladder, each 0.91 (95% CI: 0.87-0.95), and lowest for the diaphragm at 0.63 (95% CI: 0.60-0.67). EVIT U-Net achieved the highest DSC for kidney, liver, and spleen, performed comparably to the highest-performing models for bladder, and had a mean inference time of 54 milliseconds per image. In previously unlabeled pediatric FAST clips, experts rated model-generated organ masks as acceptable for localization in 73%-95% of clips across organs.

ConclusionWe describe the automatic segmentation of key abdominal organs in pediatric FAST with limited annotated data. This represents an important advancement in our image processing pipeline and can accelerate the development of large, robust datasets with segmentation for anatomy and pathology. Experts found that model-generated masks provided acceptable localization in most previously unlabeled pediatric clips, supporting the potential use of automated segmentation in pediatric FAST image analysis.

papers.title: How reliable is deep learning segmentation of the infant brain? Variability and failure analysis of segmentation pipelines under a common protocol in 51 infants aged 1 to 9 months
papers.text:
How reliable is deep learning segmentation of the infant brain? Variability and failure analysis of segmentation pipelines under a common protocol in 51 infants aged 1 to 9 months. Abstract

Background Deep learning segmentation increasingly supplies the brain volumes used in infant neuroimaging, yet pipelines are usually ranked by a single mean Dice score, which hides variability and rare failures. Objective To quantify how much of the apparent difference between infant brain MRI segmentation pipelines reflects retraining variability, cross-validation partitioning, aggregation choice and rare failures, and to derive a reporting template for validating such tools. Materials and methods Four pipelines (nnU-Net, 3D TransUNet, Swin UNETR, 2.5D STSNet) and a cross-fitted consensus were trained and evaluated on the public Baby Open Brains dataset (71 T1 and T2-weighted MRI visits from 51 infants aged 1.0 to 9.4 months, 31 expert-corrected labels) with subject-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, subject-weighted summaries and Holm-corrected paired tests. Results Mean Dice was 0.8867 (95% confidence interval 0.8802–0.8932) for the consensus, 0.8805 for TransUNet, 0.8772 for Swin UNETR, 0.8722 for nnU-Net and 0.7868 for STSNet. Among the 3D pipelines the pipeline term explained 0.134% of Dice variation (𝑝 = 0.177), all paired effects were small (|𝑑| ≤ 0.22) and every mean-difference confidence interval included zero. TransUNet exceeded Swin UNETR in 46 of 51 infants; for nnU-Net versus Swin UNETR the mean (−0.0050) and median (+0.0072) disagreed in sign. Fold-level differences (−0.0490 to +0.0169) exceeded retraining standard deviations (0.0005–0.0016). Two scans drove the reversal and most failures; the consensus produced none. Conclusion Three competently configured 3D pipelines segmented the infant brain accurately with small mutual differences and no detected age dependence. Choosing among them mattered less than reporting variability and failures; a simple consensus removed all failures.

papers.title: Automatic generation of training data from dual-energy CT scans: a new approach to train renal vessel segmentation models.
papers.text:
Automatic generation of training data from dual-energy CT scans: a new approach to train renal vessel segmentation models..

Objective

To investigate the feasibility of automatic training data generation using virtual non-contrast (VNC) images of dual-energy CT and to evaluate the performance of medical segmentation models trained on auto-generated data.

Methods

Training images were generated from contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scans using VNC algorithm. Corresponding training labels were generated from iodine-density images via intensity thresholding. The paired VNC images and labels constituted the dataset (791 cases in total) for training non-enhanced CT (NECT) segmentation models. We attempted to train segmentation models with VNC images alone, as well as the combination of VNC and real NECT images.

Results

Models trained with auto-generated data effectively performed renal vein segmentation on NECT images, achieving Dice score of 69.60%. It identified 100% (70/70) vein main trunks and 54.5% (6/11) accessory veins in the test set. The models' performance on artery segmentation was not satisfactory, with Dice score of 44.56%. It only identified 41.4% (29/70) artery main trunks and 4.54% (1/22) accessory arteries. However, the combination of generated data and labeled data greatly improved model's artery Dice to 71.23%. Combined model identified 100% (70/70) vein main trunks, 98.6% (69/70) artery main trunks, 68.2% (15/22) accessory arteries and 63.6% (7/11) accessory veins. Its accessory artery detection is significantly higher than the model trained with labeled data (15/22 vs. 5/22, p < 0.01), closing the gap with human radiologist (15/22 vs. 18/22, p = 0.250).

Conclusion

VNC and Iodine-density images can be utilized to automatically generate training data for segmentation models. This pipeline shows promise for training segmentation models on NECT images.

papers.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.text: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

papers.title: Benchmarking Classification Tasks of Chest X-ray AI Across Multinational Public and Private Datasets: a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study
papers.text: Benchmarking Classification Tasks of Chest X-ray AI Across Multinational Public and Private Datasets: a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study. Chest X-ray (CXR) AI models are increasingly proposed for triage, screening, and rule-out, where the operating point is fixed to miss few abnormalities. Most evaluations instead report threshold-free discrimination on a few public benchmarks, leaving clinically usable performance and generalisability to unseen institutional cohorts poorly characterised. We retrospectively evaluated 10 published CXR classification models on 12 datasets from six countries: seven public benchmarks and five institutional cohorts from China, Japan, and Germany. Models spanned convolutional networks, vision-language models, a question-answering foundation model, and a repurposed encoder. Only image-level classification was assessed; segmentation, detection, and report generation were out of scope. Source labels were harmonised to a common vocabulary. The primary outcome was specificity at 95% sensitivity; PPV at 95% sensitivity and AUROC were secondary outcomes. Estimates weighted each diagnostic task equally, with 95% CIs. MAVL and MedKLIP had the highest overall specificity at 95% sensitivity (0.37 [95% CI 0.31-0.44] and 0.37 [0.30-0.44]) and kept that ranking on tasks evaluable for every model. Their PPV was 0.18 (0.13-0.24) and 0.19 (0.13-0.25): most flagged examinations would be false positives. Specificity was lower on institutional cohorts than on public benchmarks for most models, by 0.13 for MAVL, 0.15 for DenseNet, and 0.09 for MedKLIP. No model was best for every finding, country, lesion extent, or prevalence stratum; specificity fell from 0.34 for diffuse to 0.15 for focal findings. At 95% sensitivity, the best current models clear only about a third of truly negative examinations, and public-benchmark performance overstates what they achieve on unseen institutional data. Operating-point-aware evaluation and external validation on institutional cohorts should precede deployment.

papers.title: PadChest-GR: A Bilingual Chest X-Ray Dataset for Grounded Radiology Report Generation.
papers.text:
PadChest-GR: A Bilingual Chest X-Ray Dataset for Grounded Radiology Report Generation..

Background

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered radiology report generation (RRG) aims to create free-text radiology reports from clinical imaging. Grounded radiology report generation (GRRG) augments RRG by including the localization of individual findings on the image. Currently, to our knowledge, no manually annotated chest x-ray (CXR) datasets exist on which to train GRRG models.

Methods

In this article, we present a dataset called PadChest-GR (grounded reporting), which is derived from the CXR dataset, PadChest, and aimed at training GRRG models to analyze CXR images. First, we selected a subset of studies from PadChest that contained images with frontal projection; studies that were originally labeled as suboptimal and those involving pediatric patients were excluded. Then, using Generative Pretrained Transformer 4 in Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service, we processed reports to extract sentences with single findings, translate them from Spanish into English, link them to the existing PadChest finding and location labels, and classify the finding progression. A team of 14 radiologists discarded studies with poor image quality or issues relating to the report or findings list and then manually annotated the findings using bounding boxes to surround regions of interest in each image.

Results

We curated a public bilingual dataset of 4555 CXR studies with grounded reports, of which 3099 were abnormal and 1456 were normal. Each report contains complete lists of sentences describing individual present (positive) findings and absent (negative) findings in English and Spanish. In total, PadChest-GR contains 7037 positive-finding sentences and 3422 negative-finding sentences. Every positive-finding sentence is associated with up to two independent sets of bounding boxes labeled by different readers and has categorical labels for finding type, locations, and progression.

Conclusions

PadChest-GR is a manually curated dataset designed to train GRRG models to understand and interpret radiological images and generated text. By including detailed localization and comprehensive annotations of all clinically relevant findings, PadChest-GR provides a valuable resource for developing and evaluating GRRG models from CXR images. (Funded by the Microsoft Corporation.).

papers.title: PromptForSegCXR: Prompt-Driven Multi-Organ and Multi-Disease Segmentation in Chest X-rays using a Multi-stage Fusion Mechanism
papers.text: PromptForSegCXR: Prompt-Driven Multi-Organ and Multi-Disease Segmentation in Chest X-rays using a Multi-stage Fusion Mechanism. Image segmentation is central to automated medical image analysis, enabling precise identification of anatomical structures and pathological regions. Conventional segmentation models typically target a single organ or disease, limiting their adaptability across clinical scenarios. While multi-organ and multi-disease segmentation has been explored, building such datasets requires extensive manual annotation by medical experts. Prompt-driven segmentation offers a flexible, user-guided alternative that speeds up annotation, yet no prior work has addressed prompt-based interactive segmentation across multiple organs and diseases in chest X-rays. This study makes two main contributions. First, we introduce a novel dataset of expert-designed doodle prompts spanning 23 classes (six organs and seventeen diseases), curated from multiple public chest X-ray datasets for prompt-driven segmentation. Second, we propose PromptForSegCXR, a lightweight dual-input segmentation framework that combines the chest X-ray with user-provided doodle prompts to accurately segment diverse anatomical and pathological regions. The model uses a multi-stage feature fusion strategy to integrate spatial and semantic representations, along with a depthwise-pointwise-residual convolution block with squeeze-and-excitation attention for efficient hierarchical feature extraction and adaptive recalibration. Experimental results show the model achieves a Dice score of 81.62 percent on the full dataset, outperforming SAM-based prompt segmentation models by up to 10 percent and conventional segmentation architectures by up to 23 percent, while remaining lightweight. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for accurate, flexible, prompt-driven chest X-ray segmentation.

papers.title: Faithful, Interpretable Chest X-ray Diagnosis with Artifact-free B-cos Networks
papers.text: Faithful, Interpretable Chest X-ray Diagnosis with Artifact-free B-cos Networks. Faithfulness and interpretability are essential for deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical domains such as medical image analysis. B-cos networks modify the parameterization of convolutional and classification layers to measure class evidence via feature-weight alignment, enabling built-in, class-specific contribution maps without post-hoc explanations. While maintaining diagnostic performance competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs, standard B-cos networks exhibit severe aliasing artifacts in their explanation maps, rendering them unsuitable for clinical use, where clarity is essential. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing anti-aliasing strategies using ASAP and BlurPool (BP) to significantly improve explanation quality. Our experiments on chest X-ray datasets demonstrate that the modified $\text{B-cos}_\mathrm{ASAP}$ and $\text{B-cos}_\mathrm{BP}$ preserve strong predictive performance while providing faithful and artifact-free explanations suitable for clinical application in multi-class and multi-label settings. Code is available at: https://github.com/shrebox/Artifact-free-B-cos-Networks.

papers.title: Eyes on the Image: Gaze Supervised Multimodal Learning for Chest X-ray Diagnosis and Report Generation
papers.text: Eyes on the Image: Gaze Supervised Multimodal Learning for Chest X-ray Diagnosis and Report Generation. Medical vision-language models still struggle to match radiologists' attention and to verbalize findings with explicit spatial grounding. We address this gap with a two-stage multimodal framework for chest X-ray interpretation built on the MIMIC-Eye dataset. In the first stage introduces a gaze-token classifier that fuses image patches, bounding-box masks, transcription embeddings, and radiologist fixations. A curriculum-scheduled, trust-calibrated composite loss supervises the gaze token, boosting both accuracy and spatial alignment. Adding fixation supervision raises AUC 4.4% and F1 13.3%, and Pearson correlation rises to 0.306, confirming clinically relevant focus. In stage 2, classifier predictions are translated into region-specific diagnostic sentences. Confidence-weighted keywords are extracted, mapped to 17 thoracic regions through an expert dictionary, and expanded with a prompted large language model, boosting clinical-term BERTScore and ROUGE scores over keyword baselines. All components are toggle-able for ablation, and the full pipeline is reproducible, offering a new benchmark for interpretable, gaze-aware chest-X-ray analysis. Integrating eye-tracking signals demonstrably enhances both diagnostic accuracy and the transparency of generated reports.

papers.title: RadJEPA: Radiology Encoder for Chest X-Rays via Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture
papers.text: RadJEPA: Radiology Encoder for Chest X-Rays via Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture. Vision-language pretraining has driven progress in medical image representation learning, but it depends on paired image-text data and can inherit reporting bias from clinical narratives. We study whether language-free predictive pretraining can produce an image encoder that transfers effectively to radiology report generation. RadJEPA is a chest-X-ray adaptation of I-JEPA, pretrained on approximately 840K unlabeled radiographs using latent context-to-target prediction. Our primary contribution is an extensive empirical evaluation of this language-free encoder for report generation: the frozen image encoder is coupled to a trainable two-layer projector and language decoder, and is also substituted into four established vision-language backbones. Across MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, RadJEPA matches or exceeds the evaluated image-only and image-text baselines on lexical, entity-relation, and clinical-label metrics. Controlled MIMIC-only comparisons provide evidence that the predictive objective contributes beyond domain-specific pretraining, while broader comparisons also reflect differences in pretraining data, model capacity, and input resolution. Complementary classification and segmentation experiments assess transfer beyond report generation.

papers.title: Can saliency maps flag chest radiograph classifier errors at a new hospital? An external validation study
papers.text: Can saliency maps flag chest radiograph classifier errors at a new hospital? An external validation study. Saliency maps are offered as a safeguard for medical image classifiers, but whether they reveal individual errors at a new hospital remains largely untested. We trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and at two external sites, in the USA and Vietnam, with radiologist-consensus labels. We scored each explanation by its anatomical enrichment, the area-normalized concentration of attribution in a segmented thoracic region, and tested whether it detects errors beyond the model's confidence. Grad-CAM localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888). Adding enrichment to a confidence-based error detector calibrated at the training hospital never raised its area under the curve by more than 0.011, and for the convolutional network the relation between enrichment and correctness reversed between hospitals, degrading the transferred detector. Model confidence, not saliency, should anchor deployment monitoring.

papers.title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images
papers.text: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images. We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.

papers.title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
papers.text: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification. Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

papers.title: Expert Perspectives on Transparency and Trust in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis: Qualitative Study.
papers.text:
Expert Perspectives on Transparency and Trust in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis: Qualitative Study..

Background

The integration of AI-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (AI-CDSS) into clinical practice has expanded rapidly, particularly in medical imaging. Beyond algorithmic performance, growing evidence suggests that clinicians' engagement with AI-CDSS is shaped by how transparently systems communicate their outputs, and how trust is formed through human-AI interaction. However, a limited understanding of how these concepts are perceived by end users and developers continues to hinder real-world implementation.

Objective

This study aims to explore expert perspectives on transparency and trust in AI-CDSS for chest X-ray diagnosis, with a focus on the two-dimensional lens: user interface and users' mental models.

Methods

A qualitative study was conducted using semistructured interviews with a total of 21 experts, including 11 radiologists and 10 AI experts experienced in AI-CDSS. Data were analyzed thematically to explore factors perceived to influence transparent communication and trust.

Results

Three themes emerged: (1) perspective of transparency and trust, (2) user interface, and (3) users' mental models. Findings reveal that trust is a dynamic calibration process developed through repeated use, feedback loops, and alignment with clinicians' mental models, rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. Significant discrepancies were identified between how developers design system transparency and how clinicians interpret AI outputs.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates that transparency and trust are achieved through interpretable outputs, clear communication of system limitations, and alignment with clinical workflows. Designing trustworthy AI-CDSS requires integrating transparent interface design with consideration of users' knowledge, experience, and attitudes to support effective human-AI interaction.

papers.title: RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models.
papers.text:
RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models..

Purpose

Variability in chest X-ray (CXR) reporting hinders training and evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology report generation. Our previous study showed that Structured Radiology Report Generation (SRRG)-style supervision improves VLM-based CXR reporting over free-text supervision. Here, we examine this finding in a larger multi-institutional setting and address a key preprocessing challenge: reliable free-text-to-structured-report conversion using open-source small language models (SLMs).

Methods

We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-3B using free-text and SRRG-style structured supervision across 10 institutions covering 97K samples. We then propose RadStructAgent, an agentic framework that converts free-text CXR reports into structured reports using SLMs, combining LLM-based orchestration, judge feedback, and feedback-guided revision. RadStructAgent is evaluated on 1,000 free-text CXR reports using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.

Results

For the report generation task, structured supervision improves Qwen2.5-VL-3B over free-text supervision, increasing GREEN from 0.494 to 0.539, with similar gains across other clinical metrics. For the structuring task, RadStructAgent improves both clinical quality (GREEN) and anatomy-level assignment (RadFAA): for Qwen3-4B, from 0.844 to 0.867 and 0.883 to 0.891; for Qwen3-8B, from 0.863 to 0.881 and 0.889 to 0.902.

Conclusion

Structured supervision remains effective for VLM-based CXR report generation when evaluated in a larger multi-institutional setting. RadStructAgent shows that open-source SLMs can be strengthened through agentic verification and refinement, providing a resource-efficient approach for offline and privacy-preserving structured report preparation. Our code, prompt templates, and configuration files are publicly available at: https://github.com/badhon1512/RadStructAgent .

papers.title: FASA-Net: A Frequency-Domain-Enhanced and Anatomically Constrained Vision-Language Framework for Automated Chest X-ray Report Generation.
papers.text: FASA-Net: A Frequency-Domain-Enhanced and Anatomically Constrained Vision-Language Framework for Automated Chest X-ray Report Generation.. Automated radiology report generation can reduce radiologists' workloads by producing preliminary reports from medical images. However, generating chest X-ray reports remains challenging. Subtle lesions and organ boundaries may be underrepresented, visual regions may be poorly aligned with medical terminology, and long reports require coherent clinical descriptions. To address these challenges, we propose FASA-Net, a vision-language framework that combines frequency-domain enhancement with anatomical semantic constraints. Its Frequency-Domain Pyramid Attention Network (FPAN) integrates frequency-domain analysis and a multiscale feature pyramid to enhance local structures and high-frequency visual details. The Anatomical Semantic Constraint Attention (ASCA) module guides cross-modal interactions between visual regions and anatomy-related terms to reduce the risk of regional misalignment and semantic hallucination. The Context Aggregation Module (CAM) incorporates a summary of the text generated so far into decoding to improve coherence and terminological consistency. Experiments on the public IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR datasets show competitive performance on natural language generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, together with improved clinical label consistency measured using CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics. Ablation studies, visualizations, and case studies further illustrate the contributions of FPAN, ASCA, and CAM to visual detail enhancement, anatomical semantic alignment, and contextual aggregation. FASA-Net therefore has potential as an auxiliary tool for chest X-ray report generation, although clinical deployment requires further validation using multicenter data, radiologist assessments, and prospective studies.

papers.title: AI-Enhanced Super-Resolution Handheld Ultrasound for Carotid Plaque Detection in Community Screening
papers.text: AI-Enhanced Super-Resolution Handheld Ultrasound for Carotid Plaque Detection in Community Screening.

papers.title: Interpretable Prostate Cancer Detection using a Small Cohort of MRI Images
papers.text: Interpretable Prostate Cancer Detection using a Small Cohort of MRI Images. Prostate cancer is a leading cause of mortality in men, yet interpretation of T2-weighted prostate MRI remains challenging due to subtle and heterogeneous lesions. We developed an interpretable framework for automatic cancer detection using a small dataset of 162 T2-weighted images (102 cancer, 60 normal), addressing data scarcity through transfer learning and augmentation. We performed a comprehensive comparison of Vision Transformers (ViT, Swin), CNNs (ResNet18), and classical methods (Logistic Regression, SVM, HOG+SVM). Transfer-learned ResNet18 achieved the best performance (90.9% accuracy, 95.2% sensitivity, AUC 0.905) with only 11M parameters, while Vision Transformers showed lower performance despite substantially higher complexity. Notably, HOG+SVM achieved comparable accuracy (AUC 0.917), highlighting the effectiveness of handcrafted features in small datasets. Unlike state-of-the-art approaches relying on biparametric MRI (T2+DWI) and large cohorts, our method achieves competitive performance using only T2-weighted images, reducing acquisition complexity and computational cost. In a reader study of 22 cases, five radiologists achieved a mean sensitivity of 67.5% (Fleiss Kappa = 0.524), compared to 95.2% for the AI model, suggesting potential for AI-assisted screening to reduce missed cancers and improve consistency. Code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: Preliminary Study on Stromal Nodule Detection Using B-Mode Ultrasound Images and Deep Learning.
papers.text: Preliminary Study on Stromal Nodule Detection Using B-Mode Ultrasound Images and Deep Learning.. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a common condition among aging men. Currently, transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS) is used for detecting BPH but frequently falls short in accuracy. In this study, we investigated the use of a deep learning network for stromal nodule detection in prostate specimens exhibiting BPH using B-mode ultrasound (US) imaging. B-mode US data was captured from ex-vivo prostate specimens of human patients. Expert annotations differentiating between stromal and non-stromal regions for each prostate specimen were correlated with corresponding B-mode data and used as the reference for validation. The Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) network was trained and applied to segment stromal versus non-stromal tissue within B-mode ultrasound images. An 80/20 patient-level train/test split was used to evaluate model performance. Preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of using SAM2 to identify stromal nodules directly from B-mode ultrasound data, achieving a Dice score of 0.76. Ongoing work focuses on increasing the dataset and improving segmentation accuracy. The study provides an approach to validate the capability of ultrasound imaging for BPH detection. More image data are needed to improve the segmentation performance.

papers.title: Computer-Assisted Detection (CADe) of colonic polyps during colonoscopy reduces cancer-related healthcare costs - a single Singaporean institution cost effectiveness analysis.
papers.text:
Computer-Assisted Detection (CADe) of colonic polyps during colonoscopy reduces cancer-related healthcare costs - a single Singaporean institution cost effectiveness analysis..

Background and aims

Colonoscopy remains as an invaluable diagnostic and therapeutic tool used for the screening and evaluation of colonic pathologies. Periodic endoscopic screening allowing for early detection and removal of pre-malignant lesions, resulting in significant overall decreased incidence and mortality from colorectal cancer. Despite its added costs, artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly utilized in the field of endoscopy, boasting benefits of improving adenoma detection rates while reducing endoscopists' mental fatigue intra-procedurally. As such, further evaluation of the financial impact of such AI-usage in screening colonoscopies was performed to assess if routine use of AI-guidance in screening colonoscopies was justifiable.

Methods

This study conducted a cost effectiveness analysis of the GI Genius™ CADx Intelligent Endoscopy Module (US-DG-2000309, 2021 Medtronic) system in our local Singaporean tertiary public healthcare institution. A decision tree model was used to calculate Incremental Cost Effectiveness Ratio (ICER), comparing cancer-related costs for patients who underwent conventional colonoscopy versus colonoscopy with AI guidance.

Results

With a calculated ICER value of 0.72, our study suggests that AI-assisted colonoscopy was indeed cost effective. Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY) values derived for each subgroup of patients further demonstrated overall improved quality of life reported by patients who underwent AI-assisted colonoscopy, as compared to conventional colonoscopy.

Conclusion

Our study supports the incorporation of AI guidance into routine colonoscopic evaluation in view of increased cost effectiveness and improved overall quality of life achieved. However, further studies and analysis must be undertaken before reliably determining the cost-effectiveness of AI on regional or international scales.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Lesion Segmentation Models
papers.text: Rethinking Evaluation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Lesion Segmentation Models. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease that can significantly reduce the quality of life of a patient. Existing treatment options can only help slow down the progression of the disease. Therefore, early detection and precise monitoring of disease progression are important. Deep learning offers state-of-the-art models for detecting and segmenting MS lesions in brain MRI scans. However, most of these models are evaluated using the Dice score, without accounting for lesion-wise detection and segmentation performance or other metrics that quantify model performance in cases that are complex or confusing for human annotators, or in cases that are essential for disease detection and progression monitoring. In this paper, we highlight the need to rethink the evaluation of MS lesion segmentation models. In this context, we first present problem fingerprinting in detail to highlight what neurologists look for in brain MRI scans for MS detection and progression monitoring, and which metrics are required to properly quantify model performance in these contexts. Additionally, we present an analysis of state-of-the-art models on two open-source datasets using these metrics to highlight their usability for real-world deployment in hospitals.

papers.title: Prediction of Rectal Cancer Regrowth from Longitudinal Endoscopy
papers.text: Prediction of Rectal Cancer Regrowth from Longitudinal Endoscopy. Clinical trial studies indicate benefit of watch-and-wait (WW) surveillance for patients with rectal cancer showing a complete or near clinical response (CR) directly after treatment (restaging). However, there are no objectively accurate methods to early detect local tumor regrowth (LR) in patients undergoing WW from follow-up exams. Hence, we developed Temporal Rectal Endoscopy Cross-attention (TREX), a longitudinal deep learning approach that combines pairs of images acquired at restaging and follow-up to distinguish CR from LR. TREX uses pretrained Swin Transformers in a siamese setting to extract features from longitudinal images and dual cross-attention to combine the features without spatial co-registration between image pairs. TREX and Swin-based baselines were trained under two settings: (a) detecting LR or CR at the last available follow-up and (b) early detection of LR at 3--6, 6--12, and 12--24 months before clinical confirmation. TREX achieved the highest accuracy in detecting LR with a high sensitivity of 97% $\pm$ 6% and a balanced accuracy of 90% $\pm$ 3%, and outperformed all baselines in early detection at both 3--6 (74% $\pm$ 1%) and 6--12 months (62% $\pm$ 4%) prior to clinical detection. Clinical validation via a surgeon survey showed that TREX matched attending-level overall accuracy (TREX: 86.21% vs.\ Clinicians: 87.84% $\pm$ 1.28%). Finally, we explored TREX's ability to predict treatment response by combining pre-treatment (pre-TNT) and restaging endoscopies, achieving a balanced accuracy of 73% $\pm$ 12%. These results show that longitudinal deep learning analysis of endoscopy may improve surveillance and enable earlier identification of rectal cancer regrowth.

papers.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Identify Oropharyngeal Cancer During Fiberoptic Endoscopy.
papers.text:
Using Artificial Intelligence to Identify Oropharyngeal Cancer During Fiberoptic Endoscopy..

Objective

Oropharyngeal tumors with a propensity for submucosal spread can be difficult to detect and delineate during endoscopy. To facilitate their detection, we developed an Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithm to segment tumors and other anatomically significant structures within the oropharynx.

Study design

Model development and validation study.

Setting

Tertiary academic medical center.

Methods

We collected videos from 106 patients undergoing pharyngolaryngoscopy, extracted 942 images, and annotated each pixel as one of 12 classes, such as tumor, uvula, and healthy mucosa. We trained an AI algorithm and evaluated its performance in multiclass and tumor-based segmentation.

Results

The AI algorithm achieved a recall statistic of 0.93 and a Dice score of 0.79 for tumor detection. High Dice scores were observed for pharyngeal mucosa (0.90), epiglottis (0.88), and vocal cords (0.82).

Conclusions

This study demonstrates that AI can semantically segment all the structures visualized during endoscopy, paving the way for computer-assisted systems for tumor identification and computer-assisted navigation during endoscopy or intubation.

papers.title: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers
papers.text: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers. T1-T2 correlation MRI has strong potential to quantify microstructural compartments without imposing a biological model. Traditionally, full T1-T2 spectra per voxel are reconstructed with an ill-conditioned and time-consuming Inverse Laplace Transform. We propose to view this challenge as an object detection task: A Detection Transformer (DETR) takes 64 TI/TE signals and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2, and signal fraction. We achieve a mean average precision mAP@10 of 76.8% on simulated data, outperforming both our previous model design (53.8%) and regularized NNLS (66.1%). We show that our DETR approach outperforms NNLS in almost every setting across compartment count, compartmental signal fraction, and SNR. Reconstruction is orders of magnitude faster than NNLS. The results are fully reproducible from our public code: github.com/SebastianEndtTHI/t1t2-detr

papers.title: Identification of local nonlinear shear-wave dynamics using Volterra kernels: application to prostate cancer detection.
papers.text: Identification of local nonlinear shear-wave dynamics using Volterra kernels: application to prostate cancer detection.. Cancer remains a major health concern worldwide. Shear-wave elastography (SWE) holds promise for cancer detection by quantifying linear elastic changes in tissue through shear-wave (SW) velocity estimation. However, shear viscosity and nonlinearity are often over-looked, despite their potential as additional biomarkers. This study evaluates the visco-hyperelastic properties of soft tissue, including linear shear modulus, shear viscosity, and shear nonlinearity. We propose using Volterra kernels to characterize local nonlinear SW dynamics, with kernel identification based on SW particle velocity measurements at adjacent locations. The method was validated using in-silico simulations and in-vitro gelatin phantoms. To evaluate its clinical relevance, we applied the method for prostate cancer (PCa) detection. To our knowledge, this is the first in-vivo assessment of voxel-based visco-hyperelastic properties of the prostate. In 90 patients, our results indicated that the linear kernel correlated with the linear shear modulus, while the quadratic kernel reflected both viscosity and nonlinearity. A convolutional neural network trained on these parameters with registered histopathology as ground truth achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.60 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57, 0.62) and 0.66 (95% CI: 0.64, 0.68) for PCa detection, respectively-both significantly outperforming the linear shear modulus (AUC of 0.54; 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.56). Our findings suggest that Volterra kernels reflect information related to the visco-hyperelastic properties of prostate tissue, highlighting the potential of viscosity and nonlinearity as additional biomarkers for PCa detection.

papers.title: Improving PI-RADS Prediction and Prostate Cancer Detection from Multiparametric MRI with Anatomical Guidance
papers.text: Improving PI-RADS Prediction and Prostate Cancer Detection from Multiparametric MRI with Anatomical Guidance. Accurate prediction of Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) scores from multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) remains challenging, more so than clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection. Given the importance of lesion location in PI-RADS scoring, we evaluated whether incorporating prostate zonal masks improves PI-RADS prediction and csPCa detection across multiple architectures (3D ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT) using a large-scale internal dataset. Anatomical guidance generally improved performance across architectures, with the best results achieved by ResNet-18 with 2-zone guidance for PI-RADS prediction (QWK = 0.511) and ResNet-50 with 5-zone guidance for csPCa detection (AUC = 0.809). Fine-tuned results on external datasets further demonstrated the benefits of anatomical guidance. Furthermore, models with anatomical guidance improved the utility of model-predicted PI-RADS scores for PI-RADS-based csPCa detection (positive defined as PI-RADS>=3). Combining model-predicted and expert-assigned PI-RADS scores significantly increased the AUC from 0.711 to 0.756 (p < 0.05), suggesting that AI-derived PI-RADS scores may provide complementary information to expert assessment for csPCa detection. Overall, our findings highlight the value of incorporating prostate zonal anatomy into deep learning-based prostate MRI assessment.

papers.title: Determination of total free acids in UiO-66 via extraction-decoupled gas-evolvement headspace detection.
papers.text: Determination of total free acids in UiO-66 via extraction-decoupled gas-evolvement headspace detection.. The accurate quantification of free acidic species occluded within metal-organic frameworks (i.e., UiO-66) is essential for evaluating synthesis completeness, material purity, and post-synthetic processing. In this work, a rapid and automated headspace gas chromatography (HS‑GC) method was developed for the determination of total free acids in MOFs. The strategy couples ultrasound‑assisted methanolic extraction with a selective phase‑conversion reaction: the extracted carboxylic acids react stoichiometrically with bicarbonate in a sealed headspace vial to liberate carbon dioxide, which is then detected by HS‑GC. Under systematically optimized conditions, the method exhibited excellent linearity, high sensitivity with a low limit of detection, and satisfactory precision. Accuracy was confirmed by near‑quantitative spike recoveries and by close agreement with a well‑established spectrophotometric reference method. Leveraging the automated headspace platform, the procedure substantially reduced sample cycle time and enabled high‑throughput operation while markedly decreasing organic solvent consumption relative to conventional wet‑chemical protocols. This approach provides a reliable, efficient, and environmentally favorable tool for routine monitoring of free acid content in MOFs (i.e., UiO-66), facilitating quality control in both laboratory‑scale research and scaled‑up synthesis.

papers.title: Panognostics-Plus: An Integrated Multi-Task AI Framework for Automated Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation with Dental Charting and Structured Reporting-Development and Technical Validation Study.
papers.text: Panognostics-Plus: An Integrated Multi-Task AI Framework for Automated Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation with Dental Charting and Structured Reporting-Development and Technical Validation Study.. Dental charting from panoramic radiographs is essential for clinical assessment, yet remains time-consuming. This study presents Panognostics-Plus, an automated cloud-based AI framework for panoramic radiograph analysis integrating dental charting and structured radiological reporting. Panognostics-Plus was developed using a retrospective dataset of 1,595 panoramic radiographs and a YOLO-based architecture comprising modules for dental anatomy, dental treatment, and periapical diagnostics. Anatomical structures and dental treatments were analyzed using a two-stage pipeline, whereas periapical lesions were analyzed by detection-and-classification. YOLOv8m, YOLOv9m, YOLO11m, and YOLO26m were benchmarked. Detection was evaluated by precision, sensitivity, F1-score, AP, and mAP; segmentation by IoU and Dice; and processing time. Model differences were assessed using Friedman tests with Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons. YOLO26m achieved the highest overall performance. The largest mAP0@50:0.95 gains were observed for crowns (+ 21.3%), radicular cysts (+ 20.5%), root canal treatments (+ 17.3%), bridges (+ 14.3%), periodontal bone level (+ 14.3%), and periapical granulomas (+ 13.5%). Dental implants achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.99, 0.98, and 0.98, respectively. Radicular cysts achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.95, 0.93, and 0.94 versus 0.92, 0.90, and 0.91 for periapical granulomas. Significant differences were observed in 8 of 10 detection tasks and all segmentation tasks (all p < 0.001); periodontal bone level (p = 0.193) and dental fillings (p = 0.073) were nonsignificant. Dice coefficients reached 0.97 for dental anatomy and 0.96 for dental treatments. The workflow generated a segmentation overlay, dental chart, and structured radiological report in 15 ± 1.4 s per radiograph. Panognostics-Plus may improve panoramic radiograph analysis and clinical efficiency, although further validation is required.

papers.title: Labeled Numerical Phantom of Abdominal Wall for Wave-Physics-Based Ultrasound Imaging: Applications to Image Reconstruction.
papers.text: Labeled Numerical Phantom of Abdominal Wall for Wave-Physics-Based Ultrasound Imaging: Applications to Image Reconstruction.. The transabdominal ultrasound imaging requires acoustic wave propagation through the abdominal wall, which consists of a complex organization of tissue layers that degrade imaging of underlying organs such as the liver. A priori knowledge of the acoustic properties of this medium could enable adaptive imaging techniques, but the underlying ground-truth properties in a living patient are a fundamentally unknown quantity. Numerical simulations can offer a solution to this challenge by modeling the propagation of ultrasound imaging pulses in media with known acoustic properties and can therefore provide a quantitative relationship between the received ultrasound echoes and the underlying tissue structure. However, to be comparable with clinical scenarios, in silico phantoms of the abdominal wall must be geometrically and quantitatively accurate, with rigorous tolerances. Here, we describe a dataset generation approach to produce experimentally calibrated ultrasound data for transabdominal imaging. Semantically labeled 3-D in silico phantoms with 0.33-mm isotropic resolution, along with physical parameters from the literature of the human abdominal wall, are used to model the acoustic propagation through human tissue. We perform 2-D numerical simulations of the Westervelt equation to generate a dataset of raw ultrasound data for liver imaging consisting of 1027 samples. We then discuss the applications of this dataset for facilitating abdominal ultrasound imaging research. The labeled abdominal dataset, simulated data, and the simulation tools that model wave propagation are made publicly available.

papers.title: Developing Foundation Models for Universal Segmentation from 3D Whole-Body Positron Emission Tomography
papers.text: Developing Foundation Models for Universal Segmentation from 3D Whole-Body Positron Emission Tomography. Positron emission tomography (PET) is a key nuclear medicine imaging modality that visualizes radiotracer distributions to quantify in vivo physiological and metabolic processes, playing an irreplaceable role in disease management. Despite its clinical importance, the development of deep learning models for quantitative PET image analysis remains severely limited, driven by both the inherent segmentation challenge from PET's paucity of anatomical contrast and the high costs of data acquisition and annotation. To bridge this gap, we develop generalist foundational models for universal segmentation from 3D whole-body PET imaging. We first build the largest and most comprehensive PET dataset to date, comprising 11041 3D whole-body PET scans with 59831 segmentation masks for model development. Based on this dataset, we present SegAnyPET, an innovative foundational model with general-purpose applicability to diverse segmentation tasks. Built on a 3D architecture with a prompt engineering strategy for mask generation, SegAnyPET enables universal and scalable organ and lesion segmentation, supports efficient human correction with minimal effort, and enables a clinical human-in-the-loop workflow. Extensive evaluations on multi-center, multi-tracer, multi-disease datasets demonstrate that SegAnyPET achieves strong zero-shot performance across a wide range of segmentation tasks, highlighting its potential to advance the clinical applications of molecular imaging.

papers.title: Variable Bregman Majorization-Minimization algorithms for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization, with application to Poisson imaging
papers.text: Variable Bregman Majorization-Minimization algorithms for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization, with application to Poisson imaging. In this work, we introduce a unifying Bregman-based majorization-minimization (MM) framework for solving nonconvex nonsmooth optimization problems. The proposed approach leverages Bregman divergences, possibly varying across iterations, to construct tailored surrogate functions that majorize the objective. We establish the convergence of the iterates of the resulting variable Bregman MM algorithm to critical points under the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, relaxing standard assumptions such as the Lipschitz smoothness of the nonconvex objective function. We derive a constructive methodology to build a broad class of variable Bregman majorants with tractable minimizers. Our study encapsulates various existing majorization techniques, in particular those derived for Poisson data fidelity terms in imaging inverse problems. Numerical experiments on Positron Emission Tomography (PET) image reconstruction with a nonconvex regularizer showcase the practical feasibility of the proposed scheme.

papers.title: Mechanically Anisotropic Multi-modal Phantoms for Elastography Imaging.
papers.text: Mechanically Anisotropic Multi-modal Phantoms for Elastography Imaging.. Mechanical anisotropy is a promising biomarker of tissue health because many tissues contain organized fibrous structures that can be disrupted by injury or disease. Elastographic imaging methods have recently emerged to noninvasively quantify anisotropic mechanical properties in soft fibrous tissues like brain white matter or muscle. Calibrated phantoms that reproduce anisotropic tissue behavior are necessary for clinical translation of these methods, but durable, validated, anisotropic, elastography phantoms are not currently available. To address this need, we fabricated mechanically anisotropic lattice composite phantoms by embedding directionally scaled, 3D-printed, polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) lattices in polyacrylamide (PAA) gel matrix. Apparent shear moduli governing deformations parallel and perpendicular to the scaling direction in these phantoms were estimated using magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) and ultrasound shear wave elastography (SWE). The properties of the phantom composite materials were independently characterized by benchtop dynamic shear testing (DST). All measurements were repeated over a four week period to assess stability of the phantoms over time. Both elastography imaging methods (MRE and SWE) detected anisotropy in lattice composite phantoms and identified differences in properties between different phantoms. Some quantitative differences were also observed between estimates of shear moduli and anisotropy obtained by MRE, SWE and DST, attributable to different features of each method. These phantoms and their fabrication protocols are available at the National Medical Phantom Library (NMPL) [1], to serve as assessment and calibration tools for anisotropic elastography imaging methods.

papers.title: Virtuality VS Reality: Testing a virtual approach for the exploratory analysis of Bronze Age urns from Northern Italy.
papers.text: Virtuality VS Reality: Testing a virtual approach for the exploratory analysis of Bronze Age urns from Northern Italy.. Cremation is among the most destructive funerary practices. Over the past 30 years, radiographic imaging has increasingly been used to non-destructively extract information from cremation burials. Advances in scanners and imaging software have enhanced the quality of data retrievable through this method. However, scanning cremated remains, particularly when urned, presents challenges due to their fragility, size, material density overlaps, and the high cost of imaging equipment. These factors often result in low-quality images where distinguishing different materials becomes difficult and time-consuming. This exploratory research aims to provide and assess qualitative and quantitative information from tomographic images on burials' taphonomy, biological profiles (sex and age at death), Minimum Number of Individuals (MNI) and thermal alterations to the bones and to evaluate a relatively simple segmentation strategy to analyse the spatial distribution of the remains in the vessels. For this purpose, 10 non-micro-excavated urns from the Middle-Late Bronze Age necropolis of Vicofertile (Parma, Italy) were scanned using Computerised Tomography (CT), subsequently micro-excavated, and the remains analysed to compare the information obtained from the two approaches. When extracted, data about the age classes, burial taphonomy, and heat-induced changes to the bones (e.g., fractures) were confirmed by the physical analysis, while the MNI, hypothesised to be 10 from the scans, was increased by one. Sex estimation was not possible from the scans. The vertical and horizontal distribution of the remains was estimated for cranial, long, spongy bones, upper, lower limbs, and trunk elements, with the vertical cranial distribution being the most accurately predicted category. Overall, the physical analysis proved essential to refine the results of virtual analysis and deal with the drawbacks of low-quality images. Despite the limitations discussed here, this research presents the largest systematic comparison of tomographic imaging and physical analysis of urned cremations to date, highlighting both the potential and the current limitations of CT-based investigation.
