papers.title: OPTARI: An open-source software framework for clinical translation of optoacoustic imaging
papers.text: OPTARI: An open-source software framework for clinical translation of optoacoustic imaging. Combined optoacoustic (OptA) and ultrasound imaging is a promising modality across a wide range of pathologies. Its use in clinical research, however, is limited by a lack of analysis software accessible to users without programming expertise. Existing tools are either script-based engineering frameworks or proprietary vendor applications. We present OPTARI, an open-source graphical software application to facilitate large-scale clinical optoacoustic-ultrasound (OPUS) studies. OPTARI builds on the napari image viewer and the PATATO toolkit for OptA data processing. It supports native vendor and open HDF5 data formats, aligns with the IPASC standard, and is distributed as a standalone executable. Features include region-of-interest annotation, reconstruction, chromophore unmixing, deep-learning-based tissue segmentation, and temporal and spectral analysis modules. OPTARI offers a combination of features for clinical study analysis that none of the compared tools provide. The automated tissue segmentation produced results comparable to expert labeling for muscle tissue, and batch processing reduced analysis time from minutes to under one second per scan. The tool is used in ongoing clinical OPUS studies. OPTARI connects engineering frameworks with medical research and provides an open-source basis for reproducible and standardized analysis in clinical OptA imaging studies.

papers.title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon
papers.text:
MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon. BackgroundMedical imaging research increasingly combines specialized artificial intelligence models for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation. For three-dimensional CT and MRI, these workflows typically run on NVIDIA GPUs with substantial memory. On-device AI on widely available Apple Silicon computers could broaden access to these models for clinical researchers. These computers share a large memory pool between the CPU and GPU, which suits workflows that combine several models. However, few established imaging models run natively on Apple Silicon. Adapting a model to new hardware also requires verifying that its results match the original software.

MethodsWe developed MedMLX, a collection of 21 established medical imaging models rewritten for Apple Silicon in MLX, Apples machine learning framework. The collection includes nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM2 and SAM 3. The models segment organs and tumors, detect lung nodules, generate synthetic images and draft radiology reports from CT, MRI, PET/CT, radiographs and endoscopic images. Using public cases from 11 imaging datasets, we compared the models results with those of the original software run on an Intel CPU and an NVIDIA GPU. Agreement required a Dice coefficient of at least 0.99 for every segmentation label and equivalent criteria for other outputs. We measured memory use and processing time on an Apple M1 Max computer with 64 GB of memory.

ResultsMedMLX agreed with the original software in 211 of 212 comparisons. The single exception was a brain MRI segmentation. On this case, the original software itself gave different results on the two devices. We illustrated sequential workflows, including anatomical segmentation of a synthetic brain MRI and lesion synthesis guided by organ segmentation. With a memory-saving setting, 19 of the 21 models used less than 16 GB of memory. This setting reduced memory use by a median of 49% and increased processing time by a median of 13%.

ConclusionsMedMLX enables on-device AI with established medical imaging models on Apple Silicon computers rather than specialized NVIDIA hardware. The models agree closely with the original software, and most need less than 16 GB of memory.

papers.title: Radiochemical Synthesis of 18F-Meta-Fluorobenzylguanidine (18F-mFBG) for PET/CT Imaging in Patients with Pheochromocytoma.
papers.text: Radiochemical Synthesis of 18F-Meta-Fluorobenzylguanidine (18F-mFBG) for PET/CT Imaging in Patients with Pheochromocytoma.. Pheochromocytoma (PCC) is a relatively rare neuroendocrine tumor. Due to its diverse and often nonspecific clinical manifestations, PCC is frequently missed or misdiagnosed in clinical practice. As a positron-emitting tracer, <sup>18</sup>F-meta-fluorobenzylguanidine (<sup>18</sup>F-mFBG) specifically targets and binds to the human norepinephrine transporter (hNET), and is used for disease diagnosis, lesion localization and assessment, and treatment planning. This study provides a detailed description of the entire process for <sup>18</sup>F-mFBG, including radiolabeling, quality control, patient preparation, and positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging. The radiolabeling of <sup>18</sup>F-mFBG was performed using a fully automated labeling module. Patient preparation followed a standardized protocol, which included patient instructions, explanation of the protocol, and intravenous administration of the radiopharmaceutical. The PET/CT imaging section details the acquisition and reconstruction parameter settings. Validated through 32 cases, the study demonstrated that key metrics such as maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) and target-to-background ratio (TBR) effectively distinguished PCC lesions and their uptake characteristics. The results indicate that <sup>18</sup>F-mFBG PET/CT imaging is a non-invasive and rapid method that provides information on tumor burden in PCC, offering a basis for auxiliary diagnosis and treatment planning.

papers.title: ConfUSIus: an accessible and scalable toolkit for functional ultrasound imaging analysis
papers.text: ConfUSIus: an accessible and scalable toolkit for functional ultrasound imaging analysis. Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) maps brainwide hemodynamics at high resolution, yet analysis requires expert knowledge as pipelines remain fragmented across laboratories. We introduce ConfUSIus, an open-source Python package and graphical interface for accessible, scalable, and reproducible fUSI analysis. Its common data model unifies heterogeneous fUSI recordings across beamformed IQ processing, motion correction, registration, denoising, and statistical analysis. ConfUSIus lowers barriers and facilitates method development, comparison, and sharing.

papers.title: PDGFRβ-Targeting VHH Tracer Enables Noninvasive PET Imaging of Kidney Fibrosis.
papers.text: PDGFRβ-Targeting VHH Tracer Enables Noninvasive PET Imaging of Kidney Fibrosis.. With a prevalence above 10% worldwide, chronic kidney disease is one of the leading medical burdens. Independent of the underlying cause, kidney fibrosis emerges as the common final endpoint and serves as the most robust predictor of disease progression and long-term prognosis. Fibrosis is driven by extracellular matrix-producing mesenchymal cells, which are characterized by platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ) expression. PDGFRβ also mediates fibrogenesis in these cells and represents a potential therapeutic target for direct intervention or a potential anchor for selective delivery of antifibrotic drugs. Diagnostic approaches assessing PDGFRβ expression in kidneys are missing. Here, we developed and evaluated a novel tracer using a PDGFRβ-targeting biparatopic variable domain of a heavy-chain-only antibody construct, designated SP02SP26-ABD, for in vivo, noninvasive, molecular imaging of kidney fibrosis. Methods: PDGFRβ expression was assessed in human kidney biopsies and publicly available transcriptomic datasets. In vivo imaging studies were performed in 2 distinct murine models of kidney fibrosis using fluorescence imaging and 89Zr-labeled PET. Specificity and dose dependency were evaluated using a nonspecific control variable domain of a heavy-chain-only antibody construct, R2R2-ABD, and coinjection of increasing amounts of unlabeled SP02SP26-ABD. Ex vivo biodistribution and correlation with histologic and molecular markers of fibrosis were performed. Results: PDGFRβ was increased in fibrotic human kidneys across multiple disease entities, predominantly localized to pericytes and fibroblasts, supporting its relevance as a translational imaging target. In vivo imaging demonstrated significantly higher tracer accumulation in fibrotic compared with nonfibrotic kidneys across both models, whereas tracer accumulation in nonrenal organs was low, with minimal uptake in the spleen. We found no difference between fibrotic and nonfibrotic kidneys when using a nonspecific R2R2-ABD control construct, whereas increasing amounts of unlabeled SP02SP26-ABD led to a dose-dependent decrease in tracer accumulation, consistent with a saturation effect. Tracer signal correlated with PDGFRβ expression, confirming the specificity of the approach. Conclusion: We provide the first proof of concept for noninvasive PET imaging of PDGFRβ-expressing fibrogenic cells in kidney disease, supporting further development of this approach for specific, noninvasive assessment of kidney fibrosis.

papers.title: Performance of Machine Learning Classification in Sonomammogram Images using BI-RADS
papers.text: Performance of Machine Learning Classification in Sonomammogram Images using BI-RADS. This research aims to investigate the classification accuracy of various state-of-the-art image classification models across different categories of breast ultrasound images, as defined by the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS). To achieve this, we used 2,945 sonomammogram images for training and 936 images for validation, with the source cohort reported as comprising 1,540 patients. In order to conduct a thorough analysis, we employed six advanced classification architecture families, including VGG19 \cite{simonyan2014very}, ResNet50 \cite{he2016deep}, GoogleNet \cite{szegedy2015going}, ConvNeXt \cite{liu2022convnet}, EfficientNet \cite{tan2019efficientnet}, and Vision Transformers (ViT) \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}, instead of traditional machine learning models. We evaluate models in three different settings: full fine-tuning, linear evaluation and training from scratch. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness and capability of our Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) system, with a remarkable accuracy of 76.39\% and an F1 score of 67.94\% in the full fine-tuning setting. Our findings indicate the potential for enhanced diagnostic accuracy in the field of breast imaging, providing a solid foundation for future endeavors aiming to improve the precision and reliability of CAD systems in medical imaging.

papers.title: Integrating AI for Human-Centric Breast Cancer Diagnostics: A Multi-Scale and Multi-View Swin Transformer Framework
papers.text: Integrating AI for Human-Centric Breast Cancer Diagnostics: A Multi-Scale and Multi-View Swin Transformer Framework. Despite advancements in Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems, breast cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths among women worldwide. Recent breakthroughs in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown significant promise in development of advanced Deep Learning (DL) architectures for breast cancer diagnosis through mammography. In this context, the paper focuses on the integration of AI within a Human-Centric workflow to enhance breast cancer diagnostics. Key challenges are, however, largely overlooked such as reliance on detailed tumor annotations and susceptibility to missing views, particularly during test time. To address these issues, we propose a hybrid, multi-scale and multi-view Swin Transformer-based framework (MSMV-Swin) that enhances diagnostic robustness and accuracy. The proposed MSMV-Swin framework is designed to work as a decision-support tool, helping radiologists analyze multi-view mammograms more effectively. More specifically, the MSMV-Swin framework leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to isolate the breast lobe, reducing background noise and enabling comprehensive feature extraction. The multi-scale nature of the proposed MSMV-Swin framework accounts for tumor-specific regions as well as the spatial characteristics of tissues surrounding the tumor, capturing both localized and contextual information. The integration of contextual and localized data ensures that MSMV-Swin's outputs align with the way radiologists interpret mammograms, fostering better human-AI interaction and trust. A hybrid fusion structure is then designed to ensure robustness against missing views, a common occurrence in clinical practice when only a single mammogram view is available.

papers.title: Optimizing Breast Cancer Detection in Mammograms: A Comprehensive Study of Transfer Learning, Resolution Reduction, and Multi-View Classification
papers.text: Optimizing Breast Cancer Detection in Mammograms: A Comprehensive Study of Transfer Learning, Resolution Reduction, and Multi-View Classification. Mammography, an X-ray-based imaging technique, remains central to the early detection of breast cancer. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have enabled increasingly sophisticated computer-aided diagnostic methods, evolving from patch-based classifiers to whole-image approaches and then to multi-view architectures that jointly analyze complementary projections. Despite this progress, several critical questions remain unanswered. In this study, we systematically investigate these issues by addressing five key research questions: (1) the role of patch classifiers in performance, (2) the transferability of natural-image-trained backbones, (3) the advantages of learn-to-resize over conventional downscaling, (4) the contribution of multi-view integration, and (5) the robustness of findings across varying image quality. Beyond benchmarking, our experiments demonstrate clear performance gains over prior work. For the CBIS-DDSM dataset, we improved single-view AUC from 0.8153 to 0.8343, and multiple-view AUC from 0.8483 to 0.8658. Using a new comparative method, we also observed a 0.0217 AUC increase when extending from single to multiple-view analysis. On the complete VinDr-Mammo dataset, the multiple-view approach further improved results, achieving a 0.0492 AUC increase over single view and reaching 0.8511 AUC overall. These results establish new state-of-the-art benchmarks, providing clear evidence of the advantages of multi-view architectures for mammogram interpretation. Beyond performance, our analysis offers principled insights into model design and transfer learning strategies, contributing to the development of more accurate and reliable breast cancer screening tools. The inference code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/dpetrini/multiple-view.

papers.title: A Versatile Foundation Model for AI-enabled Mammogram Interpretation
papers.text: A Versatile Foundation Model for AI-enabled Mammogram Interpretation. Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women globally. Mammography is essential for the early detection and diagnosis of breast lesions. Despite recent progress in foundation models (FMs) for mammogram analysis, their clinical translation remains constrained by several fundamental limitations, including insufficient diversity in training data, limited model generalizability, and a lack of comprehensive evaluation across clinically relevant tasks. Here, we introduce VersaMammo, a versatile foundation model for mammograms, designed to overcome these limitations. We curated the largest multi-institutional mammogram dataset to date, comprising 706,239 images from 21 sources. To improve generalization, we propose a two-stage pre-training strategy to develop VersaMammo, a mammogram foundation model. First, a teacher model is trained via self-supervised learning to extract transferable features from unlabeled mammograms. Then, supervised learning combined with knowledge distillation transfers both features and clinical knowledge into VersaMammo. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we established a benchmark comprising 92 specific tasks, including 68 internal tasks and 24 external validation tasks, spanning 5 major clinical task categories: lesion detection, segmentation, classification, image retrieval, and visual question answering. VersaMammo achieves state-of-the-art performance, ranking first in 50 out of 68 specific internal tasks and 20 out of 24 external validation tasks, with average ranks of 1.5 and 1.2, respectively. These results demonstrate its superior generalization and clinical utility, offering a substantial advancement toward reliable and scalable breast cancer screening and diagnosis.

papers.title: The Impact of Longitudinal Mammogram Alignment on Breast Cancer Risk Assessment
papers.text:
The Impact of Longitudinal Mammogram Alignment on Breast Cancer Risk Assessment. Regular mammography screening is crucial for early breast cancer detection. By leveraging deep learning-based risk models, screening intervals can be personalized, especially for high-risk individuals. While recent methods increasingly incorporate longitudinal information from prior mammograms, accurate spatial alignment across time points remains a key challenge. Misalignment can obscure meaningful tissue changes and degrade model performance. In this study, we provide insights into various alignment strategies, image-based registration, feature-level (representation space) alignment with and without regularization, and implicit alignment methods, for their effectiveness in longitudinal deep learning-based risk modeling. Using two large-scale mammography datasets, we assess each method across key metrics, including predictive accuracy, precision, recall, and deformation field quality.
  Our results show that image-based registration consistently outperforms the more recently favored feature-based and implicit approaches across all metrics, enabling more accurate, temporally consistent predictions and generating smooth, anatomically plausible deformation fields. Although regularizing the deformation field improves deformation quality, it reduces the risk prediction performance of feature-level alignment. Applying image-based deformation fields within the feature space yields the best risk prediction performance.
  These findings underscore the importance of image-based deformation fields for spatial alignment in longitudinal risk modeling, offering improved prediction accuracy and robustness. This approach has strong potential to enhance personalized screening and enable earlier interventions for high-risk individuals. The code is available at https://github.com/sot176/Mammogram_Alignment_Study_Risk_Prediction.git, allowing full reproducibility of the results.

papers.title: OncoVision: Integrating Mammography and Clinical Data through Attention-Driven Multimodal AI for Enhanced Breast Cancer Diagnosis
papers.text: OncoVision: Integrating Mammography and Clinical Data through Attention-Driven Multimodal AI for Enhanced Breast Cancer Diagnosis. OncoVision is a privileged-information training framework that uses mammography images and clinical features during training and performs inference from mammographic images alone. Employing an attention-based encoder-decoder backbone, it jointly segments four regions of interest (masses, calcifications, axillary findings, and breast tissue) with accuracy exceeding the nnU-Net baseline and predicts ten structured clinical features, including BI-RADS category. We developed two late-fusion strategies, Independent and Dependent, that integrate imaging, radiomic, and clinical information during training to improve diagnostic precision and potentially reduce inter-observer variability. Radiomic features extracted from predicted masks provide shape, intensity, and texture descriptors that complement the learned CNN representations. We evaluated OncoVision in a retrospective multi-reader study with six board-certified radiologists, assessing diagnostic confidence, reading time, and segmentation accuracy with and without AI assistance. In a paired reader-assistance evaluation, OncoVision was associated with higher diagnostic confidence for junior and senior radiologists, reduced reading time by up to 61%, and achieved segmentation accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of radiologists for mass lesions. We operationalized OncoVision as a secure web application, now deployed at a partner hospital, that generates structured reports with dual-confidence scoring and attention-weighted visualizations for real-time diagnostic support. The platform is designed for integration into clinical workflows, with the goal of supporting screening access in underprivileged regions. By combining accurate segmentation with clinical intuition, OncoVision advances AI-assisted mammographic interpretation, offering a scalable and accessible approach to earlier and more consistent image interpretation.

papers.title: A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography.
papers.text:
A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography..

Objectives

Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) is the standard for breast cancer screening but has reduced sensitivity in dense breasts. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves cancer detection compared to 2D mammography but is limited by cost and longer reading times. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mammography has demonstrated improved sensitivity compared to 2D mammography. This study compares AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) with DBT in recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs).

Methods

: A multi-reader, multi-case crossover study was conducted using the Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset, which includes paired FFDM and DBT images with biopsy-proven outcomes. Six radiologists reviewed 53 IBC and 53 screen-detected cancer (SDC) cases, with random assignment to DM+AI or DBT, followed by crossover after a washout period. Primary outcomes included recall rate of IBCs. Secondary outcomes included recall rate of SDCs, interpretation time, and subgroup analysis by breast density.

Results

: For IBCs, DM+AI and DBT demonstrated similar recall rates (41.5% vs 40.9%) and detection rates (14.8% vs 11.9%). DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) cancers. For SDCs, recall and detection rates were comparable across modalities. In fatty breasts, recall was higher with DM+AI (91.7% vs 50.0%), while DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts. DM+AI enabled faster interpretation, averaging 24.1 seconds less per case.

Conclusion

: AI-enhanced 2D mammography demonstrated comparable performance to DBT with shorter interpretation times, supporting a stratified screening approach.

Advances in knowledge

This study is the first direct comparison of AI-enhanced mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis for IBC detection.

papers.title: Observer agreement in sonographic glandular tissue component classification and sonographic breast density assessment: a multi-institutional study.
papers.text:
Observer agreement in sonographic glandular tissue component classification and sonographic breast density assessment: a multi-institutional study..

Purpose

The sonographic glandular tissue component (GTC) is a potential imaging biomarker for stratifying breast cancer risk in women with dense breasts. This study evaluated the reproducibility, reliability, and clinical applicability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment in a multicenter observer study.

Methods

Fifteen readers (nine physicians and six sonographers) from 12 institutions independently assessed 100 paired ultrasound images twice, 1 month apart, with the dataset rearranged for the second reading. GTC was qualitatively classified into four categories according to its estimated proportion within the fibroglandular tissue (FGT): minimal, mild, moderate, and marked; minimal/mild were grouped as low GTC and moderate/marked as high GTC. Sonographic breast density was categorized as sonographic dense breast (high GTC), sonographic non-dense breast (visible fat lobules), or intermediate, with intermediate cases further divided into high or low categories using an FGT-to-FAT (subcutaneous and retromammary fat) ratio cutoff of 1. Interobserver and intraobserver agreement was evaluated using κ statistics.

Results

Substantial interobserver agreement was observed for the four-class GTC classification, the two-class GTC classification, and sonographic breast density assessment. Intraobserver agreement was moderate for the four-class GTC classification and substantial for the two-class GTC classification and sonographic breast density assessment. The majority-vote sonographic breast density assessment showed substantial agreement with the mammographic ground truth, whereas individual-reader assessments showed moderate concordance with mammographic breast density both overall and in intermediate-density breasts. No significant differences in agreement were observed between physicians and sonographers.

Conclusion

Substantial interobserver agreement and moderate-to-substantial intraobserver agreement support the reproducibility and reliability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment.

papers.title: Nonlinear association between age and volumetric breast density in Japanese women.
papers.text:
Nonlinear association between age and volumetric breast density in Japanese women..

Background

Volumetric breast density (VBD) is influenced by age, body mass index (BMI), and reproductive factors, yet the shape of the age-VBD association and age-specific VBD distributions in Japanese women remain incompletely characterized. We examined the associations of age, BMI, menopausal status, and parity with software-derived VBD and characterized age-specific VBD distributions, including the proportion of women with VBD ≥ 7.5%.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 719 asymptomatic Japanese women undergoing screening mammography (mean age, 58.7 ± 12.6 years; range, 20-87 years) in whom no breast lesion was identified. VBD was quantified using Volpara Density. Age was modeled using restricted cubic splines, adjusted for BMI, menopausal status, and parity. Regression analyses used 672 complete cases. Mean VBD ≥ 7.5% defined volumetrically dense breasts.

Results

Overall, 72.7% (523/719) had VBD ≥ 7.5%. Mean VBD was 17.34%, 13.41%, 11.01%, and 11.72% at ages 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79 years, respectively, and 16.81% versus 11.85% in pre- versus postmenopausal women. Age was associated with VBD (P < 0.001), with significant nonlinearity (P = 0.027); adjusted VBD was lower with increasing age until the mid-60s and then largely plateaued. Higher BMI (β = -1.08; 95% CI, - 1.20 to - 0.97; P < 0.001) and parity (β = -2.21; 95% CI, - 3.43 to - 0.98; P < 0.001) were independently associated with lower VBD, whereas menopausal status was not (β = -1.07; 95% CI, - 2.85 to 0.71; P = 0.239).

Conclusions

Age was nonlinearly associated with VBD in Japanese women, plateauing after the mid-60s. VBD ≥ 7.5% was common, while BMI and parity remained independently associated with lower VBD.

papers.title: Clinical Implications of Background Parenchymal Enhancement on Breast MRI.
papers.text: Clinical Implications of Background Parenchymal Enhancement on Breast MRI.. Breast MRI is an essential tool for breast cancer detection, evaluation, and characterization, offering greater sensitivity than mammography and ultrasound. Normal breast tissue demonstrates variable enhancement on MRI, known as background parenchymal enhancement (BPE), which reflects the physiologic enhancement of fibroglandular tissue after gadolinium administration. Initially considered an incidental finding, BPE is now recognized as a dynamic imaging feature influenced by several factors, including age, menopausal status, exogenous hormone use, and prior breast cancer treatments. Increasing evidence supports its clinical relevance since variations in BPE have been associated with differences in breast cancer risk, lesion detection, and imaging interpretation. Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is emerging as an important imaging biomarker with potential applications in risk stratification, evaluation of disease extent, and monitoring response to neoadjuvant therapy. Differences in BPE patterns may also correlate with tumor biology and molecular subtypes, further supporting its role in personalized breast imaging assessment. This article provides a comprehensive review of BPE, highlighting its biologic basis, imaging characteristics, and clinical implications in breast cancer care. It also examines the evolving role of artificial intelligence tools in the assessment and quantification of BPE, which may improve standardization and integration into clinical decision-making and research.

papers.title: Evaluation of artificial intelligence algorithms from Lunit for detection of breast cancer with mammogram in a South-East Asian population.
papers.text: Evaluation of artificial intelligence algorithms from Lunit for detection of breast cancer with mammogram in a South-East Asian population.. PurposeTo conduct a pre-clinical evaluation of a commercially available artificial intelligence system, Lunit AI, as an independent mammography reader and compare its performance with human readers.Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study analyzed a double-reader population-based mammographic screening cohort of women at an academic women's hospital in Singapore from 2010 to 2017. Lunit AI performance was compared with single-reader (SRR) and double-reader radiologist (DRR) assessment using AUC-ROC, specificity, sensitivity and accuracy.Results1,982 women 35-87 years without breast implants or prior breast cancer were included. The cohort comprised 193 histopathologically confirmed breast cancers, 1,299 healthy controls and 490 histopathologically proven benign recalls. Mean age was 55.7 ± 9.7 years for with cancer and 52.9 ± 8.5 years without cancer.Lunit AI achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.874 (95% CI: 0.843-0.905) compared with 0.811 (95% CI: 0.783-0.840) for SRR assessment and 0.863 (95% CI: 0.846-0.880) for DRR assessment. Compared with SRR, Lunit AI demonstrated higher specificity (81.0% vs 72.6%, p < 0.001), lower sensitivity (80.3% vs 89.6%, p = 0.013) and higher accuracy (80.9% vs 74.3%, p < 0.001). Compared with DRR, Lunit AI demonstrated higher specificity (81.0% vs 72.6%, p < 0.001), lower sensitivity (80.3% vs 100%, p < 0.001) and higher accuracy (80.9% vs 75.3%, p < 0.001). The apparent 100% sensitivity of DRR reflects the retrospective study design and should not be interpreted as true screening sensitivity. Lunit AI detected 156 of 193 cancers and missed 34 cancers of which the majority of the missed cases were 22 cases (64.7%) of microcalcifications.ConclusionLunit AI model shows promising performance in a Southeast Asian population with high AUC-ROC, specificity and accuracy. However it shows lower sensitivity for subtle microcalcifications. These results suggest that Lunit AI may not be suitable as a fully independent reader but as an adjunct to enhance existing clinical workflows in mammographic screening.

papers.title: How Generalizable Are Foundation Models When Applied to Different Demographic Groups and Settings?
papers.text: How Generalizable Are Foundation Models When Applied to Different Demographic Groups and Settings?. AbstractRETFound is a retinal image-based foundational artificial intelligence (AI) model that can be fine-tuned to downstream tasks. However, its generalizability to Asian populations remains unclear. In this study, we fine-tuned RETFound on an Asian-specific dataset. We then evaluated the performance of RETFound versus a conventional Vision Transformer model (pretrained on ImageNet) in diagnosing glaucoma and coronary heart disease and predicting the 3-year risk of stroke in an Asian population. When fine-tuned on a "full" dataset, RETFound showed no significant improvement compared with a conventional Vision Transformer model (area under the curves [AUCs] of 0.863, 0.628, and 0.557 vs. 0.853, 0.621, and 0.543, respectively; all P≥0.2). Furthermore, in scenarios with limited training data (fine-tuned on ≤25% of the full dataset), RETFound showed a slight advantage (up to a maximum AUC increase of 0.03). However, these improvements were not statistically significant (all P≥0.2). These findings indicate the challenges foundational AI models face in adapting to diverse demographics, emphasizing the need for more diverse data in current foundation models and the importance of global collaboration on foundation model research.

papers.title: Towards Accurate and Lightweight Peripheral Neuroblastic Tumor Diagnosis via Contrastive Multi-scale Pathological Image Analysis
papers.text: Towards Accurate and Lightweight Peripheral Neuroblastic Tumor Diagnosis via Contrastive Multi-scale Pathological Image Analysis. Peripheral neuroblastic tumors (pNTs) are among the most common extracranial solid tumors in children, and accurate pathological subtyping is important for risk stratification and treatment planning. However, pNT subtyping on hematoxylin-eosin whole-slide images (WSIs) remains challenging because of limited pediatric tumor cohorts, marked histological heterogeneity, inter-observer variability, and the computational burden of existing WSI classifiers. To address these challenges, we propose CoPath, a framework consisting of CoHisNet and PathVote. CoHisNet is a lightweight multi-scale feature-fusion network for patch-level histopathological classification. By replacing the multilayer perceptron components in Swin Transformer blocks and the classification head with Kolmogorov-Arnold Network layers, CoHisNet improves nonlinear feature modeling under a compact architecture. Its multi-scale interaction and contrast-driven feature-enhancement design enables the model to capture both tissue-level structures and fine-grained cellular morphology. PathVote further incorporates pathology-informed tissue-component priors to aggregate patch-level predictions into WSI-level decisions. We validated CoPath on a private two-branch PpNTs cohort and the public BreakHis breast cancer histopathology dataset. Experimental results show that CoPath achieves competitive or superior performance compared with general image classifiers, pathology foundation models under linear probing, and pathology-specific classification models, while maintaining substantially lower computational complexity. The source code is available at https://github.com/JSLiam94/CoPath.

papers.title: Streamline pathology foundation model by cross-magnification distillation
papers.text: Streamline pathology foundation model by cross-magnification distillation. Foundation models (FM) have transformed computational pathology but remain computationally prohibitive for clinical deployment due to their massive parameter counts and high-magnification processing requirements. Here, we introduce XMAG, a lightweight FM developed through corss-magnification distillation that transfers knowledge from state-of-the-art 20x magnification teacher to an efficient 5x magnification student architecture. XMAG employs a compact backbone and operates entirely at 5x, requiring 11.3 times fewer patches per whole slide image (WSI) compared to existing approaches. Our Novel distillation framework incorporates dual-level knowledge transfer, aligning both global image representations and local spatial token mapping. We trained XMAG on 3.49 million images curated from publicly available datasets and evaluated performance across six clinically relevant histopathology analysis tasks spanning multiple cancer types. XMAG achieved diagnostic accuracy within 1% of substantially larger foundation models while delivering 30-fold processing acceleration, reaching 8.8 WSIs per minute processing speed. Our cross-institutional validation confirmed robust generalization. Further, we developed an end-to-end training strategy to further boost our model's performance to approach the larger FMs' performance. These results establish cross-magnification distillation as a viable approach for deploying FM capabilities in resource-constrained clinical environments, potentially enabling real-time pathology AI integration.

papers.title: Accurate and Scalable Multimodal Pathology Retrieval via Attentive Vision-Language Alignment
papers.text: Accurate and Scalable Multimodal Pathology Retrieval via Attentive Vision-Language Alignment. The rapid digitization of histopathology slides has opened new opportunities for computational tools in clinical and research workflows. Content-based slide retrieval can help pathologists identify morphologically and semantically related precedent cases, supporting expert diagnosis and example-based education. Effective retrieval of whole-slide images (WSIs), however, remains challenging because gigapixel slides contain abundant irrelevant content, focal diagnostic patterns and slide-level semantic information that must be represented at a practicable search cost. Here we present PathSearch, a retrieval framework that combines fine-grained attentive mosaics with slide-level embeddings aligned through vision-language contrastive learning. Trained on 6,926 slide-report pairs, PathSearch captures both fine-grained morphological cues and high-level semantic patterns to enable accurate and flexible retrieval. The framework supports two key functionalities: (1) mosaic-based image-to-image (I2I) retrieval, ensuring accurate and efficient slide search; and (2) multimodal retrieval, where text queries can directly retrieve relevant slides. PathSearch was evaluated on eight tasks comprising 5,021 evaluation slides, spanning malignancy assessment on frozen and hematoxylin and eosin (H\&E)-stained slides, lymph-node metastasis detection, tumor subtyping, mixed-gallery rare-cancer retrieval, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk stratification. Internal and external experimental results demonstrate that PathSearch consistently outperforms the strongest existing methods without compromising multimodal accuracy. A multi-center reader study further demonstrated increases in task-level mean diagnostic accuracy, confidence, and inter-observer agreement with PathSearch's support. Together, these results support the effectiveness of PathSearch across diverse retrieval tasks and evaluation settings.

papers.title: MedGPT-oss: Training a General-Purpose Vision-Language Model for Biomedicine
papers.text: MedGPT-oss: Training a General-Purpose Vision-Language Model for Biomedicine. Biomedical multimodal assistants have the potential to unify radiology, pathology, and clinical-text reasoning, yet a critical deployment gap remains: top-performing systems are either closed-source or computationally prohibitive, precluding the on-premises deployment required for patient privacy and PHI compliance. We introduce MEDGPT-OSS, an open-weight, 20B-parameter generalist vision-language model designed to facilitate open research in clinical AI. Rather than relying on architectural complexity, MEDGPT-OSS pairs the GPT-oss language backbone with a visual front-end via a optimized, three-stage training curriculum. By progressively domain-adapting these modules through rigorous data curation and long-context multimodal alignment, we demonstrate that a 20B model can bridge the capacity gap. It successfully outperforms larger open medical models on out-of-distribution (OOD) multimodal reasoning and complex text-only clinical tasks. By unifying diverse modalities under a single instruction-following interface, MEDGPT-OSS maintains a parameter-efficient footprint fully compatible with commodity GPUs. We release the complete training recipe, open-weight checkpoints, and a rigorous evaluation harness to serve as a verifiable foundation for privacy-preserving, institution-specific clinical AI research.

papers.title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
papers.text: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder. Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches 0.565 mean intersection over union (mIoU) against 0.502. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

papers.title: VQ-CSDN: A Vector Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network for Stain Normalization of H&E Histopathology Images.
papers.text: VQ-CSDN: A Vector Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network for Stain Normalization of H&E Histopathology Images.. Stain normalization is a fundamental preprocessing technique in digital and computational pathology, and it is important for improving the consistency of clinical diagnosis by reducing color heterogeneity. However, existing stain normalization methods are often limited by content-stain entanglement and an ambiguously modeled content-stain relationship, resulting in unstable structural preservation, cross-center adaptation burden, and sensitivity to template selection. To address these limitations, we propose a Vector-Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network (VQ-CSDN) that decouples structure-defining content from stain appearance and learns a center-specific content-to-stain mapping, enabling structure-preserving, template-free stain transfer from unseen source centers without source-specific retraining. VQ-CSDN employs two independent encoders to extract content and stain features respectively and a generator for reconstruction. To better characterize cross-center content feature spaces and capture staining styles, we introduce vector quantization with a global content codebook shared across centers and center-specific stain codebooks. Moreover, a content-to-stain module directly infers stain features from the content feature and a target staining style, enabling end-to-end stain transfer without template selection. To further promote structural fidelity and enhance staining style separability, we propose center-specific gradient-driven discriminators that jointly assess center-level stain conformity and the morphological consistency of generated images. Extensive experiments on multiple public and private pathology datasets show that VQ-CSDN consistently enhances normalization quality, reflected by increased SSIM/PSNR and decreased FID, and further improves downstream benign-malignant classification performance (AUC 0.9738) over state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Pathology foundation-model embeddings reveal a morphological landscape of breast lesions beyond diagnostic categories
papers.text:
Pathology foundation-model embeddings reveal a morphological landscape of breast lesions beyond diagnostic categories.

Background

Despite rapid advances in computational pathology, including foundation-model embeddings, most approaches remain classifier-based. Breast lesion pathology is an area of unmet clinicopathological need and a compelling setting for morphology-based modeling: diagnostic categories occupy overlapping morphological spectra and reflect heterogeneous pathways of tumor development, thereby posing substantial challenges for pathological diagnosis and subsequent clinical decision-making. However, approaches to delineate morphological continua across diagnostic categories and tumor development remain understudied. Here, we leveraged morphology-based foundation-model embeddings to define a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories and dissect how these embeddings could reflect a pathobiological continuum or sequence associated with tumor development.

Methods

To model breast lesion categories in continuous morphology space, we established a leakage-controlled, patient-aware workflow using the frozen foundation model Prov-GigaPath and the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a pathologist-annotated hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) breast lesion dataset spanning normal tissue, benign proliferative lesions, atypical lesions, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive carcinoma (IC). Using the BRACS training split, we defined a train-derived principal component analysis (PCA) morphology space. We then performed two complementary analyses: normal-rooted k-nearest-neighbor (kNN)-Dijkstra graph-distance scoring to derive a trajectory-like morphology score without imposing the full ordinal diagnostic sequence; pairwise Energy distance and squared maximum mean discrepancy with a radial-basis-function kernel (RBF-MMD²) to quantify order-free distributional separation among diagnostic categories. Validation and test data were projected into the train-defined reference space to assess reproducibility.

Results

Prov-GigaPath embeddings defined a train-derived morphology space with category-associated organization. Without imposing the full diagnostic sequence, normal-rooted kNN-Dijkstra graph distances recovered a trajectory-like morphology arrangement from normal/benign to malignant lesions. Order-free Energy distance and RBF-MMD² further supported graded separation among lesion categories. Validation and test datasets preserved the pathological organization. Furthermore, morphological embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma, without requiring additional molecular information.

Conclusions

Leveraging morphology-based foundation-model embeddings, we defined a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories, allowing nuanced positioning of breast lesions along a pathobiological continuum associated with tumor development. Our approaches pave the way for extracting biologically and clinically relevant information from routine histopathology to guide molecular testing, individualized risk assessment, and cost-efficient clinicopathological decision-making.

Highlights

Overlapping morphological features challenge breast diagnostic categorization Foundation-model embeddings defined a morphologic state space Embeddings allow nuanced positioning along morphological continua across categories Embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma Latent morphological signals in H&E slides may refine individualized risk assessment

papers.title: PathoS2VD: From 2D Histopathology to Pseudo Z-Stack Representations
papers.text: PathoS2VD: From 2D Histopathology to Pseudo Z-Stack Representations. For decades, diagnostic pathology has relied on thin two-dimensional (2D) tissue sections, despite biological tissues exhibiting inherently three-dimensional (3D) morphological organization. Because a single section captures only one focal plane, important morphological cues along the z-axis are inevitably discarded, limiting tissue representation for both human interpretation and computational analysis. In this work, we propose a generative framework that learns z-axis morphological priors from pathology z-stack data, offering a cost-effective alternative to dedicated volumetric imaging, and transfers this knowledge to conventional single-plane histopathology. Specifically, an image-to-video (I2V) latent diffusion model (LDM) is trained to synthesize a pseudo z-stack from a single 2D image, capturing plausible morphological variations across adjacent focal planes rather than reconstructing physical tissue volumes. To enable deployment on large-scale clinical datasets without native z-stack acquisition, we further introduce a prior-preserving mixture fine-tuning strategy that adapts the model to new domains while retaining the learned z-axis morphological prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized pseudo z-stacks exhibit realistic cross-plane morphological continuity and consistently improve downstream prostate cancer classification compared with conventional 2D representations. Our results suggest that learning transferable z-axis priors from limited z-stack data provides a practical way to enrich routine pathology images with complementary morphological information. Code: https://github.com/QuIIL/PathoS2VD.

papers.title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
papers.text: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift. Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

papers.title: The APL Doesn't Fall Far From The Tree: Unsupervised Artefact Prototype Learning in Histopathology
papers.text: The APL Doesn't Fall Far From The Tree: Unsupervised Artefact Prototype Learning in Histopathology. Histopathology foundation models provide rich representations of tissue morphology, but technical artefacts in whole slide images introduce noise that may impact diagnostic accuracy. We introduce Artefact Prototype Learning (APL), a novel approach to detecting these artefacts that exploits the geometry of pre-trained embedding spaces without manual labels or fine-tuning. Rather than treating artefacts as isolated outliers, APL computes prototypes of out-of-distribution patches and uses them to distinguish artefact-associated patterns from tissue. Evaluation on a single-centre dataset shows that APL outperforms prior methods GrandQC and HistoART in detecting artefacts such as blur, dark spots, slide edges and pen marks, but struggles with tissue folds and blood. These results show that frozen pre-trained embeddings already carry information that allows artefact detection without expensive labels or vast computational resources.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
papers.text: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists. Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

papers.title: A web modular AI interface for brain tumor MRI classification using deep learning models.
papers.text: A web modular AI interface for brain tumor MRI classification using deep learning models.. In order to improve patient outcomes and treatment processes, early and precise diagnosis of brain tumors is crucial. Despite the strong performance shown by deep learning models in classifying brain tumors from MRI scans, integrating these models into user-friendly clinical workflows remains challenging. This study presents a web-based AI platform designed for brain tumor classification using MRI images. The platform enables users to upload MRI scans, apply standardized preprocessing, select between different deep learning models, and receive real-time predictions. A custom convolutional neural network (CNN), pretrained VGG19, and pretrained Xception were evaluated using a publicly available T1-weighted contrast-enhanced brain MRI dataset of approximately 7,000 images across four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The dataset lacks patient demographic and clinical metadata, limiting assessment of clinical generalizability. The models achieved test accuracies of 96.03%, 98%, and 96%, respectively, with VGG19 demonstrating the best performance. The study is limited by the use of a single public, slice-based dataset and the absence of external clinical validation; future work will focus on multi-sequence MRI and independent clinical cohorts.

papers.title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
papers.text: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging. Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
papers.text: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity. Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

papers.title: Geometric Modeling of Hippocampal Tau Deposition: A Surface-Based Framework for Covariate Analysis and Off-Target Contamination Detection
papers.text: Geometric Modeling of Hippocampal Tau Deposition: A Surface-Based Framework for Covariate Analysis and Off-Target Contamination Detection. We introduce a framework combining geometric modeling with disease progression analysis to investigate tau deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) using positron emission tomography (PET) data. Focusing on the hippocampus, we construct a principal surface that captures the spatial distribution and morphological changes of tau pathology. By projecting voxels onto this surface, we quantify tau coverage, intensity, and thickness through bidirectional projection distances and interpolated standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR). This low-dimensional embedding preserves spatial specificity while mitigating multiple comparison issues. Covariate effects are analyzed using a two-stage regression model with inverse probability weighting to adjust for signal sparsity and selection bias. Using the SuStaIn model, we identify subtypes and stages of AD, revealing distinct tau dynamics: the limbic-predominant subtype shows age-related nonlinear accumulation in coverage and thickness, whereas the posterior subtype exhibits uniform SUVR increases across disease progression. Model-based predictions show that hippocampal tau deposition follows a structured spatial trajectory expanding bidirectionally with increasing thickness, while subtype differences highlight posterior hippocampal involvement consistent with whole-brain patterns. Finally, directional signal patterns on the principal surface reveal contamination from the choroid plexus, demonstrating the broader applicability of the proposed framework across modalities including amyloid PET.

papers.title: A foundation-model approach to pediatric headache classification from resting-state fMRI.
papers.text: A foundation-model approach to pediatric headache classification from resting-state fMRI.. Headache is the most common neurological disorder in children and substantially affects quality of life. We investigated whether resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) can support pediatric headache classification using machine learning. We encoded rs-fMRI data using NeuroSTORM, a recent foundation model, and fine-tuned it to distinguish healthy controls from children with headache and subsequently classify headache subtypes. We then compared NeuroSTORM with a standard neuroscience approach that uses functional connectivity (FC) matrices derived from brain activity as predictors. Using 189 rs-fMRI scans from 110 individuals collected across two visits (prevalence of any headache: 74%), NeuroSTORM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.82-0.82) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) in discriminating headache from non-headache. In contrast, models trained on FC matrices showed limited performance (AUROC, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.67-0.67]; AUPRC, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.85-0.85]). In a multiclass setting, when tasked with classifying individuals as healthy controls, individuals with chronic migraine, or individuals with non-chronic headaches (e.g., post-viral headache, new daily persistent headache, post-traumatic headache), NeuroSTORM achieved a macro-AUROC of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.68-0.69). The results suggest this approach can distinguish chronic migraine, the most common headache syndrome, but has difficulty differentiating other headache subtypes from chronic migraine. Overall, under limited-data conditions, NeuroSTORM appears to capture latent rs-fMRI representations that transfer to headache-related tasks. The findings provide proof-of-concept for fMRI-based prediction of pediatric headache using a foundation model without relying on functional connectivity features and highlight the potential of this approach for subtype identification. Further development of such tools may help clinicians improve diagnosis based on brain activity and tailor treatment strategies to individual patients.
