papers.title: Medial temporal lobe tau-neurodegeneration mismatch from structural imaging and plasma biomarkers.
papers.text: Medial temporal lobe tau-neurodegeneration mismatch from structural imaging and plasma biomarkers.. Although tau pathology is closely associated with neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease, our prior work using multi-modality imaging revealed that mismatch between tau (T) and neurodegeneration (N) might reflect contributions from non-Alzheimer's disease processes. The medial temporal lobe (MTL), an early site of Alzheimer's disease pathology, is also a common target of co-pathologies, such as limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathological change (LATE-NC), often following an anterior-to-posterior atrophy gradient. Given the susceptibility of MTL to co-pathologies, here we explored T-N mismatch specifically within MTL using plasma ptau217 and MTL morphometry for identifying vulnerabilities and resilience in cognitively impaired or unimpaired patients with Alzheimer's disease. We parcellated the MTL into 100 spatially contiguous segments and calculated their T-N mismatch using plasma ptau217 as a measure for T and thickness as a marker of N. Based on these mismatch profiles, we clustered 447 amyloid-positive individuals from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort into data-driven T-N phenotypes. We characterized the T-N phenotypes by examining their cross-sectional and longitudinal atrophy both within the MTL and across the whole brain, in addition to cognitive trajectories. This framework was replicated in an independent cohort and, finally, translated to a real-world clinical sample of 50 patients undergoing anti-amyloid therapy. Clustering identified three T-N phenotypes with different MTL T-N mismatch profiles, atrophy patterns and cognitive outcomes, despite comparable Alzheimer's disease severity. The 'canonical' group, characterized by low T-N residuals (N ∼ T), showed Alzheimer's disease-like neurodegeneration patterns. The 'vulnerable' group, characterized by disproportionately greater neurodegeneration than tau (N > T), showed atrophy primarily in the anterior MTL that extended into temporal-limbic regions, in both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses. This group also exhibited neurodegeneration that preceded estimated tau onset and experienced faster cognitive decline across multiple domains, aligning with the typical characteristics of mixed LATE-NC with Alzheimer's disease. In contrast, the 'resilient' group (N < T) showed minimal atrophy and preserved cognitive function. These phenotypes were reproducible in an independent research cohort. Importantly, in a feasibility study applying the model developed from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative to a clinical cohort of patients receiving lecanemab, we identified vulnerable individuals with LATE-like atrophy patterns. This highlights its potential utility for identifying individuals with co-pathology in clinical settings. Our findings demonstrate that T-N mismatch within MTL using MRI and plasma biomarkers can reveal Alzheimer's disease groups with varying vulnerability/resilience, with the vulnerable group displaying structural and cognitive outcomes suggestive of LATE-NC. This approach offers a cost-effective strategy for clinical trial stratification and precision medicine for Alzheimer's disease therapeutics.

papers.title: Agatston-2.0: A next-generation AI-based coronary calcium quantification approach to improve risk stratification among individuals with zero Agatston scores - Part I: An AI-CVD Study within the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis and Framingham Heart Study.
papers.text:
Agatston-2.0: A next-generation AI-based coronary calcium quantification approach to improve risk stratification among individuals with zero Agatston scores - Part I: An AI-CVD Study within the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis and Framingham Heart Study..

Background

A coronary artery calcium (CAC) score of zero using the conventional Agatston scoring method (Agatston-1.0) is associated with very low cardiovascular risk (the "Power of Zero"); however, a small proportion of individuals with CAC=0 still develop coronary heart disease (CHD). Agatston-1.0 relies on thick slices (2.5-3 mm) and a fixed attenuation threshold (≥130 HU), which may miss early, small, low-density, or partially calcified coronary plaques. Agatston-2.0 is an artificial intelligence (AI) framework for automated coronary segmentation and continuous voxel-wise calcium quantification without fixed thresholds, applicable to CT scans with slice thickness ≥0.2 mm and generating an AI-derived CAC score (AI-CAC).

Objectives

To evaluate the prognostic value of Agatston-2.0 for risk stratification among individuals with a baseline CAC=0.

Methods

We pooled 3,965 participants with CAC=0 from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA, n=2,816) and the Framingham Heart Study (FHS, n=1,149). Associations with incident CHD were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models with up to 20 years of follow-up.

Results

An AI-CAC score>0 was detected in 862 participants (21.7%) in population with CAC=0. Participants with AI-CAC>0 had higher 20-year CHD incidence than those with AI-CAC=0 (7.7% vs. 3.8%, p<0.0001). After adjustment for traditional risk factors, AI-CAC>0 remained independently associated with incident CHD (HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.18-2.47). AI-CAC also predicted progression to positive CAC score (adjusted HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.70-2.24).

Conclusions

The Agatston-2.0 framework identifies clinically meaningful coronary calcification in individuals classified as CAC=0. If validated in additional cohorts, Agatston-2.0 could become the new standard for coronary calcium scoring.

papers.title: A latent ODE approach to full-cycle biventricular cardiac motion modeling from cine MRI
papers.text: A latent ODE approach to full-cycle biventricular cardiac motion modeling from cine MRI. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) captures rich spatiotemporal information about ventricular structure and motion, but conventional risk models use only a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases. We present a latent dynamical model that encodes bi-ventricular anatomy and full-cycle cine motion as a continuous latent trajectory, using heart-rate-aware neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics and a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct anatomically consistent 3D+t ventricular motion. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model tests whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure. We studied 72,386 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease, including 367 incident heart failure events. In a held-out evaluation subset, adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, compared with 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. Compared with non-graph and non-ODE approaches, the proposed model gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and downstream prognostic performance. These results suggest that continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, while external validation in more representative patient cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction use.

papers.title: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan
papers.text: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common MRI findings in older adults. They are widely regarded as markers of brain aging and cerebral small-vessel disease, and associated with risk for cognitive decline, Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD), and stroke. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are typically interpreted by total lesion burden, but lesions with similar volumes can occupy different anatomical locations, potentially reflecting distinct pathological processes. Here we present voxelwise topographic reference modelling (vTRM), a framework for characterizing individual WMH masks against age- and sex-stratified frequency maps derived from cognitively unimpaired individuals. Using 42,469 FLAIR-derived lesion masks from twelve adult cohorts, we mapped population-level WMH spatial vulnerability, characterized age-related changes in its distribution across periventricular, lobar and arterial-territory compartments, and constructed paired percentile charts for lesion burden and spatial typicality. A quadrant-based classification defined by these two percentile dimensions revealed graded relationships with ADRD pathophysiology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, while identifying WMH patterns differentially associated with ageing-related, vascular and neurodegenerative processes among individuals with similar lesion volumes. These reference charts establish a benchmark for normative WMH ageing, enabling quantification of individual deviations from typical age-, sex- and burden-related patterns and identification of WMH phenotypes associated with vascular, neurodegenerative or mixed etiologies. The framework, together with a deployable 3D U-Net model trained on these data for automated WMH segmentation, is available through the Brain Lesion Analytics platform (  https://brainlesionanalytics.org/ ).

papers.title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
papers.text: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes. Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.

papers.title: AI-derived cardiothoracic structures and coronary artery calcification volumes on non-contrast CT as predictors of mortality in pulmonary hypertension.
papers.text: AI-derived cardiothoracic structures and coronary artery calcification volumes on non-contrast CT as predictors of mortality in pulmonary hypertension.. To assess the prognostic value of AI-derived cardiothoracic structures and coronary artery calcification volumetric measurements in pulmonary hypertension (PH) using non-gated, non-contrast CT. Patients with suspected PH who underwent non-gated, non-contrast chest CT and right heart catheterisation within one month were retrospectively identified from the Assessing the Spectrum of PH Identified at a Referral Centre (ASPIRE) registry. Two validated deep learning models were used to segment and measure the volumes of cardiothoracic structures and coronary artery calcifications. The prognostic value of AI-derived cardiothoracic structures and coronary artery calcification volumetric measurements was assessed using univariable and multivariable Cox regression adjusted for demographics and PH subgroups and REVEAL scores. Six hundred twenty patients were included (mean age 64 ± 13 years; 62% female; 388 patients died during follow-up), comprising 202 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, 84 with PH-LHD, 112 with PH associated with lung disease, 65 with chronic thromboembolic PH, 9 with unclear PH, and 148 patients without PH. Calcifications were present in the right coronary artery (RCA), mainstem and left anterior descending artery (LAD), and left circumflex artery (LCX) in 45%, 67%, and 35% of patients, respectively. In multivariable Cox regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, and PH subgroup, right atrial (RA) volume was independently associated with mortality (HR 1.024, 95% CI: 1.009-1.039, p = 0.001), as were coronary artery calcifications in the RCA (HR 1.378, 95% CI: 1.113-1.705, p = 0.003), mainstem and LAD (HR 1.868, 95% CI: 1.441-2.421, p < 0.001), and LCX (HR 1.342, 95% CI: 1.084-1.660, p = 0.007). After further adjustment for the REVEAL risk score, these associations remained significant (RA volume HR 1.026, RCA calcification HR 1.604, mainstem and LAD calcification HR 2.339, LCX calcification HR 1.576; all p < 0.001). AI-derived RA volume and coronary artery calcifications are independently associated with increased mortality in PH patients. QuestionThe prognostic significance of AI-derived cardiothoracic volumes and coronary artery calcification measured on routine non-gated, non-contrast chest CT in patients with PH remains uncertain.FindingsAI-derived RA volume and coronary artery calcification volumes independently predicted mortality in PH patients, even after adjustment for demographics, PH subgroups, and REVEAL score.Relevance statementAutomated CT-based AI measurements can provide additional prognostic biomarkers to improve risk stratification in PH beyond established clinical scores.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer’s Disease
papers.text:
Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer’s Disease.

Background

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations.

Methods

We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5×5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE ε4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction.

Results

Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 ± 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 ± 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 ± 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume.

Conclusion

These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Quantifying "Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus"-like Brain Morphometry patterns in an Alzheimer's Disease Cohort.
papers.text:
Quantifying "Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus"-like Brain Morphometry patterns in an Alzheimer's Disease Cohort..

Background and purpose

Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is largely underdiagnosed. It is a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive decline, and cognitive improvement may occur even with comorbid Alzheimer's disease. However, iNPH-related imaging features can overlap with age-related and neurodegenerative atrophy, making differentiation difficult. Automated morphometric profiling of NPH-like patterns in biomarker-defined Alzheimer's disease cohorts has not been systematically explored. This pilot study aimed to quantify iNPH-like brain morphometry in an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort using deep-learning-based morphometry and automated callosal angle measurement.

Materials and methods

We included N=30 amyloid-negative reference iNPH patients and N=1003 ADNI participants with structural T1-weighted MRI and CSF biomarkers. Age- and sex-adjusted volumetric z-scores were obtained using a deep-learning-based morphometry algorithm. We derived an iNPH morphometric profile using principal component analysis and Gaussian modeling of the reference iNPH cohort and applied it to the ADNI participants to compute individual iNPH similarity scores. We also automated callosal angle measurement for further clinical representation. We compared scores across cognitive stages and biological Alzheimer's disease groups and evaluated against expert Radscale review.

Results

iNPH-like morphometry increased with cognitive impairment, with mean differences of 0.03 between cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment (p=0.06), 0.06 between mild cognitive impairment and dementia (p<0.001), and 0.09 between cognitively normal and dementia groups (p<0.001). Among cognitively impaired participants, scores were higher in biologically-defined Alzheimer's disease patients than biologically-defined non-Alzheimer's disease patients (mean difference=0.08, p<0.001). The iNPH similarity score correlated most strongly with ventricular enlargement features. Automated callosal angle measurements showed high agreement with expert ratings (Gwet's AC1 = 0.939) and angles below 90° occurred in 1.5% of ADNI participants.

Conclusions

Automated normative morphometric profiling and callosal angle quantification identified heterogeneous iNPH-like structural patterns in the ADNI cohort. These tools provide a scalable approach for characterizing iNPH-like imaging features in dementia cohorts where identifying a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive impairment remains relevant. Further clinical validation remains necessary.

papers.title: Systolic pressure gradient across myocardial bridge mediates the effect of bridge depth on clinical symptoms.
papers.text: Systolic pressure gradient across myocardial bridge mediates the effect of bridge depth on clinical symptoms.. The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis. Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897). MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms. Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.

papers.title: INSIGHT: Spatially resolved survival modelling from routine histology crosslinked with molecular profiling reveals prognostic epithelial-immune axes in stage II/III colorectal cancer
papers.text: INSIGHT: Spatially resolved survival modelling from routine histology crosslinked with molecular profiling reveals prognostic epithelial-immune axes in stage II/III colorectal cancer. Routine histology contains rich prognostic information in stage II/III colorectal cancer, much of which is embedded in complex spatial tissue organisation. We present INSIGHT, a graph neural network that predicts survival directly from routine histology images. Trained and cross-validated on TCGA (n=342) and SURGEN (n=336), INSIGHT produces patient-level spatially resolved risk scores. Large independent validation showed superior prognostic performance compared with pTNM staging (C-index 0.68-0.69 vs 0.44-0.58). INSIGHT spatial risk maps recapitulated canonical prognostic histopathology and identified nuclear solidity and circularity as quantitative risk correlates. Integrating spatial risk with data-driven spatial transcriptomic signatures, spatial proteomics, bulk RNA-seq, and single-cell references revealed an epithelium-immune risk manifold capturing epithelial dedifferentiation and fetal programs, myeloid-driven stromal states including $\mathrm{SPP1}^{+}$ macrophages and $\mathrm{LAMP3}^{+}$ dendritic cells, and adaptive immune dysfunction. This analysis exposed patient-specific epithelial heterogeneity, stratification within MSI-High tumours, and high-risk routes of CDX2/HNF4A loss and CEACAM5/6-associated proliferative programs, highlighting coordinated therapeutic vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Imaging-anchored multiomics in cardiovascular disease: integrating cardiac imaging, bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics
papers.text: Imaging-anchored multiomics in cardiovascular disease: integrating cardiac imaging, bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics. Cardiovascular disease arises from interactions between inherited risk, molecular programmes, and tissue-scale remodelling that are observed clinically through imaging. Cardiac MRI (CMR), computed tomography (CT), and echocardiography are integral to routine cardiovascular care, while bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics are providing increasingly detailed molecular characterization of cardiac tissue. Yet, these imaging and molecular data are still analysed in largely separate pipelines. This review examines joint representations that link cardiac imaging phenotypes to transcriptomic and spatially resolved molecular states. An imaging-anchored perspective is adopted in which echocardiography, CMR, and CT define a spatial phenotype of the heart, and bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics provide cell-type- and location-specific molecular context. We define the representation requirements of each modality, compare multimodal fusion strategies, and synthesize integrative pipelines for radiogenomics, spatial alignment, and image-based gene-expression prediction, together with their validation requirements, limitations, and failure modes. Spatial multiomic maps of human myocardium and atherosclerotic plaque, together with single-cell, spatial, and multimodal medical foundation models, are advancing imaging-anchored multiomics; however, cost, scalability, and tissue availability remain substantial barriers to large-scale cardiovascular translation.

papers.title: ProtoPathway: Biologically Structured Prototype-Pathway Fusion for Multimodal Cancer Survival Prediction
papers.text: ProtoPathway: Biologically Structured Prototype-Pathway Fusion for Multimodal Cancer Survival Prediction. We introduce ProtoPathway, an interpretable-by-design multimodal framework for cancer survival prediction that unifies whole slide imaging and transcriptomics through encoders producing biologically grounded representations on both sides of the fusion. On the histopathology side, $K$ learnable morphological prototypes, trained end-to-end with the survival objective, serve as the slide representation itself: patches flow into prototype tokens via soft assignment, compressing variable-length patch sets into fixed task-adaptive tokens. On the genomic side, a bipartite graph neural network encodes gene expression within the Reactome pathway hierarchy, producing pathway embeddings that reflect both constituent genes and their broader biological context through bidirectional message passing over a shared gene--pathway graph. Cross-modal attention then operates over a compact prototype $\times$ pathway matrix in which prototypes query pathways, modeling the biological direction in which molecular programs give rise to tissue morphology. Because both axes carry stable task-learned identity, the attention matrix is itself an interpretability output, yielding native inference-time attribution across the full biological hierarchy, from genes through pathways and prototypes to spatial tissue maps. We evaluate on five TCGA cancer cohorts, demonstrating competitive or superior survival prediction with substantially improved biological interpretability and reduced computational cost, with interpretability claims validated through fold-stratified rank-based population-level analysis. Our source code, model weights, and Reactome pathways, together with a unified codebase reimplementing all multimodal survival baselines under identical preprocessing and evaluation, are available at: https://github.com/AmayaGS/ProtoPathway.

papers.title: BioFact-MoE: Biologically Factorized Mixture of Experts for Vision-Language Prognostic Modeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
papers.text: BioFact-MoE: Biologically Factorized Mixture of Experts for Vision-Language Prognostic Modeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is biologically heterogeneous, shaped by the interplay between hepatic functional reserve and tumor-related oncologic factors; thus, similar survival outcomes may reflect fundamentally different underlying biological processes. Prognostic modeling in HCC is informed by rich multimodal information from multiparametric MRI and radiology reports from routine clinical practice. Existing prognostic vision-language models (VLMs) learn a single entangled latent representation that blends hepatic and tumor-related factors, limiting both accuracy and biological interpretability. We present BioFact-MoE, a biologically factorized Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework that explicitly decomposes liver and tumor factors via biologically supervised experts within a residual MoE survival architecture. On a HCC cohort of N=588 patients (pretrained on 4,582 3D MRI image-report pairs), BioFact-MoE consistently improves survival prediction over all baselines across time horizons, achieving 12-, 18-, and 24-month AUCs of 75.33%, 75.85%, and 73.96%. Beyond scalar risk prediction, gated expert weights enable phenotype-aware risk stratification. Pathway-informed gating uncovers clinically meaningful treatment-associated survival heterogeneity. In held-out validation, hepatic and tumor embeddings show selective associations with liver function and tumor burden markers, respectively (p<0.05), without supervision. The code is available at https://github.com/jy-639/BioFact-MoE.

papers.title: GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash: Efficient Pathology Foundation Models for Whole-Slide and Tumor Microenvironment Analysis
papers.text:
GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash: Efficient Pathology Foundation Models for Whole-Slide and Tumor Microenvironment Analysis. Foundation models have emerged as a driving force in computational pathology, with the potential to transform cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection by learning transferable representations from large-scale histopathology data. A growing landscape of pathology foundation models now spans diverse data sources, architectures, and downstream applications. However, most pretrained models operate only at the image-tile level, use restrictive licenses, and remain computationally expensive, limiting large-scale slide-level clinical and research use.
  Here, we introduce GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash, efficient models for whole-slide pathology AI and spatial proteomics prediction. GigaPath-Flash combines a 22M-parameter ViT-S tile encoder with a 21M-parameter LongNet slide encoder, both pretrained on large-scale real-world histopathology data. Its compact tile encoder is distilled from the billion-parameter GigaPath (ViT-g) teacher and shared by both models. GigaPath-Flash retains 97% of GigaPath's average slide-level performance with 50x less compute. GigaTIME-Flash extends this backbone to predict the tumor immune microenvironment directly from routine H&E images. It surpasses the original CNN-based GigaTIME in prediction quality while running 6x faster and using 8x less GPU memory.
  Together with GigaPath and GigaTIME, these models form an open-weight, Apache-2.0-licensed family pretrained on large-scale real-world clinical data. By releasing all models and weights, we provide accessible building blocks for computational pathology, immuno-oncology, and precision health.

papers.title: Giant intracranial neurocysticercosis mimicking brain tumors: Two illustrative cases with a practical neurosurgical decision-making algorithm.
papers.text:
Giant intracranial neurocysticercosis mimicking brain tumors: Two illustrative cases with a practical neurosurgical decision-making algorithm..

Background

Giant parenchymal neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a rare Taenia solium infection that can mimic neoplasms or cystic lesions. Its appearance, mass effect, and risk of neurological deterioration may complicate diagnosis and management, especially when surgery is considered.

Case description

We present two cases of giant parenchymal NCC initially diagnosed as intracranial neoplasms because of radiological findings and mass effect. Both patients underwent surgery for neurological deterioration and diagnostic uncertainty. In the first case, intraoperative findings suggested NCC, later supported by response to antiparasitic therapy. In the second, frozen section and histopathology confirmed NCC, allowing modification of the oncological procedure and avoidance of extensive resection. Both patients received antiparasitic treatment and had favorable clinical outcomes. Literature review showed that surgery in giant intracranial NCC has been driven by mass effect, neurological deterioration, or diagnostic uncertainty.

Conclusion

Giant parenchymal NCC should be included in the differential diagnosis of large cystic intracranial lesions, especially in patients exposed to endemic regions. When findings are inconclusive and deterioration or mass effect is present, surgery may confirm diagnosis and guide further treatment. Intraoperative pathology can avoid unnecessary resection.

papers.title: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
papers.text: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models. Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where each cell sits in the tissue. The inverse, what a given transcriptomic state looks like, is less explored but equally useful: it lets researchers visualize the morphological consequence of a molecular state and interpret a spatial assay's molecular calls against real tissue structure. GeneFlow, the current state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch, incurring a high cost on every new target dataset it is applied to. We instead propose GESTALT, which reformulates gene expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it as an image. Because this visual knowledge is reused rather than relearned, GESTALT trains in a fraction of the time. In both multi-cell and single-cell settings, our method outperforms the SoTA on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets. Beyond improved image quality, GESTALT natively synthesizes at 1024 x 1024, and is evaluated in three generalization settings: zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources. Coupled with a statistical model of spatial expression, GESTALT also provides, to our knowledge, the first paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with explicit control over cell type, density, and composition. Code is available at https://github.com/trongnhandev1011/Gestalt.

papers.title: Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution
papers.text:
Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution. Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors with a high migration-to-proliferation ratio ( D / k ) are associated with treatment resistance, motivating the estimation of D/k from routine pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and the investigation of mechanisms underlying its heterogeneity across patients. Unlike previous approaches based on nested spherical approximations of enhancing and non-enhancing tumor volumes, we incorporate the spatial arrangement of the enhancing and non-enhancing tumor regions by deriving a 1D tumor density distribution from their segmentations and fitting a 1D reaction-diffusion model to estimate D / k . We achieved an error of under 5% when comparing our method to synthetic density distributions and found excellent correlation with synthetic tumor segmentations (Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.996). We then evaluated associations between patient-specific D / k values and their clinical, transcriptomic, and radiomic features. When applied to 102 pre-treatment MRI scans from the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2017 dataset, elevated D/k significantly correlated with reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.01), older age ( p = 0.04), and a trend toward lower Karnofsky Performance Status ( p = 0.059). In a subset of 91 patients with available microarray data, mesenchymal-like phenotypes consistently exhibited elevated D/k across three established molecular subtype classifications ( p = 0.013, p = 0.055, and p = 0.127). Elastic Net regularization followed by overrepresentation analysis revealed an enrichment of glycosylation-related pathways among genes associated with D/k variability ( p = 0.0123 and p = 0.0368). Furthermore, Multi-Omic Factor Analysis identified a radiomic factor correlated with D / k (r = 0.57, p = 4×10 - 9 ), with the highest-weighted features corresponding to smoothness of the non-enhancing tumor region on T2 and FLAIR.

Author Summary

Glioblastoma tumors vary considerably in their growth patterns, with some forming relatively compact masses while others spread more diffusely into surrounding brain tissue. These patterns can be observed in a single pre-treatment MRI scan, where enhancing and non-enhancing regions approximate tumor cell density. Our method measures average tumor density in concentric spherical shells centered on the tumor core. It then fits a radially symmetric model of tumor growth to this distribution to estimate the ratio of tumor cell migration to proliferation (D/k). We validated our method using simulated tumors with known migration and proliferation characteristics. We then applied our method to the publicly available BraTS 2017 dataset. We also used matched patient gene expression data to investigate molecular differences associated with variation in D/k. We found that tumors with higher D/k were associated with poorer overall survival and a greater tendency toward the mesenchymal molecular subtype. We also identified an association between variation in D/k and genes involved in glycosylation-related pathways. Together, these findings connect tumor growth patterns visible on MRI with patient outcomes and molecular characteristics.

papers.title: <sup>18</sup>F-FGln PET/CT Imaging of Glutamine Uptake Has Potential for Predicting Immunotherapy Response in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
papers.text: <sup>18</sup>F-FGln PET/CT Imaging of Glutamine Uptake Has Potential for Predicting Immunotherapy Response in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.. We investigated whether glutamine (Gln) uptake, imaged by <sup>18</sup>F-(2S,4R)-4-fluoroglutamine (<sup>18</sup>F-FGln) PET/CT, could predict and modulate immunotherapy response in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Analysis of the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (LIHC) dataset revealed that SLC1A5 expression-which encodes a primary Gln uptake channel in HCC cells-was significantly associated with poor prognosis, higher tumor grade, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In murine HCC models, tumors with high <sup>18</sup>F-FGln uptake exhibited elevated Slc1a5 expression and poor response to anti-PD-1 therapy, whereas low-uptake tumors were more sensitive to immunotherapy. Genetic knockdown of Slc1a5 reduced <sup>18</sup>F-FGln uptake, enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy, increased cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, and decreased regulatory T cell abundance. Transcriptomic and single-cell analyses revealed activation of antitumor immune pathways and reprogramming toward an immune-inflamed phenotype after Slc1a5 suppression. V-9302 decreased tumor Gln uptake, as measured by <sup>18</sup>F-FGln PET/CT, and sensitized HCC to PD-1 blockade. In patient-derived organoid-T cell co-culture systems, low-SLC1A5 organoids were susceptible to PD-1 blockade, whereas high-SLC1A5 organoids were resistant, consistent with <sup>18</sup>F-FGln PET/CT findings. These results identify Gln uptake as a checkpoint of immune evasion in HCC and support that <sup>18</sup>F-FGln PET/CT has the potential to predict and monitor immunotherapy response.

papers.title: Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Theranostics and Therapeutic Decision-Making of Lung Cancer.
papers.text: Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Theranostics and Therapeutic Decision-Making of Lung Cancer.. Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) is central to lung cancer staging and can alter treatment intent by detecting occult nodal and distant disease. FDG PET/CT contributes to treatment planning, biopsy targeting, radiotherapy delineation and assessment of metabolic response. Quantitative PET parameters provide complementary information on tumor burden, biological aggressiveness, and prognosis. Programmed death-ligand 1, fibroblast activation protein, and somatostatin receptor PET extend molecular imaging toward noninvasive assessment of tumor phenotype and potential theranostic targets. Artificial intelligence and radiomics may characterize tumor heterogeneity and predict molecular phenotype and treatment response but require further standardization and validation.

papers.title: MONKEY Challenge: Machine-learning for Optimal detection of iNflammatory cells in KidnEY transplant biopsies.
papers.text:
MONKEY Challenge: Machine-learning for Optimal detection of iNflammatory cells in KidnEY transplant biopsies..

Purpose

Accurate quantification of inflammatory cells in Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-stained kidney transplant biopsies is essential for Banff classification but remains subjective and labor-intensive. To address this, the MONKEY challenge benchmarked deep learning (DL) methods for automated detection of mononuclear leukocytes and their subtypes.

Materials and methods

A multicenter dataset of 118 biopsies with co-registered PAS and immunohistochemically restained slides, comprising over 131,000 annotated cells, was used. The algorithms were evaluated on hold-out validation and test set using Free-response Receiver Operating Characteristic (FROC) analysis, alongside precision, recall, and F1-scores.

Results

Across diverse architectures, performance converged, with the top models achieving F1-scores up to 0.75 for overall detection. Lymphocyte detection performed well (F1 up to 0.78), whereas monocyte detection remained more challenging (F1 up to 0.47). To explore the potential clinical applicability of automated inflammatory cell detection, the winning model was integrated with renal tissue segmentation models, enabling compartment-specific evaluation and quantitative assessment of Banff-related lesions. In an independent multicenter cohort of 180 kidney transplant biopsies, DL-derived quantitative measurements demonstrated strong correlations with consensus pathologist scoring for several inflammation-related Banff lesions, particularly total inflammation and interstitial inflammation.

Conclusions

This study establishes the first multicenter, PAS-based, IHC-validated benchmark for inflammatory cell detection and provides a clinically grounded resource to support the development of robust, generalizable AI systems for transplant pathology. Beyond benchmark performance, our extended tissue-specific analyses demonstrate that inflammatory cell detection on routine PAS slides can be anatomically contextualized and translated into quantitative measurements that align with conventional Banff lesion assessment, providing a foundation for future AI-assisted evaluation of kidney transplant biopsies.

papers.title: Medical AI Encodes a "Feeling of Error": Verifying Cancer Segmentation via Internal Concepts
papers.text: Medical AI Encodes a "Feeling of Error": Verifying Cancer Segmentation via Internal Concepts. Cancer segmentation models can fail silently, generating plausible but incorrect masks that risk missed findings or unnecessary biopsies. A critical question arises: Do AI models "know" when they are wrong, and if so, can we use the signal to predict their own failures? Humans do have a "Feeling of Error" (FOE): a spontaneous sense of unease that flags a potential error during thinking. We investigate whether cancer segmentation models exhibit an analogous internal signal. Unlike output-level cues (e.g., prediction confidence or uncertainty), which offer no insight into why a failure occurs and suffer from a sensitivity-quality tradeoff where high detection sensitivity could degrade overall segmentation quality. We instead propose to capture the model's FOE from its inner workings. Using mechanistic interpretability tools, specifically Sparse Autoencoders, we decompose internal neural activations into a dictionary of human-interpretable concepts and show that failure cases exhibit a distinct latent signature: fewer active concepts with lower activation magnitudes compared to successful segmentation. By training a classifier on these concept activations, we achieve accurate failure detection along with explanations for the model's mistakes. Experiments on prostate, pancreatic, and brain cancer segmentation demonstrate that our approach outperforms output-based methods in failure detection while preserving segmentation quality.

papers.title: MUSegNet: Automated detection of clinically significant prostate cancer on micro-ultrasound.
papers.text:
MUSegNet: Automated detection of clinically significant prostate cancer on micro-ultrasound..

Background

Micro-ultrasound (microUS) is a non-inferior alternative to multi-parametric MRI for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) diagnosis, yet cancer's subtle features result in missed cancers and large inter-reader variability. We seek to automate the detection of csPCa on microUS by developing the microUS Prostate Cancer Detection Network (MUSegNet).

Methods

Implemented using the well-established segmentation framework, nnUnet, MUSegNet automatically outlines the prostate, transitional zone, and csPCa. Our study explored strategies to train such segmentation models given reduced data, which is common with new imaging modalities such as microUS and/or when labeling data is tedious. MUSegNet was trained using three datasets: (1) 53 microUS exams manually labeled using MRI and pathology references (53 patients), (2) 565 unlabeled microUS exams (106 patients), and (3) 2749 conventional b-mode ultrasound exams (2281 patients). We evaluated MUSegNet in 73 independent patients from two institutions, against manual labels and in direct comparison with six expert readers.

Results

MUSegNet was significantly better at detecting csPCa than the baseline models trained using manual labels (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - AUROC; 0.85 vs. 0.73, Delong p-value < 0.01, sensitivity: 0.74 vs. 0.27, dice similarity coefficient: 0.29 vs. 0.09, Wilcoxon p-value < 0.001). MUSegNet was better at detecting posterior vs. anterior lesions (AUROC: 0.94 vs. 0.72, sensitivity: 0.86 vs. 0.49, Dice: 0.31 vs. 0.11) and outperformed the six human readers for all lesions (AUROC: 0.85 vs. 0.78, sensitivity: 0.74 vs. 0.63). While evaluation in a larger cohort is needed, MUSegNet found csPCA in 33% of cases with csPCa and MRI invisible cancers (1 in 3).

Conclusions

MUSegNet reliably detected the extent of clinically significant prostate cancer on micro-ultrasound exams, paving the way for improving cancer detection for biopsy targeting and reducing inter-reader variability. MUSegNet was best at capturing posterior cancers, with some benefit for the challenging anterior cancers.

papers.title: Subtype-specific screen-detected and interval breast cancer rates in population screening: a BreastScreen Queensland cohort study.
papers.text:
Subtype-specific screen-detected and interval breast cancer rates in population screening: a BreastScreen Queensland cohort study..

Objectives

To quantify subtype-specific rates of screen-detected and interval breast cancers based on hormone receptor and HER-2 status in population-based breast cancer screening participants.

Methods

Clinical and administrative data collected by BreastScreen Queensland (a biennial screening program) for consecutive mammography screens between 2017 and 2020 were analysed. Invasive cancer diagnosis and hormone receptors and HER-2 status were determined using BreastScreen Queensland Register and data linkage with the Queensland Cancer Register. Screen-detected and interval cancer rates for each subtype were determined overall and by age group.

Results

Amongst 971,231 screening episodes in 557,110 women, 5635 screen-detected and 1702 interval cancers were diagnosed. Overall, cancer detection rate (CDR) at screening was 58.0 per 10,000 screens and interval cancer rate (ICR) was 17.5 per 10,000 screens. Hormone receptor (ER and/or PR) positive (HER-2 negative) CDR was 47.5 per 10,000, HER-2 positive (ER, PR any) CDR was 6.1 per 10,000, and triple-negative (ER, PR and HER-2 negative) CDR was 3.7 per 10,000 screens. Hormone receptor positive ICR was 12.0 per 10,000, HER-2 positive ICR was 2.5 per 10,000, and triple-negative ICR was 2.3 per 10,000 screens. Hormone receptor positive screen-detected cancers were particularly overrepresented in older age groups and overrepresentation of triple-negative interval cancers was constant across all age groups.

Conclusions

To our knowledge, we report the world's first population-based estimates of both subtype-specific screen-detected and interval cancer rates respectively. These data provide a benchmark for investigating effects of new early detection strategies for breast cancer screening including those related to risk-based interventions.

papers.title: Big Data Analytics Framework for Early Breast Cancer Detection Using Optimized MapReduce and Deep Learning on Large-Scale Mammographic Data.
papers.text: Big Data Analytics Framework for Early Breast Cancer Detection Using Optimized MapReduce and Deep Learning on Large-Scale Mammographic Data.. The paper presents a framework that is aimed at addressing the large-scale data challenge with a particular focus on early prediction of breast cancer based on mammography image data. The abundance of large-scale medical imaging data in healthcare has opened the way to intelligent diagnostic systems through its ability to analyze and process large-scale mammography data. The proposed framework, the metaheuristic optimization based large-scale breast cancer detection (MO-LSBCD) framework provides a complete solution to the extraction of discriminative features that can be used to predict the disease correctly. Early and accurate diagnosis of breast cancer is one of the most critical factors in improving survival rates and reducing treatment costs for patients. The MO-LSBCD framework is divided into three phases: (1) The CBIS-DDSM mammography dataset consists of 10,239 image files with a size of 6 GB, but for classification, the analytical unit is the annotated region of interest (ROI), with 3568 ROI-level abnormality records from 1566 unique patients (normal, malignant, benign, and benign-without-callback); (2) solving the large-scale data problem by implementing an optimized MapReduce model to efficiently distribute and process the large volumes of breast cancer mammography images in parallel; and (3) effective deep learning techniques to classify breast cancer pathology. The experimental findings indicate that the enhanced MapReduce model reduces total processing time and improves F-measure in comparison with the standard MapReduce model. Among different deep learning models tested on the CBIS-DDSM dataset, the classification of EfficientNet-B3 and ResNet-50 was better with an accuracy of 99.64% and 98.91%, respectively, compared with the other models on all evaluation metrics. The results of this paper confirm that MO-LSBCD framework can be used to provide a robust and scalable solution to large-scale breast cancer detection to help clinicians in the early diagnosis of breast cancer and eventually help in the improved patient outcome.
